source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on the N-facing slope of a ridge. A slightly raised circular area (diam. c. 20m) defined by a scarp (H 0.4m) along the N and W arcs and by an earthen bank (Wth 4m; int. H 0.9m; ext. H 1m) along the S and E arcs. There is a shallow external fosse at the base of the scarp along the N and W arcs. Remains of stone facing is evident on the external face of the bank and on the internal face in parts. The interior is partially overgrown and slopes gently down to N. From cartographic evidence (the 1914 OS 6-inch map) the bank along the S and E arcs appears to have been incorporated into a field boundary system. Linear deep drains on E-W and N-S axes, lying to the S and E of the bank respectively, separate it from recently constructed field boundaries.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on top of a ridge. Sections of field boundaries to the NW, E and SE of Drumcolumb church and graveyard (SL027-141001-; SL027-141002-) may be the remains of an ecclesiastical enclosure (diam. c. 350m E-W). They occur as a series of segments, rather than a single continuous field boundary. The field boundaries coincide NW-N with the base of the hill but NE-SE cut across the slope. The boundaries are vertical-sided earthen banks (Wth 2m; H 0.8m) scarped into the slope with accompanying drains (Wth 2m) on the upslope side. From NW-N the field boundary is topped with a hawthorn hedgerow. A segment of fence at the ESE has a noticeably more substantial external face (H 1.8m). The curving segment of the field boundary indicated to the SE of the church on the 1910-11 OS 6-inch map has been levelled but remains visible as a slight scarp. There is a small broken high cross (SL027-141003-) in the centre of the graveyard. A holy well (SL027-141004-) associated with St Columb, recorded near the church in 1836 (OSL, 254), remains unlocated.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

On a flat tract of ground, on the slopes below the S end of the Bricklieve Mountains with an outlook to the SE across Lough Key. source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a NW-facing slope. The ruin of a four-storey structure consisting of a rectangular block (int.: 6m NE-SW; 4.3m NW-SE) with a circular tower (diam. 4.7m) at each corner (see plan in Waterman 1961, fig. 14.6; photograph Ó Muraíle 2002, 236; photo, plans and drawings Harbison 2002, 98-100 and figs 81-4). It is built of limestone rubble in a lime mortar with a gentle base-batter. The structure was substantially repaired by the OPW c. 1940 when nearly every embrasure was rebuilt to some extent and concrete lintels inserted. The walls of the corner towers stand mostly to full height but the NE and SE walls of the main block are missing and the SW and NW walls are largely rebuilt, especially on the inside. The internal floors were all wooden but none have survived. Also gone is the spiral wooden stairs housed in the W tower.
The lowest floor may have been an unlit basement as there is no apparent access door or windows. The only surviving features are three gun loops: one in the main NW wall and one each in the E and S towers facing each other and covering the front face of the main SE wall. The loops are small splayed embrasures with plain rectangular openings in front (H c. 0.15m; Wth c. 0.5m). The entrance doorway on the first floor at the SW end of the NW wall is almost entirely rebuilt but a socket for a drawbar survives. According to Waterman (1961, 271), the door was reinforced by 'a sliding gate working portcullis-wise which could be raised into a recess at second floor level'. This recess (D c. 0.2m) is the exact width of the doorway and directly above it on the inside. However, there is no vertical slot on the side of the doorway to house a sliding gate. The first floor has a large plain fireplace in the centre of the SW wall, and there are window embrasures in each corner tower. In the stairs tower there are three gun loops, two covering the entrance door. According to Waterman (ibid.), 'the towers could at each floor be closed against the main block by a door secured with a draw-bar'; this was judged from the surviving drawbar-sockets as very little of any doorway is left. 
At second-floor level each tower room has a fireplace, a window ope and numerous gun loops. There are also gun loops in the stairwell and two windows. The third floor has a similar arrangement but with far fewer gun loops. Most of the windows at higher levels have stone seats set into their embrasures. On the outermost face of each tower is a small box machicolation just below the rooftop level. Tall plain chimney stacks survive on top of the E and N towers.
Built in 1590 by Sir Richard Bingham to command the 'Red' Earl's Road (SL033-147---) where it goes through the Curlew's pass (O'Dowd 1991, 40), it may be identified with the 'strong new fort in the strait of the Curlews' recorded in his report to the Privy Council in September of that year (CPSI 1588-92, 264). The fort was garrissoned by ten men commanded by Captain John St Barbe. It was partially destroyed by Red Hugh O'Donnell in 1595 and again sacked during the 1641 rebellion. It was again garrisoned by Crown forces in the mid-1650s as part of a system of fortifications protecting the land settlements that followed the restoration of Charles II (O'Dowd 1991, 60, 118, 131, 137). It was out of use by 1680. By 1684 it was described as 'an auncient castle and great fortifications' (Ó Muraíle 2002, 242); recent excavations by M. A. Timoney (1998, 2000b, 2002e) did not find evidence for the fortifications in the field across the stream to the E. A grave-memorial at Aghanagh graveyard (SL040-17102-), which is dated 1659, is dedicated to Winifred Hughes wife of Henry Hughes, governor of Ballinafad Castle (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney); in the same graveyard is the grave of Captain St Barbe.

This is a national monument in State care (No. 342).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, at the base of a slight S-facing slope and on the N bank of a stream. The well (diam. 0.8m; max. D 0.95m at the N side) is cut into the stream bank and the sides and base, which is flat, are of rock and earth. The well water runs in a muddy irregular flow from the S side of the well to the stream. A tree, which stands immediately to W, is adorned with old and new rags which are tied to the branches. Recent use of the well is evidenced by the presence of euro coins of various denominations embedded in the trunk of the tree. Access is via a rough path, paved with stones from the stream bed, that leads to a gate 5m W of the well. An area (c. 0.8m x 0.8m) around the well has been fenced off and has not been disturbed by livestock. In 1942-4 it was recorded that the pilgrimage day was 15th August and that the well was said to hold cures for any diseases, there being no particular prayers (ITA). A rath (SL034-044----) lies c. 60m to NW and Templemore church and graveyard (SL034-048001- and SL034-048002-) are c. 300m to E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In level pasture, 750m N of Lough Arrow. This passage tomb is a National Monument (No. 152) in state ownership. It is a massive round cairn (diam. 62m N-S, 60m E-W; H c. 6m) retained by a kerb of substantial kerbstones. Twenty-three are exposed from S around to NW and seven more are visible from N around to SE. Considerable quarrying has taken place along the perimeter of the site. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 94). A possible rath (SL034-128----) lies c. 90m to NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

On a low rise on a natural promontory on the NW shoreline of Lough Arrow. A raised roughly oval area (24m NW-SE; 43m NE-SW) defined by arcs of two earthen banks with an intervening fosse and by a scarp adjacent to the shoreline. The curved inner bank (Wth 4m; int. H 1.1m; ext. H 2m) is evident NW-N, the intervening fosse (Wth 4m) is evident NW-NE and the outer bank (Wth 3m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 1.4m) is evident NW-NE. A scarp (H 1.3m), faced with large boulders, defines the shoreline NE-SW. There is a possible entrance (Wth c. 10m) at NW between the shore to SW and the end of the bank to NW. The interior is level. A crannog (SL034-199----) in Lough Arrow lies c. 100m to SE. Subsequent to the site inspection, the earthen banks were levelled in May 2000 (pers. comm. C. Fredengren).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In the NW arm of Lough Arrow, c. 150m from the shore and near the outflow into the River Unshin, with a clear view of the heights of Moytirra to E and Carrowkeel to SW. A roughly circular high-cairn crannog (29.9m N-S; 28.2m E-W; H 1.95m above the muddy lake-bed) with a central plateau (10.5m N-S; 14.5m E-W) consisting of small stones (diam. 0.3m) which form a flat but somewhat unstable surface. Slightly off-centre on the E portion of the plateau is a pile (1.6m N-S; 2m E-W; H 0.55m) of loosely arranged stones. The plateau drops down under the water to a berm and the edges of the crannog are quite distinct. Wood-Martin (1886, 246) mentioned observing fractured bones on the surface. An enclosure (SL034-198----) is situated on a promontory, c. 100m to NW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In a demesne, overlooking Lough Arrow to the S. The present early 19th-century Ballindoon House (Bence-Jones 1988, 18) is reputed to be on the site of a 17th-century house (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). That house may have been the small rectangular structure (roughly on the site of the present house) indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map at the SE end of a tree-lined linear avenue (L c. 400m) (SL034-253----). This avenue (Wth 16m) is cambered and flanked on either side by a drain (Wth 2.5m; int. D 0.2m; ext. D 0.5m to the top of the external bank) with a low broad external earthen bank (Wth 2m; ext. H 0.6m). The central portion has a gravel surface but otherwise it is entirely an earthen construction. It is similar to the avenue at Annaghmore (SL026-049----) and is probably 17th/early 18th-century in date. Another house, named 'Kingsborough Ho.', which no longer survives, is indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map, c. 50m to the S of the present Ballindoon House. According to local information, stones from the nearby Ballindoon Castle (SL034-220001-), c. 0.9km to the SE, were taken to build Ballindoon House.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Listed in the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified 'Castle'. In mature deciduous forest, on top of a high rounded central point of Annaghgowla Island in Lough Gara. A rectangular one-storey, gable-ended structure built of stone in lime mortar with brick details. The S gable stands almost to full height and the W wall is also well preserved but most of the N and E walls have fallen. There is a central doorway in the S wall, which was framed in brick. There is a brick string course c. 0.8m above ground level and another on the gable at the height of the side walls. There is a brick framed occulus in S gable. There is the possible remains of a fireplace, flanked by windows, in the N wall. This is probably of 18th century date. The structure is not marked on the 1938 edition of the OS 6-inch map. This, together with the architectural features recorded above, strong suggest that this structure is post-1700 AD in date.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Listed in both the SMR (1989) and the RMP (1995) and classified 'Barrow Possible'. In pasture, on top of a gentle rise at N end of Inishmore Island in Lough Arrow. A roughly kidney-shaped area (22m NW-SE), indenting deeply at NE, enclosed by an earthen bank (Wth 0.68m at top; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.6m) and external fosse (Wth 0.8m; D 0.3m). Drystone facing is evident on the external face of the bank at S and WNW. There is a gap in the bank at NW. The interior slopes gently down to SW and is overgrown with long grass and nettles. There are young beech trees in the interior and along the edge of the bank. This feature is likely to be an 18th/19th-century landscape feature. This is probably post-1700 AD in date.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the W shoreline of Inishmore Island in Lough Arrow. A grass-covered flat-topped mound (diam. at top 4m N-S; 5.7m E-W; diam. at base c. 23m; H 4.5m) with steeply sloping sides. The mound is highest on the W side due to the natural slope down to the shoreline. There is a flat-bottomed fosse around the base of the mound except along the W arc where the edge of the mound slopes down to the shoreline. Rock outcrop is evident in the fosse at NE. An external flat-topped bank (Wth 3.6m; int. H 2m to base of fosse; ext. H 1.1m) is evident NW-NNE. Immediately outside the fosse at S is a roughly rectangular platform (12.5m N-S; 15m E-W) or bailey (SL034-232001-) defined by a fosse along the N and S sides, that on the S side being less well defined, and by a steep-sided scarp on the W side; the E side is indistinct. The nature of irregular lines of submerged boulders noted at the shoreline immediately to N of the mound remains unclear. The form of the mound and the attached platform are consistent with a small earthwork castle.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, at a break of slope just below the summit of Mullaghfarna Hill, with good views of undulating lowlands on the shores of Lough Arrow to E but overlooked to NW by the steep slopes of the Bricklieve Mountains. A roughly circular area (31.8m N-S; 34.5m E-W) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 3m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.95m) with a low internal rim NW-SW and by a scarp (H 0.8m) SW-NW. The remains of an outer earth and stone bank (Wth 3m; int. H 1m; ext. H 0.2m) are evident W-S with a waterlogged intervening fosse (Wth 3m), marked by a dense growth of rushes. At NE, a 14m wide section of the outer bank has been levelled. The NW portion of the interior is slightly raised to compensate for the slope, however, the interior retains a slight slope down to NW. Faint outlines of NE-SW cultivation ridges are evident. The rath overlooks a rectangular enclosure (SL040-033001-) and another rath (SL040-034----) c. 450m and c. 300m to NNW respectively. There is an enclosure (SL040-036----) visible on rising ground c. 450m to WNW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, straddling a break of slope on a NE-facing slope, with excellent views over Lough Arrow to E. Indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map by an arc of hachures SW-NE. Remains consist of a subcircular area (c. 25m NE-SW; c. 30m NW-SE) of uneven ground engulfed in long grass, brambles and hawthorn bushes and truncated at SW by a field boundary bordering a road. Low remains of a bank (Wth c. 2m; ext. H c. 0.5m) are evident in an arc W-NE, marked by a denser band of overgrowth. A linear band of field clearance debris engulfed in overgrowth completes the circuit E-S. The NE portion of the interior retains a slight slope even though it has been raised to compensate for the hillslope. Outside the bank N-NE, at a distance of c. 3.5m, is a raised band of dense overgrowth, possibly the remains of an outer bank though it does appear to merge with the inner bank at NW.

source_data.original_text: ‘Bellarush Bridge’ is not included in the SMR (1989) or the RMP (1995). It is located at the intersection of three townlands: Bellarush; Cartronroe and Annagh. Wood-Martin (1892, 200) recorded that ‘The oldest bridges now standing in the County are those at Bellarush, near the north end of Lough Arrow, and Drumcliff. No date can be assigned for the building of either, but from their narrow arches and style of masonry, they must have been long in existence.' It is a road bridge (Wth 7.9m; long axis NE-SW) over the Arrow or Unshin River immediately N of Lough Arrow. The bridge comprises three segmental arches with rough voussoirs. The corbels to support the centering of the arch are visible. The piers are very thick and have cutwaters. There are two narrow lintelled opes on the NE side. There is an arched ope on river bank on SW side with rough voussoirs. The main arches on the upstream side and the voussoirs are better dressed with some concrete repair. The parapet wall has flat-bedded coping.  It is not marked on the Down Survey (1655-6) barony map but is shown quite clearly on a map surveyed in 1777 (Taylor and Skinner 1778, 64). However, Mr. Gary Salter, an accredited conservation engineer has recently been tasked with undertaking minor repairs and maintenance of the bridge on behalf of Sligo County Council and has undertaken a detailed survey of the monument which he has kindly forwarded on to our Department. He believes ‘that the original bridge (circa 15’ wide) has the shape, characteristics, proportions, material shape and workmanship of a structure most likely to have been built in the period between 1200 and 1600AD. The bridge was widened subsequently to approximately twice its original width, but even this work has the character of pre-1840 construction. The ‘New Bridge’ (Markievicz Br.) in Sligo town, dating to 1680 was extant at this time, indicating that Wood-Martin considered the bridge at Bellarush to pre-date it. Mr. Salter’s survey, together with the Wood-Martin reference, strongly suggest that Bellarush bridge is a pre-1700 structure.

source_data.original_text:
On a low ridge close to the W shore of Lough Arrow. The tomb stands in a low oval mound (25.5m SSE-NNW; 9m ENE-WSW). A court (min. L 5m) to the SSE is represented by four stones, one at the outer and one at the inner ends of both arms. Two jambs mark the entrance to a gallery (L 8m), a segmenting jamb on the N side of which indicates a division into two chambers. One stone remains of the N side of the first chamber and there are two on the S side. A stone outside the inner of these two seems to represent a doubling of the gallery side. Two orthostats at the S are the only remains of the inner chamber. A large slab in the front chamber may be a lintel displaced from above the entrance jambs. There is also a displaced slab at the back of the gallery.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In upland grazing, at the base of a NE-facing limestone escarpment in the foothills of the Bricklieve Mountains and on a low terrace bordered to E by an expanse of heather-covered bog. The NE edge of the cashel straddles the break of slope at the NE edge of the terrace. A circular area (24.6m NW-SE; 26.5m NE-SW) enclosed by a moss-covered stony bank which is most substantial (Wth 4.3m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.9m) E-WSW. There is a break (Wth 1.5m) at NW and another low area or break (Wth c. 2.6m) at ENE, partially obscured by a field boundary wall. The centre of the interior incorporates a low gently domed rise (Wth c. 8m) without clearly defined limits. There is a shallow depression (2.3m x 2m; D 0.25m) on the N side of the central rise. An E-facing limestone scarp (H c. 1m) representing the natural edge of the terrace extends on a NNW-SSE axis through the E half of the interior giving it a split-level profile. A NE-SW field boundary wall crosses the SE edge of the cashel. Traces of a NW-SE field boundary wall, which bisected the interior, are also evident as are possible E-W cultivation ridges. One of a line of cashels (SL040-156---, -15901-, -161---) spaced at intervals along the long axis of the terrace. Another cashel (SL040-158001-) lies c. 130m to E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In a strip of hazel woodland, located on a terrace on the E-facing slope of a NNW−SSE limestone ridge, on the lower E flank of the Bricklieve Mountains, overlooking Lough Arrow. 
This cashel is shown on the 1837 OS 6-inch map, but not on the 1914 edition. It consists of a roughly circular area (c. 21m E−W; c. 19m N−S) defined by remnants of a stone wall. On the W arc, the wall consists of a substantial stone bank (Wth 2-2.5m; H 1.2m) of limestone boulders and large stones, which may incorporate field clearance stones. Elsewhere around the circuit, the wall is reduced to a low jumble (Wth 1.5-2m; H 0.3m) of moss-covered stones. On the E arc, the wall merges in a shallow curve with the natural break of slope of the terrace, where the ridge slope falls away steeply for several meters. Here the wall can be traced as a low, slumped scarp (Wth slope 1.5m; H 0.8-1m), covered with stone tumble.
The interior is split level, with the E third at a lower level. A low, gently slumped N−S stony scarp (Wth slope 1.5-2m; H 0.5-0.6m) marks the division between the two levels. Straddling this internal division is a souterrain (SL040-162001-), located in the SE quadrant of the interior. The visible remains of the souterrain consist of a simple length of passage (L c. 7-8m E−W) faced with drystone walling. No roofing slabs are evident. The E end of the passage projects to E of the N−S dividing scarp, and is banked up to compensate for the lower ground level.
A N−S field wall (Wth 0.6m; H 0.6m) extends across the W half of the cashel interior. The perimeter of the cashel is densely ringed with hazel trees, which grows in and on the moss-covered stones of the enclosing wall; hazel trees and dense pockets of brambles and undergrowth obscure much of the interior and the souterrain. 
A possible cashel (SL040-247----) is located c. 200m to NW on the crest of the ridge, another cashel is located 240m to N, and two cashels (SL040-163001-; SL040-164----) and an enclosure (SL040-163004-) are located c. 300m to S towards the S end of the ridge.

SL040-162----_03: Enclosing wall on E side of cashel, viewed from N

source_data.original_text:
The Red Earl's Road, probably of medieval origin, linked the towns of Ballymote, Co. Sligo and Boyle, Co. Roscommon, by a route around the N and E sides of the Bricklieve Mountains (M. A. Timoney 1998, 155), a distance of c. 21km. It is said to have been built by Richard de Burgh, The Red Earl of Ulster, after the Norman conquest, to link his castle (SL033-092----) at Ballymote with Boyle Abbey (RO006-068005-), Co. Roscommon. The road traverses a number of townlands over a number of 6-inch sheets (OS 33: Bellanascarrow West/Roscrib East/Roscrib West/Ballinvoher; OS 34: Drumcormick/ Bricklieve/Tiraree; OS 40: Cloghoge Lower/Carrowkeel/Mullaghfarna/ Doonaveeragh/Knockroe/Cuilsheeghary More/Mountgaffeny/Ballinafad/Gortalough/ Ballaghboy/Cartron; OS 45: Ballaghboy/Cartron).

Sections of the road are recorded under five records (SL033-147----; SL034-159----; SL040-023----; SL040-197----; SL040-190----) commencing at Ballymote and following the route E and then S to the county boundary with Roscommon. Only sections of the road are indicated on the 1914 and 1941 OS 6-inch maps even though it was, of course, continuous. A possible link road between Bothar an Iarla Ruaid and Bothar an Corran (SL033-145----) goes from Greenan townland, around the S side of the Bricklieve Mountains, to Ballinafad. At its nearest point, Bothar an Corran is c. 0.8km to the SW. 

This section (SL040-190----) is c. 3.2km in total length. The northern 2km stretch is represented on the OS 6-inch maps as following the course of the townland boundaries SE from Ballinafad and crosses the national primary route (N4). The S 1.1km stretch of this road extends over hilly terrain which is largely covered in coniferous forestry. There is no surface evidence of the initial stretch in a field of pasture but it may be partially preserved in a N-S field boundary. Just after the point where it is crossed by the N4 (the main Sligo/Boyle road), the old road is traceable for a stretch of c. 250-300m. It survives as a grassed-over track (Wth 5.5m) bordered by field fences of earth and stone and flanked by mature and semi-mature coniferous forestry. The track is covered in rough upland vegetation and is soft underfoot in parts. The most S section is under forestry and is impassable. According to O'Rorke ([1889], vol. 2, 299-301), this section through the townland of Ballaghboy, is known as the 'Yellow Pass' and due to the steep gradient it was not 'practicable for horses'. In an effort to overcome this Manus O'Donnell, encamping on the Curlew Mountains in 1540, 'set his forces to work in levelling it off' (ibid.). O'Rorke (ibid.) also relates that in 1691 when Lord Granard was bearing down on Sligo, the horses failed to draw the cannon and the soldiers were obliged to get into harness and do the horse's work.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of revision: 1 June 2011

source_data.original_text:
In a demesne, overlooking Lough Arrow to the S. The present early 19th-century Ballindoon House (Bence-Jones 1988, 18) is reputed to be on the site of a 17th-century house (SL034-213----) (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). That house may have been the small rectangular structure (roughly on the site of the present house) indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map at the SE end of a tree-lined linear avenue (L c. 400m). This avenue (Wth 16m) is cambered and flanked on either side by a drain (Wth 2.5m; int. D 0.2m; ext. D 0.5m to the top of the external bank) with a low broad external earthen bank (Wth 2m; ext. H 0.6m). The central portion has a gravel surface but otherwise it is entirely an earthen construction. It is similar to the avenue at Annaghmore (SL026-049----) and is probably 17th/early 18th-century in date. Another house, named 'Kingsborough Ho.', which no longer survives, is indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map, c. 50m to the S of the present Ballindoon House. According to local information, stones from the nearby Ballindoon Castle (SL034-220001-), c. 0.9km to the SE, were taken to build Ballindoon House.

Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC with revisions by Patrick F. O'Donovan and Paul Walsh

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on the narrow top of a NNW−SSE ridge, on the E flank of the Bricklieve Mountains, overlooking Lough Arrow to E−SE. The ridge slopes falls away steeply immediately to E, and somewhat more gradually on the W side, and to N, the spine of the ridge inclines gradually downwards. At E, the ridge slope drops to a lower ridge or broad terrace, where a cashel (SL040-126----) is located c. 150m to NE. Several other cashels are located within a radius of a few hundred meters, with a particular cluster c. 300m to W.
This enclosure is not shown on the 1837 and 1914 OS 6-inch maps. It has been levelled, but its outline can still be traced. It consists of a circular area (19m E−W; 19m N−S) defined by a slight mossy rise (Wth 1-1.4m), which represents the remnants of an enclosing wall/bank. It encompasses most of the available E-W width of the narrow ridge top, and on the E side coincides with the natural break of slope, where the ridge slope drops steeply.
The enclosing element seems most likely to have been a wall; the mossy cropmark would suggest this, and the majority of ringforts/enclosures in this area of the Bricklieves are cashels or stone enclosures. It is almost entirely levelled at SE−SSW, but is more easily traced at SW−NE. It appears to have been truncated at ESE−E by a shallow, subcircular depression (diam. c. 5m), now largely obscured by brambles. 
In the N half of the interior there is an irregular-shaped, grassed-over pit or depression (4m NE−SW; 1m NW−SE; D 0.4m), with a shallower, narrower extension (L 1m) to NW at its SW end. It is bordered at top by a slightly raised rim. Its significance is uncertain, but there is no obvious evidence of stone lining or any structural features to suggest that it is a souterrain.
Slight remnants of a field wall, on an ENE-WSW axis, abut the enclosing wall at SW and NE, and extend downslope beyond the cashel.

Attached image: SL040-248----_01.JPG: viewed from N.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 30 May 2018

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on level ground at the N end of a ridge top plateau, on the E flank of the Bricklieve Mountains. The location provides excellent views, especially to W and N along a valley backed by higher ridges of the Bricklieves. A few meters to N of the hut site, the plateau drops in a series of small rocky ledges to a lower elevation. On the W side of the plateau ground falls away steeply towards the W shore of Lough Arrow.
The hut site is evident as a subcircular, slightly sunken area (6m N−S; 6m E−W) defined by the remnants of a sod-covered bank (Wth 1.5-2m; H 0.2m). There is a poorly defined break (Wth c. 1.5m) at E, which may be an original entrance. The bank is evident as a low, broadly slumped rise, reduced in parts to a barely discernible undulation: it is overlain by, and has been partly levelled and cut by a series of later cultivation ridges and furrows, on a roughly E-W axis. A low, barely discernible undulation lies 4m to S, which may be the S side of second room or annex (c. 5-6m E−W; c. 4m N−S). 
There is a cashel (SL040-112001-) 160m to WSW, and an enclosure (SL040-150----) 140m to SE.

source_data.original_text:
Near the W end of Drumcolumb graveyard (SL027-141002-) and within the N half of a possible ecclesiastical enclosure (SL027-141----). A rectangular church (12m E-W; 7m N-S) reduced to sod-covered foundations (H c. 0.6m) except for a section of upstanding walling (L c. 4m), built of limestone blocks, near the E end of the S wall. Remnants of a splayed window are evident at its E end. At the W end are the sod-covered foundations of a rectangular annexe (7m N-S; 6m E-W), which may have been a residence for the cleric (M. A. Timoney 2002b, 57). Running S from the SE corner are remnants of a wall, reduced to foundation level. A high cross (SL027-141003-) is 4m to E. In 1836 it was suggested that this church was probably the remains of Drumcolumb parish church (OSL, 254-5). According to local information, it was thatched within living memory and was approached by a bridle path from the S (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In the centre of a graveyard (SL027-141002-), 4m E of the ruin of Drumcolumb church (SL027-141001-) and within the N half of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL027-141----). Described by Crawford (1918, 177) as the 'head of a plain cross with solid recessed ring… broken in two places'. A sketch from 1914 shows these two breaks, one above and the other below the ring (SMR (1989) file). The cross (H 0.5m; Wth 0.45m; T 0.1m), which is set upright in a low cairn of stones, is now eroded and weathered and the projecting arm above the ring (at the old break) has broken off. The arms project beyond the ring on one side but not on the other. Harbison (1992b, vol. 1, 74) noted that the four 'depressions' between the arms and the ring which are present on one face are only pecked out on the other face. He also stated that 'the cross-head could be later than 1200' (ibid.).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Incorporated into a farmyard, on an E-facing upland terrace overlooking Lough Arrow to the NE. Two discrete sections of walling survive which appear to be the end-walls of a rectangular building (ext. L 17.5m N-S). Both sections (T 1.1m) are similar in construction; mortared limestone rubble laid in intermittant courses. The N section (L 5.5m; H 2.25m) contains the NW corner of the building, with a short return of the W wall (L 1.25m). Through the N wall is a blocked-up opening (Wth 1m; H 1.55m) which may have been a doorway. This wall forms the end-wall of a small shed. The S section (L 2.2m; H 2.3m) is very fragmentary and has also been used as the wall of a small shed. On the internal wall-face, 0.65m above ground level, is a wall-press (Wth 0.65m; H 0.55m; D 0.5m). Extending E from this section, and apparently a continuation of it, are low fragmentary wall-footings (H c. 0.3m; L c. 4.5m) ending in a jumble of stones at the foot of a cedar tree. This suggests that the original structure was at least 7m in width. 
According to local information, human bones (SL040-186002-) were found on the N side of the structure during construction works. Described in 1836 as 'the remains of old walls called by the people Teach na gCaileachaidh Dúbha [the house of the Black Nuns], which they say was a nunnery' (OSL, 157). Wood-Martin (1882, 66) noted the doorway in the N wall, and also mentioned that the greater portion of the building had fallen down the precipice where its ruins lay strewn (this area is occupied by the farmyard). Listed by Gwynn and Hadcock (1970, 375) as the site of a Patrician monastery. However, surviving remains are unlikely to be earlier than the late medieval period.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, near the top of a gentle SW-facing drumlin slope; in the centre of the E half of a graveyard (SL034-048002-). Only the SE end-wall (H 1.7m; L 8.7m; T 0.75m), built of mortared random rubble with pick-dressed quoins, stands of the church shown as a rectangular building (c. 15m NW-SE) on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. Part of the base of a splayed window embrasure survives in the centre of the wall. This is flanked internally by two small plain wall-presses. A pile of cut and dressed stones along the base of the wall include the head of a window light with a pointed chamfered arch and part of a chamfered door surround. This is the remains of the medieval parish church of Kilmacallan (M. B. Timoney 1999/2000, 40). It is named 'Templemore' on the 1914 OS 6-inch map and is known locally by that name. 'Tobermoneen' holy well (SL034-045----) is c. 300m to the W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In Templemore graveyard (SL034-048002-). A number of architectural fragments were identified in the graveyard in 1994 (pers. comm. Mary B. Timoney). They included a window head, various chamfered jambs (probably from a door and window) and a rectangular block of limestone (0.2m x 0.15m x 0.4m) with one end carved in the form of a human head;the remainder squared-off in section (0.15m x 0.15m; L 0.25m). The facial features are badly eroded but the eyes, nose and mouth are just apparent. A noticeable feature is the projecting chin, the underside of which is decorated with a number of shallow radiating grooves. These fragments undoubtedly derive from the ruined church (SL034-048001-) and carved head may have been a voussoir in an arch.

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a W-facing slope; incorporated into the S wall of the garden of Killadoon House. Remains of a rectangular church (int. 17.3m E-W; 5.35m N-S), covered with scrub overgrowth. The walls (T 0.75m) are of random-rubble limestone and sandstone, bonded with lime mortar. The corners have interlocking limestone quoins and the NW corner has a slight base-batter and a foundation plinth (H 0.3m; Wth 0.2m). The N wall stands to a height of 3.6m but the NE and SW corners have collapsed. The splayed ingoing of a window is evident in the E wall. The S wall forms part of the S boundary of the walled garden. It has the chamfered base of a narrow light (Wth 0.14m) at its E end, and a blocked-up doorway (int. Wth 1.5m) at the W end of which a cut-limestone chamfered jamb and a pointed arch are visible through the overgrowth. The jamb is very weathered and appears to be punch dressed. The W wall has a large breach (Wth 3.1m) at ground level, midway along its length. The interior and parts of the exterior are inaccessible due to collapsed rubble and dense overgrowth. 
This church belonged to the Premonstratensian Canons of Trinity Island, Lough Key, Co. Roscommon and the abbot of that monastery died here in 1504 (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 207). It also probably served as the parish church of Killadoon. A graveyard (SL034-131002-) lies immediately to S. There is a bullaun stone (SL034-131003--) in a farmyard to the N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a W-facing slope, immediately to the S of Killadoon church (SL034-131001-). In 1836 'an old burial place' was recorded in the townland of Killadoon and associated with the church (OSL, 246). No burials or grave-markers are evident. There is, however, a semicircular area (22m E-W; 17m N-S), enclosed E-S by a low earthen bank (Wth 2.9m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.5m) and SW-W by a scarp (H c. 2m), immediately S of the church which could be the remains of the graveyard. The interior of this area slopes down to the W. An elongated mound (long axis NE-SW) is evident in the NE quadrant and a low linear earthen bank (L 25m) extends out to the SW from the SW edge. No graveyard is indicated here on the 1838 OS 6-inch map, while the area immediately to the N of the church is indicated as a formal walled garden.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, at the S end of a ridge overlooking Lough Arrow to the E. An oval area (32m NW-SE; 25m NE-SW) defined by the remains of two earthen banks and an intervening fosse. Elsewhere the interior is defined by a scarp. This scarp appears linear at E. The intervening fosse (Wth 3m) is evident all round. The outer bank (Wth 4.2m; int. H 0.9m; ext. H 0.6m) is evident E-SW. A NE-SW field boundary cuts across the interior. There is a souterrain (SL034-179002---) in the N quadrant adjacent to the bank. Beech trees grow along the perimeter of the rath.

source_data.original_text:
At the lower NW end of a narrow NW-SE ridge, with good views of the Bricklieve Mountains to SW and W and of Lough Arrow to the NE. A slightly raised roughly circular area (27m NW-SE; 29m NE-SW) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 3.8m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 1.15m) with a low internal rim. In a few places along the mid line of the bank where the top is eroded, a core of medium to large stones is visible, set on edge contiguously in a single line. Outside the bank at SSE and SSW are two shallow depressions (Wth 2m), 3m apart, that follow the curve of the bank. The N portion of the interior is raised to compensate for the hillslope. There is a possible souterrain (SL040-039002-) in the NW quadrant. Several animal burrows also occur in this area. A stand of conifers is planted in the interior with a ring of beech and conifers on the perimeter. The ridge itself is planted with mixed woodland, some of which, in the vicinity of the rath, have been felled.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on top of a limestone ridge and within a field system (SL040-121001-). An oval area (14.3m NW-SE; 12.5m NE-SW) enclosed by a ruinous stone wall, evident as a partially sod-covered jumble of stones (Wth 2m; H 0.4m) with traces of internal and external stone facing. The interior slopes down slightly to NW and has an uneven surface. Traces of a slight stony scarp may be the remains of an internal division in the SE quadrant. A rectangular cairn (2.6m NE-SW; 2.2m NW-SE; H 0.7m) of large stones abuts the inner wall face at SE. Abutting the wall face at SW is a slightly sunken subrectangular area (3.5m NE-SW; 2.5m NW-SE; D 0.5m) defined on the NE and SE sides by inward-facing scarps and on the NE side by a slight stony rise. Remnants of a field boundary extend to SSW from the enclosure wall at S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rough upland grazing, straddling the S slope of a rocky elevation in the foothills of the Bricklieve Mountains. On the NE edge of an expanse of boggy ground bordered c. 100m to W by a sheer limestone cliff. An oval area (30m N-S; 27m E-W) enclosed by a ruined stone wall (Wth 3.6m; int. H 0.6m; ext. H 0.3m). The wall survives E-WSW as a broad low moss-covered stony bank; elsewhere the wall is relatively clear of sod revealing a low jumble of limestone rubble with a basal course of external facing in the form of large blocks visible in parts. There is a gap (Wth 2.6m) in the wall at ESE. Remnants of an E-W field wall (H 0.4m) bisect the interior S of centre. It marks a break in slope within the interior between the level slightly elevated area to N, which has an uneven surface strewn with sod-covered stone, and lower ground to S which is grassy and clear of stone. There is a hut site (SL040-15803-), within which is a souterrain (SL040-15802-), in the E half of the interior. Scant remains of two possible hut sites (SL040-15804-), noted during a previous site inspection in 1985 (SMR (1989) file), to S and SW of the souterrain are no longer visible. Appended to the external face of the cashel wall at WNW are two adjoining subrectangular annexes defined by remnants of stone walls. The more southerly annexe (c. 8m N-S; 6.3m E-W) is bordered on the S side by the E-W field boundary wall that bisects the cashel; appended to its N side is the second annexe (c. 13.5m NNW-SSE; 6m ENE-WSW). A linear cluster of cashels (SL040-156---, -157---, -15901-, -161---) is visible to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on a gently sloping upland terrace on the S-facing slope of a ridge in the Bricklieve Mountains. The cashel is overlooked by the ridge summit to NW but there are excellent views across Lough Arrow to E. A roughly circular area (27.5m E-W) enclosed by a ruinous stony wall (Wth 9m; int. H 0.75m; ext. H 0.9m) entirely covered in moss, sod and blackthorn bushes. From SW-W, where the wall straddles rising ground, it has a pronounced inward slump (Wth c. 4m; int. H 0.95m; ext. H 0.3m). From SSE-SSW the outer edge of the wall is incorporated into an E-W field boundary wall, now ruined. The interior slopes gently down to SE and is crossed at the N edge by an E-W field boundary wall. There is a hut site (SL040-16302-) in the centre of the interior. A cashel (SL040-164---) lies c. 10m to S and an enclosure (SL040-16303-) c. 20m to N.

Mentioned in 1836 as ‘Tober Maine’ and associated with St Maine, who is said to have built the nearby monastery (SL040-171001-), and although the saint’s day was not remembered locally it was thought to be in August (OSL, 155-6). There are no visible remains of this holy well. In 1942-44 it was recorded that no pilgrimages had taken place to it within the memory of the oldest living resident and that there were no known cures (ITA). A stream flows SE from the well site to ‘O’Rourke’s Ford (SL040-170002-) c. 80m to the SSE. A saint’s stone (SL040-170003-) is said to have been nearby, adjacent to the stream.

Adjacent to a road and across a stream which flows out from the base of a limestone scarp c. 80m to the NNW at St Maine’s holy well (SL040-170001-). According to tradition, O’Rourke of Breifny was opposed to the building of the nearby monastery (SL040-171001-). St Maine, perceiving that the chief was on his way to stop the work, prayed that he would be unable to pass the ford. His prayer was heard and ever since it is said that if an O’Rourke should cross the ford, he would die within a year. A Saint’s stone (SL040-170003-) is said to have been adjacent to the stream. (Wood-Martin 1882, 205-6)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

A church is said to have been founded here by St Patrick

source_data.original_text:
On the S side of a lane and on the N side of Ballinafad Bay, overlooking Lough Arrow to the E; in the centre of Aghanagh graveyard (SL040-171002-). The ruin of a rectangular church (ext. c. 18m E-W; 9m N-S), whose walls (T c. 1.07m; H c. 3m) are standing, though covered with ivy, except for the E wall which is missing. The walls are of random-rubble limestone, with some larger stones (c. 1m x 0.7m) evident along the external base of the S wall. A window embrasure, near the E end of this wall, has a chamfered light with a pointed arch (H 1.14m; Wth 0.12m). A gap (Wth c. 2m), visible through ivy high up on the W wall, may also be a window ope. Below this the masonry has been rebuilt. A doorway, near the W end of the N wall, has a limestone surround in two plain orders and a rounded arch (Wakeman 1885-6, 48) and is probably an insertion. The interior is covered by dense scrub overgrowth. It contains some 20th-century headstones and low uninscribed grave-markers. A burial vault, near the E end of the S wall, directly under the window, has its opening blocked by a late medieval graveslab (SL040-171005-). A similar graveslab (SL040-171006-) was noted here in 1847 (Wood-Martin 1882, 206, n. 1). A broken font (SL040-171004-), mentioned by Wood-Martin (ibid.) as being inside the door of the church, was not located. A cross-inscribed stone (SL040-171008-) lies to the SE. A church is said to have been founded here by St Patrick (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 372) but the present ruin is the medieval parish church of Aghanagh. Architectural fragments have recently been assembled in a pile in the interior of the church (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney). A rectangular enclosure (SL040-141----) which, according to local information, was used as a children's burial ground (SL040-141001-), is immediately to N on the opposite side of the road.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In the ruin of the late medieval parish church of Aghanagh. An inscribed 17th-century graveslab serves as a blocking slab for a burial vault which abuts the E end of the S wall of the medieval parish church of Aghanagh (SL040-171001-). The graveslab bears the coat of arms of the Hughes family. The inscription is difficult to read but was recorded by Wood-Martin (1882, 206, n. 1) as follows: 'Here lyeth the body of Winefred Hughes wife to Captain Henry Hughes who deceased the 1st (?) day of March Anno Domini 1609. Here lyeth the body of Captain...'. The date on the inscription appears to be '1659' rather than '1609' as recorded by Wood-Martin.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In a wetland area, on the W side of a road. One of a cluster of six sites (SL040-03002-; SL040-03003-; SL040-03102-; SL040-03103-; SL040-23002-) found during monitoring of the realignment of the N4 road from Hollybrook Estate to Castlebaldwin in the Summer of 1998 (Desmond 1998, 10-11). This fulacht fia was discovered in section under the sod and a thin layer of topsoil and peat. It measured 7.7m in length and consisted of a layer of compact stone within blackened soil (D 0.6m) which tapered to N and S. Underneath this material were seen the ends of two wooden planks (Wth 0.3m; T 0.11m) and three wooden pegs. Following recording the site was covered with geo-textile, peat and topsoil and remains undisturbed. (Desmond 2000, 183-4)

source_data.original_text:
In Aghanagh graveyard (SL040-171002-) and to SE of a church (SL040-17101-). Discovered in 1995 during a graveyard clean up (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney). A photograph taken in 1995 by M. B. Timoney shows an upright, but slightly leaning, D-shaped boulder (Wth c. 1m; H c. 1m) on which is carved, in relief, a cross similar in design to the head of a high cross. The cross is a ringed cross with expanded terminals which project beyond the circle. A semicircular boss projects inwards from the inner edge of the ring in each of the four spaces between the arms of the cross. In the centre of the cross is a recessed circle. The cross occupies the entire face of the boulder on which it is carved. (Herity, Kelly and Mattenberger 1997, 118).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In wet pasture, to W of a stream and c. 20m W of a burnt mound (SL040-23802-). This fulacht fia was discovered during the construction of the Curlew bypass and excavated in 1995 (Channing 1998a, 154). It consisted of a spread (c. 12m E-W; c.16m N-S) of burnt stones in a reddish-brown silty clay matrix with a high peat content and occasional flecks of charcoal. The spread was partially truncated by machinery prior to excavation. Excavation revealed a trough (1.8m x 0.95m; D 0.3m), lined with wood, cut into the subsoil. The space between the edges of the trough and the wood lining was filled with a grey daub-like substance while the trough itself was filled with burnt stones.

source_data.original_text:
In wet pasture, on the W bank of a stream and c. 20m E of a fulacht fia (SL040-238001-). This monument was discovered during the construction of the Curlew bypass and excavated in 1995 (Channing 1998a, 154). A spread (10m x 6m) of burnt stone in a reddish-brown silty clay matrix with a high peat content and occasional flecks of charcoal. Excavation revealed a pit and two post-holes in the N half of the spread. The unlined pit (1.4m E-W; 0.7m N-S; D 0.28m) which was roughly oval in plan was cut into the subsoil, filled with burnt material and did not retain water. The post-holes were found c. 1.2m to E of the pit and both were circular in plan (diam. c. 0.1m; D c. 0.11m). The Red Earl's road (SL033-147---), which is of medieval date, follows the townland boundary immediately to E of the stream. (Channing 1996, 1-9)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the W shoreline of Inishmore Island in Lough Arrow. The motte consists of a grass-covered flat-topped mound (diam. at top 4m N-S; 5.7m E-W; diam. at base c. 23m; H 4.5m) with steeply sloping sides. The mound is highest on the W side due to the natural slope down to the shoreline. There is a flat-bottomed fosse around the base of the mound except along the W arc where the edge of the mound slopes down to the shoreline. Rock outcrop is evident in the fosse at NE. An external flat-topped bank (Wth 3.6m; int. H 2m to base of fosse; ext. H 1.1m) is evident NW-NNE. Immediately outside the fosse at S is a roughly rectangular platform (12.5m N-S; 15m E-W) or bailey defined by a fosse along the N and S sides, that on the S side being less well defined, and by a steep-sided scarp on the W side; the E side is indistinct. The nature of irregular lines of submerged boulders noted at the shoreline immediately to N of the mound remains unclear. The form of the mound and the attached platform are consistent with a small earthwork castle.

Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC with revisions by Patrick F. O'Donovan and Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 20 June 2011

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, utilising a steep-sided rocky knoll rising from the SE end of a ridge. A flat oval area (26.4m NE-SW; 17.5m NW-SE) encompassing the top of the knoll is defined by a high steep scarp (H 2.6m) broken by exposed limestone bedrock at SE and SW. The scarp drops to a gently sloping terrace or berm (Wth 4-6m) from which the natural knoll slope falls steeply for several metres (H c. 6m), giving the rath a two-tiered profile. There is an entrance (Wth 2m) at NNE. A low stony bank (Wth c. 2m) tops the scarp on either side of the entrance. In the interior, 5m SW of the entrance, a few large stones protrude from the sod, though their function could not be determined. At NE is an irregular-shaped hollow (8m N-S; 6m E-W; D 0.5m), probably the result of recent disturbance. There is a possible souterrain (SL026-140001-) in the SE quadrant. A cashel (SL026-139----) lies c. 200m to NNW on the same ridge. Immediately to S the rath is overlooked by a higher ridge crowned by 'The Cashel' hilltop enclosure (SL026-141----), c. 190m to NNW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In a meadow, on the E bank of the Owenmore River, overlooked to SE and S by undulating rising ground. A level rectangular area (35.4m NE-SW; 25m NW-SE) defined on the NE, SE and SW sides by a scarp (H 0.9m), with an intervening fosse and an outer bank. On the NW side it is defined by the vertical riverbank (H 1m). The scarp is topped by a slight grassy rise (Wth 2m), in parts along the NE side and at the N end of the SE side. The fosse (Wth 3.6m; D 0.7m) is flat-bottomed, waterlogged and marked by a dense growth of rushes. The outer bank (Wth 4.2m; int. H 1.5m; ext. H 0.45m) is broad, low and compact. The enclosing elements stop short of the riverbank on both the NE and SW sides but this appears to be the result of relatively recent disturbance. The entrance (Wth 3m), with a causeway across the fosse, is midway along the SE side where the N terminal of the outer bank is expanded. The interior is densely covered with rushes and irises except for a grassy strip (Wth 3-4m) bordering the riverbank. 
At the E corner of the interior, a small rectangular two-tiered earthen platform (5m NW-SE; 4m NE-SW) projects from the scarp into the fosse. The SE side (Wth 2m NE-SW) is at the same level as, and is a continuation of, the top of the scarp. The NE side is at a lower level forming a flat step (H 0.45m) that projects 2m into the fosse. The fosse appears to swing out slightly to accommodate the projection but is nevertheless narrower (Wth 2m) here than elsewhere. Opposite the projection the inner face of the outer bank incorporates a significant amount of stone. At the S corner of the interior the scarp incorporates a much less substantial projection (1.2m NE-SW; c. 2.5m NW-SW) into the fosse. On the N half of the SE side, a berm (Wth 4.8m) separates the outer bank from the fosse (Wth 3.5m; D 0.7m) which lies parallel to the outer bank on the SE side but at the E corner swings wide, terminating at the riverbank c. 15 to N. This is clearly visible on an aerial photograph (IASAP, 3038211) but is only barely discernible on the ground.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In level elevated pasture, with a fall of ground towards a stream c. 150m to S. A low subcircular platform (21.6m E-W; 18.5m N-S to field fence) defined NNE-NW by a scarp with a slight internal lip. An E-W field boundary truncates the N edge of the rath. The scarp (H 0.4m) is very low NE-SE and partially incorporated into a N-S field boundary. It is higher (H 1.3m at S; 0.9m at NW) and better preserved SSE-NW, retaining a slight internal lip in places to S and W. The interior is level with a very slight rise at NW. A low linear rise (Wth 0.8m) on a N-S axis crosses the interior close to the scarp at W, possibly an old field division or perhaps remains of cultivation ridges. A farm track skirts the perimeter SE-SSW. Another rath (SL026-063----) lies c. 100m to E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In elevated pasture; the ground slopes gently down towards a stream c. 150m to S. A raised circular area (34m N-S; 32m E-W) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 6m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 2.6m) with an external fosse (Wth c. 5m; D 0.8m). The bank has a high, well-defined external face but a low, slumped internal rim and is best defined N-SE where much stone protrudes from the sod on the internal face. The fosse is clearly visible SSW-NW as a broad flat-bottomed shallow depression but is infilled elsewhere. A farm track to N, an area of surface disturbance and overgrowth to E, and a small plantation of conifers at SE impinge on the line of the infilled fosse. The interior slopes down gently to S. The entrance (Wth 3m) is at SSE with a possible ramp or causeway across the fosse. The perimeter is ringed with hawthorn bushes. There is a farmyard immediately to E. Another rath (SL026-062----) lies c. 100m to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

On the edge of an open expanse of undulating grassland, obscured within a dense strip of woodland, rhododendron and scrub along the boundary of the Markree Castle estate (SL026-038----). The field boundary extends NE-SW parallel to the estate boundary wall 6m to SE. An identical parallel field bank flanked by field drains lies 2.5m to NE and appears to respect the curve of the rath. These parallel field banks are estate features apparently to delimit the woodland strip that borders the estate.

source_data.original_text:
In mature coniferous plantation in level poorly drained ground on the E bank of the Owenmore River. A strip (Wth 8m) of waterlogged grass and rushes separates the NW perimeter from the river. A large circular enclosure (62m N-S) defined by a low earthen bank and a shallow external fosse. The enclosure is planted with coniferous trees in rows c. 2m apart on a roughly N-S axis. The bank (Wth 3.5m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.75m) survives as a broad low earthen rise with a gently rounded top and broadly slumped sides. The fosse (Wth 3m; D 0.3m) is evident as a shallow depression marked in parts by pools of water. The 1913 OS 6-inch map shows a wide break in the bank NE-E but this area is engulfed in a thicket of fallen trees and overgrowth and was impossible to inspect. The interior is level. Small pools of water occur in parts within the interior and there is an area of particularly boggy ground at E. A low field boundary (Wth 2m; H 0.5m) and an infilled drain (Wth c. 2m) extend to E from the SE edge of the enclosure.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, encompassing a low natural rise on a gentle NW-facing slope with good views in all directions. A subcircular area (39m N-S; 36m E-W) enclosed SE-NW by an earthen bank (Wth 2.7m; int. H 0.1m; ext. H 1.3m) with a low internal lip, and by curving field boundary (Wth 2m; int. H 0.7m; ext. H 1.1m) NNW-SE. The bank at S and W appears to be linear. There is a break (Wth 2.3m) in the bank at SE. Outside the bank SW-NW, coinciding with a natural break of slope, is a terrace (Wth 1.5m) defined on the outer edge by a broadly sloping scarp (H 0.7m). The scarp falls to a strip of flat wet ground that may incorporate a fosse (Wth c. 2-2.5m). The damp ground is bordered to W by a road flanked by field walls but from NW-NNW there is a slight rise (Wth 2.5-3m) which may be the remnant of an outer bank. The interior has a gently domed profile; from a central N-S spine (c. 10m E-W) of level elevated ground it slopes down to the perimeter at SW-W and more markedly at NE-E. Two small heaps of stones (diam. c. 2m; H 0.4m) were noted in the E half of the interior. The perimeter is thickly ringed with hawthorn and ash trees. Another rath (SL026-058----) is visible to NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
This is the site of a High Victorian Tudor-Gothic house of polychrome brick, with gables, dormer-gables and a turret and spire, built from 1856 onwards by Capt. T. J. Meredith to the design of an architect named Montgomery (Bence-Jones 1978, 88). The house was replaced by a modern monastery and church surrounded by an asphalt car park. The original doorway of the house has been dismantled and reconstructed as the entrance to a garden patio. Above the slightly pointed arch is a coat of arms. Built into the wall next to the patio entrance is a coat of arms with the latin motto DEUS PROVIDEBIT. The right angled landscaping feature indicated with hachures on the 1913 edition of the OS 6-inch map immediately to the east of the the 19th-century house, and almost certainly associated with it, does not survive.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Date of upload: 14 December 2011

In undulating pasture, on top of a ridge with excellent views of the surrounding countryside. Named 'The Cashel' on the 19 OS 6-inch map, this hilltop enclosure, consists of an oval area (65m N-S; 50m E-W) enclosed by a stone wall. The wall, which is highest along the W arc (T 0.6m; H 1.3m), has a rubble core with a facing of stone. Condit, Gibbons and Timoney (1991, 61-2) suggest that a gap through the wall at S may be the original entrance. The interior rises towards the centre. A field boundary indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map bisecting the interior on a NW-SE axis, was not indicated on the 1913 OS 6-inch map. A rath (SL026-140----) lies c. 190m to SSE.

source_data.original_text:
Within the demesne of Markree Castle (SL026-038----), in level damp pasture, immediately N of woodland enclosed by the demesne wall. A low circular earthen platform (33m E-W; 34m N-S) defined SW-ENE by a low degraded scarp (H 0.4m) and E-SSW by a vertical scarp (H 1m). Centrally placed on top of the platform is a circular earthen plinth (diam. 10.5m; H 1.1m) topped by a ruined square stone turret (4.2m N-S; 4.3m E-W; H 4m). The turret has a brick-built chimney in the NW corner, a small splayed window in the N wall, a second window in the S wall and a door ope (Wth 0.8m) in the W wall. Encircling the base of the plinth is a shallow fosse (Wth 2m) crossed by a causeway at S. The demesne wall curves around the base of the platform E-SSW, at a distance of 1.6m from it. Though the turret is of 18th/19th-century date, the platform may be the remains of an earlier earthwork.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In level pasture on the S bank of the Owenmore River. Immediately to S is undulating rising ground, much of which has been dug away by extensive quarrying c. 50m to S. A rectangular area (29m N-S; 53m E-W) enclosed on the E, S, W sides by a bank (Wth 3m; int. H 0.6m; ext. H 1m) and an external fosse (Wth c. 3.8m; D 0.7m). On the N side there is a broad low stony scarp (Wth c. 4m; H 0.4m) that slopes to within 4m of the river. This, however, extends beyond the limits of the enclosure and appears to represent a natural break of slope incorporated into a field boundary. It is difficult to examine as a dense thicket of bushes and overgrowth line the river's edge. The bank is compact and sod-covered. The fosse is clearly marked by a dense growth of irises even though its outer edge is generally poorly defined. On the E side the bank has been levelled to a slight grassy rise and the fosse is infilled to a shallow depression. The entrance (Wth 2.3m), with a causeway across the fosse, is towards the W end of the S side. The interior is covered by long grass, rushes and irises. There is a circular flat-topped mound (19m E-W; 19m N-S; H 1.8m at N, 1.5m at S) with broadly sloping sides in the SW quadrant, the level top (diam. c.10m) of which has a slight depression. A somewhat similar but probably natural, flat-topped rise (c. 20m N-S; c. 10m E-W) protrudes from the gentle S-facing slope c.15m to NE. Another moated site (SL026-021001-) lies 20m to W and a possible rectangular enclosure (SL026-021003-) lies 20m to E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a low flat-topped ridge with broadly sloping sides, steepest on the W side, and bordered W-E by low-lying wet ground and SE-S by a gently rising ridge of higher ground. An arc of scarp (L 70m; Wth slope 1.7m; H 0.5m) S-NNW coincides with the natural break of slope at the top of the ridge. At the base of the scarp there is a terrace (Wth 4.5m) from which the ground falls in a broad slope (Wth slope 5m; H 0.95m) to the base of the ridge. This is probably the remains of a large oval rath, though no evidence of an enclosing element survives N-SE. A NE-SW field boundary crosses the probable S limits of the rath. There is a souterrain (SL026-026002-) in the S half of the interior. This rath is probably that described by O'Rorke (1878, 241) as 'a large rath or fort…oblong being 96 yards [87.78m] in length and 72 [65.84m] in breadth'. There is a possible fulacht fia (SL026-026005-) immediately to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In the S half of a rath (SL026-026001-), close to the scarp of the rath at S. A low roughly circular rise (14m N-S; 13m E-W), marked by long grass and brambles, from which loose stones protrude, especially on the E side. Within the S edge of the rise is a collapsed roofless souterrain passage (L 4m N-S, Wth 1m; D 1m), choked with brambles. At the N end is an in situ lintel covering a low opening (H 0.3m) to a drystone-built passage which extends to the N. Roughly 10m to N, protruding from the ground, are two further in situ lintels, 1.3m apart.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, on top of a ridge with excellent views of the surrounding undulating terrain. A raised roughly oval area (c. 37.5m NE-SW; c. 30m NW-SE) defined ESE-NE by a scarp (H 1.7m ) with an external fosse (Wth c. 5.5m). A possible outer bank is evident S-WSW as a barely discernible flat-topped rise (Wth c. 3m). The outer edge of the fosse W-NW is incorporated into a field boundary (Wth 1.3m; ext. H 0.8m). At NE-E there is a broad causeway (Wth 11m) across the fosse and the interior is flush with the exterior ground level. This is the result of recent modification of the rath but may mask the original entrance. The fosse appears greatly expanded (Wth 8-9m) at SE and NW due to the quarrying of part of the interior platform. A possible rath (SL026-142002-) lies immediately to N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In the demesne of Coopershill House (Bence-Jones 1988, 91-2), on the W side of the avenue leading north to the house and c. 80m SSW of the bridge that carries the avenue over the Unshin River. The ruined remains of Tanzyfort House, built by the Cooper family in the middle of the 17th century and occupied by them until Coopershill House was completed in 1774, consist of an L-shaped structure originally of two storeys with an attic (Craig and Garner 1973; Orser 2003). The structure is fragmentary and shows evidence of extensive alteration and rebuilding since its abandonment in the late 18th century (Orser 2003). In the summer of 2003 Prof. Charles E. Orser of Illinois State University conducted an archaeological excavation here as part of the ongoing Rural Lifeways Project (see Orser 2000). Preliminary excavation within the structure revealed 'the likely presence of at least two rooms, a front hall, containing 984 ft², and a kitchen, containing 690 ft². The original hall had a flagstone floor, while the kitchen floor was composed of tightly set cobbles' (Orser 2003). The excavation also revealed 'a possible back entrance almost directly opposite the front doorway, and structural evidence suggests the presence of a fireplace along the north wall of the kitchen and a second-storey fireplace in the building's northeast corner' (ibid.). Further excavation is planned for 2004.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on top of a low bluff overlooking a small stream valley, at the W end of a low ridge. A D-shaped area (c. 85m ENE-WSW; c. 95m NNW-SSE) enclosed NW-SW by a slight scarp (H 0.45m) with traces of an internal lip, and on the straight W side by a low bluff (H 3.5m) dropping to a flat strip of ground (Wth 20m E-W) bordering a stream. The scarp is best preserved NW-ENE where it coincides with a natural break of slope, and SSE-SSW where it cuts into a S-facing slope; it is barely discernible E-SE and partially truncated WNW-NW by a number of small quarry pits. A growth pattern outside the scarp at NE may indicate an external fosse. The N half of the interior is fairly level but there is a marked fall of ground from the centre to S and SW following the natural slope. The interior is bisected N of centre by a post-and-wire fence on a roughly E-W axis intersecting at W with a similar fence extending to SSW. A possible internal division on a roughly NW-SE axis is indicated by a growth pattern.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on top of a low ridge with excellent views in all directions. The barrow was densely covered with overgrowth and waterlogged when inspected. The remains consist of a slightly curved section of earthen bank (L 11m; H 1.5m; Wth 1.9m at top, 4m at base; long axis WSW-ENE). In rough pasture, in a forest clearing at the NW end of an elevated ridge with extensive views in all directions. This rath was described during a previous site inspection in 1992 as a poorly preserved roughly circular area (c. 18m N-S, c. 16m E-W) defined by a scarp (H 1.3m) with a stone core along the N arc. The remainder of the rath was barely discernible as it had been heavily disturbed by forestry cultivation ridge, a N-S farm track which crosses the E side of the interior and a field boundary which truncates the E perimeter (SMR (1989) file). This rath is now completely inaccessible due to overgrowth.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In low-lying pasture, c. 250m to N of Tawnagh church (SL034-085001-) and c. 200m N of a graveyard (SL034-085002-). A natural spring rises through limestone bedrock on the NW edge of a mound (H c. 0.8m) and feeds a fast-flowing stream to NW. Two roughly rectangular stones (0.28m x 0.25m x 0.1m and 0.35m x 0.25m x 0.15m) on top of the mound with shallow hollows cut into the surface of each are, according to local information, said to be the knee prints of St Patrick. A roughly circular area (diam. 1.6m x 1.5m) to NW in front of the mouth of the well is defined by a low setting of stones and through it the outflow of the spring flows. In 1836 it was recorded as 'St Patrick's Well, Tobar Patraig...whose day is celebrated there as Patron Saint of the Parish' (OSL, 154). In 1942-4 it was noted that very few people visit the well, there being no annual pilgrimage day (ITA). There is no evidence of recent veneration at this well.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On a small elevation in pasture broken by rock outcrop some 40m W of a small stream. The tomb stands at the S end of an oval mound (9m N-S; 7m E-W; H 0.5m). The portal-stone to the W (H 1.95m), alongside it a sillstone (H 0.45m), and a sidestone (H 1.4m) of the E side of this S-facing chamber are in situ. The eastern portal-stone lies fallen at the front of the chamber (min. L 2m). About 8m NE of the chamber there is a slightly curved line (L c. 4m) of five stones on edge. The stones, which are not set into the ground, form an inner face to a slight bank of earth. While of uncertain age and function this feature is hardly of any great antiquity. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 61-2, no. 99)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

The N portion has been raised to compensate for the hillslope. Field boundaries abut the bank at SW and NW. Another rath (SL034-091----) lies c. 20m to SW.

In pasture, on a S-facing slope. A raised circular area (24m N-S; 23m E-W) defined by an earthen bank (int. H 0.6m; ext. H 1.95m) SW-SE and elsewhere by a scarp. The entrance is via a ramp (Wth 1.4m) at SSE, revetted with a line of stones (L 3.4m; H 0.2m) on the W side. A N-S field boundary abuts the external face of the bank at W. The fosse (D 0.4m) is evident NE-SE and is infilled elsewhere. There is a field boundary along the outer edge of the infilled fosse N-NE. A small quarry (5m N-S; 7m E-W; D 0.9m), now disused, is in the infilled fosse at S. The interior is level and raised to compensate for the hillslope. The N half of the rath is densely covered with overgrowth.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).
