source_data.original_text:
On rocky pasture about 4km W of the N end of Lough Arrow. Scant structural remains of a tomb survive in a low, poorly defined oval mound (19m NE-SW; max. 12m NW-SE). Two adjoining sidestones (combined length 4m) and a jamb remain of the more southerly side of a gallery aligned NE-SW. The jamb is at the NE end of the line described by the two sidestones and just 1m beyond the opposite end there is a prostrate slab, possibly a fallen backstone. Between this and the line of stones there is an upright stone which does not appear to be in situ. There are also some prostrate stones at the site. Some 2m E of the jamb a depression in the mound may mark the position of a court. 'Toberstarley' holy well (SL034-100001-) lies c. 50m to S. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 62, no. 100)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On the summit of a ridge in pasture and commanding an outlook in all directions. The remains of a cruciform passage tomb stand in the base of a cairn. The cairn perimeter has been disturbed by two adjoining raths (SL034-108001- to NW and SL034-110---- to E). A retaining kerb is represented by three leaning stones at the NE which indicate that the cairn was of round outline. The tomb would seem to have opened to the SW. An orthostat at the NE is the backstone and another opposite it and 4.65m to the SW appears to be a sillstone. This stone may have marked a point of segmentation along the passage, now otherwise destroyed. A well-preserved chamber (0.8m x 0.7m) some 1.5m SSW of the backstone is the right-hand side-chamber of the tomb. Single stones form its sides and back and it is entered between two jamb-like stones. The opposite side-chamber is represented only by its backstone. A displaced roofstone lies against the SE side-chamber and another leans against the surviving sillstone. A number of other displaced or partly buried stones lie at the site. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 93)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
The Red Earl's Road, probably of medieval origin, linked the towns of Ballymote, Co. Sligo and Boyle, Co. Roscommon, by a route around the N and E sides of the Bricklieve Mountains (M. A. Timoney 1998, 155), a distance of c. 21km. It is said to have been built by Richard de Burgh, The Red Earl of Ulster, after the Norman conquest, to link his castle (SL033-092----) at Ballymote with Boyle Abbey (RO006-068005-), Co. Roscommon. The road traverses a number of townlands over a number of 6-inch sheets (OS 33: Bellanascarrow West/Roscrib East/Roscrib West/Ballinvoher; OS 34: Drumcormick/ Bricklieve/Tiraree; OS 40: Cloghoge Lower/Carrowkeel/Mullaghfarna/ Doonaveeragh/Knockroe/Cuilsheeghary More/Mountgaffeny/Ballinafad/Gortalough/ Ballaghboy/Cartron; OS 45: Ballaghboy/Cartron).

Sections of the road are recorded under five records (SL033-147----; SL034-159----; SL040-023----; SL040-197----; SL040-190----) commencing at Ballymote and following the route E and then S to the county boundary with Roscommon. Only sections of the road are indicated on the 1914 and 1941 OS 6-inch maps even though it was, of course, continuous. A possible link road between Bothar an Iarla Ruaid and Bothar an Corran (SL033-145----) goes from Greenan townland, around the S side of the Bricklieve Mountains, to Ballinafad. At its nearest point, Bothar an Corran is c. 0.8km to the SW. 

This section (SL034-159----) (L 800m) extends NW-SE over undulating pasture and is mostly overlain by a modern road. At the SE end where the modern road curves to the S, the old road continues to SE and is visible in places as a slightly raised band of rough vegetation (L 650m; Wth c. 2m) following the contour of the hill. Bricklieve Castle (SL034-175----) is c. 200m S of the SE end of this section of the road.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of revision: 1 June 2011

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, on slightly raised level ground near the NW bank of a stream. The only visible remains of the castle are sod-covered foundations (Wth c. 2m; H c. 0.8m) defining two conjoined rectangular areas (at N end: 7.5m E-W; 9m N-S; at S end: 14m E-W; 6m N-S). A section of stone walling (L 2.6m; H 1m), constructed of small roughly cut blocks of mortared limestone, is exposed on the E side of the N area. The N end of this wall is splayed, indicating that this may be a doorway position. In 1512 this castle was described in the annals as a 'stronghold' of the O'Donnells (O'Dowd 1991, 21). By 1593 it was in the hands of Gilbert Green (O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 235), an Elizabethan soldier who took possession of land 'when it was lying waste' (O'Dowd 1991, 94). The 'Red' Earl's Road (SL033-147----) is c. 200m to the N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture. The ruin of an L-shaped house (see plan in Waterman 1961, fig. 14.8; plan and reconstruction drawing in MacLysaght 1969, f. 96; photo M. A. Timoney 2002c, 272) consisting of a gable-ended main block (int.: 10m N-S; 5.9m E-W) with a square stairway projection at the S end of the W wall (int.: L 2.85m). The main block is two storeys with an attic over a semi-basement. It is built of rubble limestone, harled externally and plastered internally. The walls stand to full height but the structure was repaired by the OPW c. 1940 when breaches were blocked up and concrete lintels inserted over some window and fireplace opes. 
The main elevation faces E with an off-centre ground-floor doorway near the S end, and centrally placed in two bays are two ground- and two first-floor windows. Only the S side of the doorway survives, with a return socket for a drawbar and an angled slot through the side which probably housed the chain for a yett. The windows are identical plain rectangular embrasures, missing their covering wooden lintels (ibid., 272) and wooden lights. 
The interior ground level is now higher than the original giving the basement a very squat appearance. Along the base of the E wall is a footing (projecting c. 0.35m) which may be the remains of an earlier structure. Just above it is a shallow scarcement which carried a wooden floor over the basement. The basement has a rebuilt fireplace in the centre of the N wall flanked by two small splayed window embrasures with single rectangular stone lights. A wall-press in the W wall is flanked by two blocked-up opes. 
Judging by a corresponding plaster gap in the W and E walls, there was a wooden partition on the ground floor between the entrance doorway and the southernmost window. As well as the pair on the E wall, the ground floor also has a similar window in the W and E walls, as well as two small splayed windows flanking the central fireplace in the N wall. The first floor has a similar arrangement of windows with the addition of a second window in the W wall, and a very small window on the E side of the central fireplace in the S wall. The N wall fireplace is set W of centre to allow space for the flue from the fireplaces below (the stack projects on the inside of the wall-face). There is also a partition gap in the plaster in the first floor, but it is located further N than the one below. The attic has two small windows either side of the central chimney stack in the W wall, and a small central fireplace in the S wall with a window on its W side. 
Except for both gables there is a shallow internal oversail just below the top of the walls (c. 0.2m). A series of drip-stones along these walls suggest that the side walls and those of the stairs may have been topped by battlements with a wall-walk.
The inside faces of the stairway projection show the 'ghost' of a wooden stairs with a landing at each corner (scale-and-platt), rising the full height of the house. At ground-floor level in the N wall are two small splayed opes which are probably gun loops; there is another in the S wall. Otherwise the stairs is lit by four rectangular window opes in the W wall. The walls of the projection rise only to the level of the side walls of the main block.
According to local tradition the house is named after Captain Baldwin, a soldier of Cromwell, who on returning from a hunting trip found the house burned down by his servants. This folklore is without foundation (Pers. Comm. Conchubhar ÓCrualaoich, Sep. 2018), as in the seventeenth century Bellanagarrigeeny – Béal Átha na gCarraigíní ‘the approach of the ford of rocks’ is sometimes also known as Coylemore – Coill Mór ‘Big Wood’ in the early seventeenth century. The land was granted to Edward Nicholson during the Cromwellian era, and Baldwin only becomes associated with it from 1711 through the marriage of a Sarah Baldwin to an Edward Nicholson. There is a fulacht fia (SL034-245----) c. 40m to E.

This is a national monument in State care (no. 373).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of revised upload: 20 September 2018

source_data.original_text:
On the SE-facing slope of a prominent ridge. The remains consist of a semicircular terrace (c. 27m E-W; c. 20m N-S) defined by traces of a possible scarp (H c. 1.5m) cut into the natural slope, most clearly visible E-SE. At the edge of the terrace, NE-SE, is a steep fall of ground, covered with overgrowth. From SE-SW the slope is more gentle, dropping into a narrow dip that separates the terrace from the steeply rising slope of a parallel ridge. A field boundary on NNW-SSE axis, engulfed in overgrowth, obscures the W arc. An E-W field boundary wall (Wth c. 1m; H c. 0.5m), densely covered in blackthorn bushes and brambles, creates a straight N side to the terrace at the interface with the steeply rising ridge slope.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
The Red Earl's Road, probably of medieval origin, linked the towns of Ballymote, Co. Sligo and Boyle, Co. Roscommon, by a route around the N and E sides of the Bricklieve Mountains (M. A. Timoney 1998, 155), a distance of c. 21km. It is said to have been built by Richard de Burgh, The Red Earl of Ulster, after the Norman conquest, to link his castle (SL033-092----) at Ballymote with Boyle Abbey (RO006-068005-), Co. Roscommon. The road traverses a number of townlands over a number of 6-inch sheets (OS 33: Bellanascarrow West/Roscrib East/Roscrib West/Ballinvoher; OS 34: Drumcormick/ Bricklieve/Tiraree; OS 40: Cloghoge Lower/Carrowkeel/Mullaghfarna/ Doonaveeragh/Knockroe/Cuilsheeghary More/Mountgaffeny/Ballinafad/Gortalough/ Ballaghboy/Cartron; OS 45: Ballaghboy/Cartron).

Sections of the road are recorded under five records (SL033-147----; SL034-159----; SL040-023----; SL040-197----; SL040-190----) commencing at Ballymote and following the route E and then S to the county boundary with Roscommon. Only sections of the road are indicated on the 1914 and 1941 OS 6-inch maps even though it was, of course, continuous. A possible link road between Bothar an Iarla Ruaid and Bothar an Corran (SL033-145----) goes from Greenan townland, around the S side of the Bricklieve Mountains, to Ballinafad. At its nearest point, Bothar an Corran is c. 0.8km to the SW. 

This section (SL040-023----) shown on the 1914 edition of OS 6-inch map comprises a 400m stretch (long axis NW-SE) which is evident in places as a grass-covered rut (Wth 3.9m; D 0.6m) crossing the top of a drumlin. A further section (SL040-197----) of the road is c. 1.2km to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of revision: 1 June 2011

In pasture, on a gentle SE-facing slope of the Bricklieve Mountains with excellent views. An oval area (42m NE-SW; 49.6m NW-SE) enclosed by a substantial earthen bank, with an external fosse evident SE-NW. The bank (Wth 3.5m; int. H 0.6m; ext. H 1.15m) is compact and well defined, with a narrow flat top and broadly sloping sides. It appears to be primarily earthen but incorporates some stone. A field boundary wall, on a NE-SW axis, overlies the bank NW-NNE, respecting its curve. The shallow fosse (Wth 2m; D 0.35m) is cut into gently rising ground. Its outer edge is quite sharply defined SW-W where it was incorporated into the line of a now disused field boundary. The gentle slope down from W to E in the interior is broken by a central level area defined NNW-SE by a slight scarp (L c. 17m; H 0.6m). The entrance (Wth 3.7m) is at ESE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In undulating pasture, straddling a break of slope and overlooked to the NW by the steep slopes of Bricklieve Mountains. A slightly raised oval area (38.6m NW-SE; 33.6m NE-SW) defined ENE-NW by an earthen bank (Wth 3.6m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.85m) and NW-NE by a scarp (H 1.8m), built up to compensate for the natural slope. The bank is generally degraded NE-SW, retaining only a low internal lip. At SW, where it backs onto rising ground, it is barely rises above the external ground level but has a pronounced internal scarp. The interior is bisected by a NE-SW field boundary wall and is generally level though it is slightly lower in the N half, the change in level is marked by an 11m stretch of a NE-facing scarp (H 1m). There is a rectangular enclosure (SL040-033001-) c. 100m to NW.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture on an E-facing terrace on the northern slopes of the Bricklieve Mountains and commanding a view over Lough Arrow 1.6 km to the E. The scant remains of a structure, possibly a chamber (L 2.2m) aligned NW-SE, stand in a mound of subrectangular plan (8.5m NE-SW; 8m NW-SE; H 0.4m). To the NW two opposed orthostats, the taller 0.7m high, stand 1.2m apart at either side of a low stone, possibly a sill, set transversely between them. These stones may mark the front of a chamber that appears to be closed by a stone (H 0.6m) some 2.2m to the SE of and parallel to the sillstone. Another stone (H 0.65m) is set face on to the NW end of the more northerly of the opposed orthostats. A partly buried stone immediately alongside the outer face of the more southerly of the opposed orthostats is not definitely structural. There are three prostrate stones at the site, the largest 1.75m in max. dimension. Enclosure (SL040-03201-) c. 150m to SSE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In good pasture, on a steep NW-facing hillside in the lower reaches of the Bricklieve Mountains. Circular, steep-sided cairn of comprised almost entirely of small stones (diam. at base c.10m). The slope of the hill was utilised in its construction. Consequently it is lowest at the SE side (H c. 1.2m) and highest at the NW side (H c. 4m). However a stretch of the cairn (L 8.2m) at NW has been incorporated into a linear NE-SW drystone-built field boundary wall which divides it into two unequal portions. There are some large stones incorporated into the base of the wall beneath the cairn material. That portion of the cairn that lies to the NW of the wall is much smaller (dim. 2.6m NW-SE) than the remainder. This potential monument is known locally as a relatively modern field clearance cairn. However it is impossible to assign a date or function on the basis of the available evidence.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 18 August 2011

source_data.original_text:
In lowlying pasture, at the narrow S corner of a rectilinear field. Located at the S end of a broad valley, with steep slopes rising immediately to S–SW of the rath, and the flat expanse of the valley bottom stretching to N–NE towards an arc of rounded hills and ridges in the middle distance. Much of the land to E is now under forestry.
This rath is not shown on the 1838 and 1914 OS 6-inch maps, but is clearly visible in current aerial imagery. It has been partly levelled, and is bisected to E of centre by a field fence on a NE–SW axis. It consists of a slightly raised circular area (diam. 30m) defined by a scarp and enclosed by a fosse with remnants of an external bank. The circular platform is still clearly defined on the N arc, but has been severely levelled at NE–SE (the portion lying to E of the bisecting field fence). A discrete section of the original enclosing bank (Wth 2.25-2.5m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.5m) survives at SSW; elsewhere it has been levelled to a scarp with a broad external slump (ext. H 0.55m at N) dropping into the fosse, which is visible as a shallow depression (Wth 2.5-3m). A hint of a rise/cropmark (Wth 3-4m) on the outer edge of the fosse is all that remains of the external bank.

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, located on a steep SW-facing slope, which drops into a broad valley, with a small stream in its base. There are very good views into the valley, and to S, with Carrowkeel visible in the distance to SE and Kesh Corran to SSW. 
This enclosure is not indicated on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps. A broadly oval area (70m NE–SW; 60-65m NW–SE) is defined by a fosse (W c. 2m) evident as a barely-discernible depression. At S–SW a slight scarp can be traced where the arc of the enclosure coincides with the base of the natural slope. The interior is not raised relative to exterior ground level, and slopes steeply down to SW, reflecting the natural slope. A field bank/property boundary, on a NE–SW axis, cuts through the enclosure to NW of centre. Part of the W quadrant of the interior has been incorporated into a small plantation of deciduous trees. At SE the fosse is truncated by a subcircular quarry pit (diam. c. 12m), now grassed over. 
A rath (SL034-103001-) is located 175m to NW and another (SL034-104----) 250m to WSW.

In pasture, on the broad level ridge top c. 25-30m W of a break of slope where ground falls away steeply to NE−E into a valley. An ESB pole stands close to the NW edge of the enclosure. 
A roughly circular enclosure (diam. c. 60-65m) is visible in Lidar imagery and in aerial imagery (Digital globe, Google Earth). It is not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps.
The enclosure was levelled at an unknown date in the past and is almost impossible to trace at ground level; a slight undulation is visible on the NE–E arc. The interior encompasses a slight dip in ground level, and a densely rush-grown area (c. 30-35m) of damp, soggy ground and standing water covers much of the E half of the interior. The original date and function of this enclosure is unclear.

Notified to NMS by Andrew Goodison.

source_data.original_text:
On the E side of a low rise skirted to the W by a stream. The remains consist of the NW corner (5.6m E-W; 2.6m N-S) of a tower now standing to two storeys, and a large block of masonry lying on the ground immediately to its SE. These are located towards the E end of a rectangular sod-covered platform (c. 30m N-S; c. 25m E-W) which may be the remains of a bawn. Immediately E of the platform are two 19th-century farm buildings which contain carved stones derived from the tower including a sheela-na-gig (SL034-001002-) and a pick-dressed quoin. The tower is built of roughly coursed limestone in a lime mortar; the walls are gently battered, but most of the quoins are missing. The ground floor had a window in its W wall but only its N side survives which contains part of a splayed gun loop. In the corner, at first-floor level, is a mural chamber the inside wall of which is gone. At this level was a large window embrasure in the N wall but only its W side survives. On the external face, 3m above present ground level, is a horizontal slit (0.8m x 0.25m) which may be an exit for a garderobe chute. A drawing by Grose (1791, vol. 1, 52) shows the tower much as it is today but with the fallen block then standing. Grose described it as 'a square tower' and noted that the castle had been used as a quarry during the building of a nearby house (see above). Traditionally known as a MacDonagh castle (Grose 1797, vol. 1, 52; McParlan 1802, 92; O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 236).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On a low rise, on the N side of a road; in the SW quadrant of Tawnagh graveyard (SL034-085002-). The ruin of a rectangular gable-ended church (int. 16.58m E-W; 6.1m N-S), with a porch (3.35m E-W; 3.95m N-S) added to the W end, built of uncoursed limestone in lime mortar. The walls stand to full height except for the central portion of the N wall that has fallen. This space is occupied by a mound of loose stones, which includes fragments of roofing stones (two of these are in NMI along with a quernstone and a portion of another from the site (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney)). A N-S line of low stones, noted on the E side of the breach in the 1980s, may have been the remains of the E wall of a N transept (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). 
The church is entered through a central doorway in the W wall. The chamfered door-surround is late medieval in style with a pointed arch and a hood-moulding. Directly overhead is another doorway, much ruined, which must have served a gallery. Just inside the doorway, on the S side, is an octagonal stone basin set in a square recess (H 0.3m; Wth 0.35m; D 0.35m) covered by a rounded arch. The interior has four surviving window opes: two in the S wall, one in the centre of the E gable and another directly overhead in the angle of the gable. These held wooden-framed lights, none of which survive. Part of a quernstone is set into one of the windows in the S wall. Two rows of joist-holes at the W end indicate the position of a gallery. There is a bellcote, for a single bell, at the top of the W gable. 
The porch walls are butted against the W wall of the church, off-centre to the N; its S wall partially covers the jamb of the doorway. The porch has a doorway in its W wall and a window ope in its N wall. Loose but in its original position in the W wall is a roughly rectangular stone inscribed: 'THIS CHURCH WAS BUILT AN/DOM 1733 JON DODD AND WILLIAM COOPER BEING CHURCHWARDENS'. Below the inscription are three sunken panels - one with a monarch's head, one with a fleur-de-lis, and the third blank. Two quoins in the NW corner of the church are punch dressed in late medieval fashion. There are other reused stones in the fabric of both the church and porch, including what may be part of a window jamb on the NE corner of the church.
This is the ruin of the late medieval parish church of Tawnagh, rebuilt as a C of I parish church, probably by the 1620s (Hurley 1943, vol. 1, 386), with the porch and gallery added in 1733 (see above). The church seems to have been out of use by 1837 (Lewis 1837, vol. 2, 599). A Tau cross (SL034-085005-) stands just inside the E wall of the graveyard, 10.8m E of the church. St. Patrick's Well (SL034-028----) is c. 250m to the N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
A rectangular graveyard (41.2m N-S; 36.1m E-W), extended to the N before 1894, enclosed by a stone wall and accessed through a gate at the SW. The ruin of the former C of I parish church of Tawnagh, incorporating a late medieval church (SL034-085001-), stands close to the SW corner. The raised roughly rectangular platform of an earlier graveyard (c. 40m E-W; 25m N-S), defined by a gently sloping scarp, occupies the S third of the graveyard. It extends N from the entrance gate at SW and curves around to the E, c. 10m N of the church, following the border of the graveyard as indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. Immediately to the N of the church are rows of low uninscribed grave-markers. A memorial, located to the N of the church porch, is dated 1701 (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney). There are a number of chest-tombs and recumbent stones, mostly on the S side of the church. The graveyard is still in use. Just inside the E boundary wall, 10.8m E of the church, is a Tau cross (SL034-08505-). A curved scarp along the contour of the hillside, c. 27m to W of the graveyard, may indicate the line of an outer enclosure. 'St Patrick's' holy well (SL034-028----) is c. 200m to the N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In Tawnagh graveyard (SL034-085002-), just inside the E boundary wall and 10.8m E of the gable of a ruined church (SL034-085001-). A Tau cross (H 0.51m) is set upright in a line of low uninscribed grave-markers and positioned directly between two 20th-century headstones. The shaft (H 0.36m) of the cross is 0.28m wide at the base but tapers to 0.21m at the junction with the arms. The arms (H 0.15m) of the cross have rounded ends which project 0.09m on either side of the shaft. The overall width of the upper portion of the cross, is 0.41m. On the E face of the cross, just below the junction of the arms and shaft, is incised a small plain Greek cross.

source_data.original_text:
In Tawnagh graveyard (SL034-085002-). Located 4m N of the porch of Tawnagh church (SL034-085001-) is a low memorial, (present H 0.56m; Wth. 0.62m; D 8cm), now standing upright, aligned N-S. The base is set in a concrete. On the E face is a lengthy inscription. The earliest identifiable date is 1701 (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney). It bears the following inscription:
'Robert Folliott Dyed
Infant 1701
Katerin Folliott Daughter
to Mary Dyed amaid y 12 of
Novr 1701 Mary Folliott ag
ed 75 years dyed August
ye 4 1719 Babara Folliott
Daughter of Mary Dyed
maid ye 10th of April 1723'
Published in M.B. Timoney, Had me made. A study of grave memorials of Co. Sligo from c. 1650 to the present. (Keash, 2005), 166, fig. 164.

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 25 August 2011

The stones, which are not set into the ground, form an inner face to a slight bank of earth. While of uncertain age and function this feature is hardly of any great antiquity. In rough pasture, at the top of an E-facing slope of a ridge. A slightly raised circular area (diam. 25m) enclosed by the remains of four earthen banks with intervening and external fosses. The inner bank (Wth 2.5m; int. H 0.7m; ext. H 0.7m), best preserved along the E arc, is separated from the second bank by an intervening fosse (Wth 2m). The second bank (Wth 4.5m; int. H 0.8m; ext. H 0.7m) is evident all around and is separated from the third bank by an intervening fosse (Wth 3m). The remains of the third bank (Wth 3m) are evident along the S and E arcs as a low rise. The fourth bank (Wth 3m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.3m), c. 16m outside the third bank, curves along the S arc where it is incorporated into a field boundary; a low curved scarp (H 1.2m) is evident along the W and N arcs. The external fosse (Wth 3m; D 0.3m) is evident along the W arc outside the fourth bank. The interior is level and has a slight slope downwards on the E half. The linear depression of a possible souterrain (SL034-173002-) is in the NW quadrant of the interior.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In wet marshy pasture, at the base of the ENE-facing slope of a ridge and to the rear of a disused creamery at Castlebaldwin. The most northerly of three adjacent holy wells, with Tober Murry (SL034-186002-) c. 12m to SE and Tober Patrick (SL034-186003-) c. 15m to SE. A moss-covered stone retaining wall is built into the slope with a lintelled ope (H 0.2m; Wth 0.5m) at its base through which water flows out toward Tobar Murry. It was mentioned in 1836 as 'Tobar Bhríghde...over which three trees grow' (OSL, 157). Also in 1836 there was a local memory of 'stations' at the well (OSNB vol. 1, 351). Prof. R. A. S. Macalister (d. 1950), in an undated report, recorded the story that when a great ash tree which grew at the wells was blown down it was said that the sign of the cross was found 'rudely branded in the fractured section of the wood' (SMR (1989) file).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On a narrow terrace, broken by limestone pavement, on the lower NE-facing slopes of the Bricklieve Mountains, overlooking undulating pasture bordering the shores of Lough Arrow. A roughly D-shaped area (c. 25m NE-SW; c. 25.5m NW-SE) defined on the straight NE side by a low scarp (H 0.4m), on the SE side by the remnants of a field boundary wall that continues away from the enclosure to SSW and ENE, from SSW-WNW by a gently curving inward facing stony scarp (H 0.7m) and WNW-N by a low stony bank. The interior is uneven and strewn with stone; the NE half is at a slightly lower level than the remainder with the change of level marked by a stony band, possibly the remains of a field boundary. Attached externally at SW is a semicircular annexe (10.6m NE-SW; 11m NW-SE) defined SSW-WNW by a substantial inward-facing scarp (H 0.8m) cut into rising ground. The scarp peters out at the NW end leaving a gap (Wth 4m) between it and the enclosure wall. There is a field boundary c. 5m to NE of the enclosure. The enclosure is within a field system (SL040-032002-). A rectangular enclosure (SL040-033001-) and two raths (SL040-034----; SL040-037----) are visible downslope to NE, E and ESE. An unclassified megalithic tomb (SL040-229----) lies c. 150m to NNW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On a terrace, on the lower NE slopes of the Bricklieve Mountains, overlooking a broad sweep of undulating lowland pasture bordering the shores of Lough Arrow. A fragmented pattern of relict field walls enclosing irregular subrectangular fields. The layout of the system is largely dictated by natural bedrock seams and terraces, mostly on a NE-SW axis. The walls are poorly preserved and survive as low sod-covered lines of stone (Wth c. 1m; H 0.3m), barely perceptible in many cases. The terrain is uneven, broken by limestone pavement and strewn with stones. Within the field system, located c. 40m WNW of the enclosure (SL040-032001-), is the poorly preserved outline of a rectangular structure (8.7m WNW-ESE; c. 5m NNE-SSW).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On a broad undulating upland terrace, overlooked to NW by the limestone escarpments of the Bricklieve Mountains. On top of a low elevation which is defined on the SE side by a steep drop to a waterlogged depression or turlough. A roughly square area (26.8m NE-SW; 25.3m NW-SE), with rounded corners, defined by an irregular sod-covered stony spread (Wth 3-5m; H 0.45m), possibly incorporating some field clearance rubble. On the NE side and in parts to NW and SW there is a raised lip (Wth c. 1m; H 0.6m) on the inner edge of the spread. On the SE side the slight stony rise (Wth 2m; int. H 0.35m) merges on the outer edge with the steep drop to the turlough. The interior is generally level but with a slight slope from the centre down to SE. There is a break (Wth 2m) at the S end of the SW side and another (Wth 4m) at the S corner. In the SW quadrant of the interior is a square area (10.6m NW-SE; 10.4m NE-SW) (SL040-033002-) defined on the SW and NW sides by the enclosure wall, on NE side by a low sod-covered stone bank (Wth 1.7m; H 0.2m) and on SE side by a slight rise. The break in the SW wall of the enclosure opens into this partitioned quadrant. A rath (SL040-034----) lies c. 100m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In the SW quadrant of Carrowkeel enclosure (SL040-033001-). It may represent a house site but it could just be partitioning of the interior. The break at the S end of the SW wall opens into the partitioned quadrant.

source_data.original_text:
In a wetland area, c. 5m E of a stream. One of a cluster of six sites (SL040-030002-; SL040-030003-; SL040-031003-; SL040-230001-; SL040-230002-) found during monitoring of the realignment of the N4 road from Hollybrook Estate to Castlebaldwin in the Summer of 1998 (Desmond 1998, 12). A low kidney-shaped mound (6m N-S; 10m E-W; H 0.5m) of stones in charcoal blackened soil, overlain with sod and a thin layer of peat and topsoil. Following recording the site was covered with geo-textile, peat and topsoil and remains undisturbed. There is a burnt spread (SL040-031003-) immediately to S and a holy well (SL040-031----) c. 30m to W. (Desmond 2000, 183-4)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In undulating rocky pasture, straddling a narrow ridge. A circular raised area (diam. 24m) defined by an earthen bank (int. H 0.4m; ext. H 1.1m) NW-NNE and elsewhere by a scarp. An external fosse (D 0.7m) is evident NW-NE. The rath is closely surrounded on the N, E and S sides by relict drystone field walls; the N field wall lies along the outer edge of the fosse, the E field wall skirts the base of the scarp while the S field wall is 1m from the base of the scarp. The interior is under pasture and clear of overgrowth. In the interior a central strip (Wth 4m) which runs N-S is level while on either side of it the ground slopes down moderately to E and W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

The wall of an adjacent graveyard (SL028-013----) overlies the fosse SW-WNW. A moated site (SL028-016001-) lies c. 250m to E in the adjacent townland of Carrowmore.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, at the base of a ridge. A clear spring rises at the base of the ridge and flows S. Modern holy plaques and statues indicate that this well is still visited. A recently built stone wall encloses it. In 1836 it was noted that the Patron day was 25th July and that 'stations' were still performed at it (OSL, 245). In 1942-4 a local tradition was recorded that the well was moved by a local friar from a site beside Geevagh Creamery, c. 3.5km to SE, to its present location after the landowner objected to pilgrims visiting it (ITA). A tree now grows adjacent to the well.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On a tract of level pasture on the lower W-facing slopes of a hill-range along the boundary between counties Sligo and Leitrim. The tomb is in an oval mound (21m E-W; max. 13.5m N-S; H 0.75m.). A fence runs into the N side of the mound from E and W. The remains of a gallery are preceded at the E by the S arm of an open court (L 6m), represented by four stones, which joins two stones of a flat facade. A single courtstone flanking the gallery entrance survives on the opposite side. Two jambs form the entrance to the gallery. A stone jammed between them is not in situ. The N side of the gallery is represented by an irregular line of stones extending for 5.5m to the W. Three stones at the opposite side of the gallery show that it extended at least 1m further in the same direction. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 59, no. 94)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In undulating wet pasture, immediately N of Geevagh village. Traces of a relict field system, underlying the modern field system, are spread over a rectangular area c. 300m x c. 250m which is characterised by rock outcrops and bushes. In the NW quadrant is a roughly pentagonal field (c. 50m N-S; 55m E-W) defined on its W side by an earth and stone field boundary and elsewhere by a disused sod-covered limestone rubble wall (H 0.7-1.2m). Adjoining the NE side of this field is a roughly rectangular field (20m N-S; 20m E-W) defined by an earth and stone bank (H 0.3-0.6m). Two linear earth and stone banks (L c. 50m; H 0.5m) lie c. 150m to SSE. Traces of other field boundaries, visible in an aerial photograph (GSIAP, G 273-2), are not visible at ground level.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified 'Sweathouse'. In wet upland pasture, on an E-facing slope overlooking the Camoge River 20m to S. It is not marked on the 1838 edition of the OS 6-inch map. A D-shaped depression (1.5m NE-SW; 1.2m NW-SE; D 0.8m), covered with overgrowth, with an entrance (Wth 0.4m; L 0.75m) on the straight SE side. The sides of the depression are lined with rough courses of unmortared limestone rubble and the base is muddy and covered with limestone rubble. According to local information, the sweathouse originally had a domed stone roof. This is probably post-1700 AD in date.

source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified as 'Enclosure' and 'Settlement Deserted' respectively. It is in wet elevated pasture, on a slight NE-facing slope with a sharp natural break of slope immediately to the N. A deserted settlement of six rectangular stone structures, all aligned NE-SW, is delimited to the W and N by a NE-SW earth and stone bank (H 1.1m) and on E side by a drain (D 0.4m). The smallest structure measures 3.2m x 3.8m while the largest measures 15.9m x 2.8m, the latter being divided into three rooms by crosswalls. Two of the structures have no obvious entrances, and two additional structures are c. 60m SW of the main complex. These structures are all shown on the 1st edition OS 6-inch map (1837) and are probably of 18th or 19th century date.

Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, on a SE-facing slope. A human burial was discovered in 1959 during works at 'Slagfield' quarry and was investigated by Rynne (1960-61, 71-3), though some disturbance to the burial had occurred prior to his investigation. A roughly cut grave (L 2m; Wth 1m; D 1m; long axis E-W) contained the skeleton of a young adult. Investigation of the grave-fill revealed 'some animal bones, two small potsherds, a small blue glass bead and three pieces of bottle glass' all possibly thrown accidentally into the grave with the fill (ibid., 71). The potsherds were dated to the fourteenth or fifteenth centuries and indicate that the burial could not be earlier than this. Analysis of the skeleton indicated a chronic tuberculous condition.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On rolling pasture and c. 100m NNE of a wedge tomb (SL035-063----) and c. 10m S of the site of an unclassified megalithic tomb (SL035-061----). A U-shaped court (L at least 5.5m; Wth c. 7.5m) at the SSE leads to a gallery (L 9m). Three stones remain of the more easterly arm of the court and five of the opposite arm. Two jambs mark the entrance to the gallery which is divided by three other pairs of jambs into four chambers. There is a sillstone between the jambs separating the second and third chamber. The gallery sides are quite well-preserved and the backstone is in place. The tomb is in a poorly preserved long mound (L c. 33m). About 2m outside the E arm of the court there is a kerbstone and another 1.5m outside the W arm. Seven probable kerbstones are exposed along the northern half of the W side of the mound. The backstone and southern sidestone of what appears to be a small lateral subsidiary chamber stand at the W side of the mound almost 5m beyond the back of the gallery. A field fence extends along both arms of the court, the E side of the gallery and from the gallery backstone northwards along the mound. There is a small quarry to the E of this fence behind the gallery. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 66-7, no. 106)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Near the crest of a low ridge in rolling pasture. Part of a WSW-facing gallery (L c. 3m; Wth 1.2m) and the remains of outer-walling and a facade survive here. Two orthostats are visible on the S side of the gallery. Opposite the western of these there is another orthostat and to the E of this two corbels rising above fill continue the line of the gallery side. Just beyond these there is a partly concealed stone which may also be a corbel. There are five outer-wall stones to the S of the gallery, two of them together at the W and three alongside at the E. The N side of the outer-walling is represented by a single stone. Two facade stones adjoin the W end of the outer-wall at the S. Two roofstones cover the surviving length of gallery. A third roofstone which lay to the E of these and also the northern half of the façade have been lost since the later half of the 19th century (Wood-Martin 1883-4, 453-4; 1888, 172-4). A stone protruding from a fence crossing the NW corner of the structure and another alongside it may be displaced facade stones. A stone at the E end of the structure could indicate the back of the outer wall but is not definitely in situ. Traces of a mound, not more than 0.5m high, are visible along the S side of the monument. A court tomb (SL035-062----) is c. 100m to NNE and the site of an unclassified megalithic tomb (SL035-061----) is c. 150m to NNE. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 65-6, no. 105)

source_data.original_text:
This destroyed monument stood on rocky pasture just over 200m W of a court tomb (SL035-079----). The tomb is marked on the 1838 OS 6-inch map but had been demolished when Wood-Martin (1883-4, 458-60, no. 20; 1888, 180-82, no. 2) visited the area later in the same century. He was informed that this tomb was similar in plan to the court tomb (SL035-079----) 200m to E. Some large stones visible in a fence at the site in 1956 may have originally formed part of the monument (Ó Nualláin 1989, 68, no. 109). An account in 1836, which seems to refer to this tomb, describes it as '... now eighteen or twenty feet [c. 6m] long, and about five feet [c. 1.5m] broad, having flags fixed around it' and claims that it had been opened some years earlier when human bones were reportedly found in it (OSL, 171-4). The report also records a claim that a 'golden breast plate' was found either in the tomb or nearby. The indications are that this destroyed monument was a court tomb.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On rocky pasture commanding an extensive outlook to the S. This court tomb is a National Monument in state ownership (no. 465). A U-shaped open court (L c. 7m) at the NNE leads to a well-preserved gallery (L 13m; Wth 1.5-2.9m) of four chambers. There are some poorly defined traces of mound around the structure. The two entrance jambs of the gallery function as courtstones and, in addition, one orthostat of the more westerly arm of the court survives and two remain on the other side. At the outer end of this side of the court there is a low moss-covered courtstone and just beyond and at right angles to it another low stone, apparently part of the tomb facade. A stone, split in two, and set more or less along the main axis of the structure stands in the gallery entrance and divides it in two. Another stone at right angles to the last closes the eastern half of the entrance gap. The divisions between the first three chambers are marked by single jambs, in each case at the W. The third and fourth chambers are separated by a sillstone. The chamber sidestones and the backstone of the gallery survive intact. There are three blocks of stone of uncertain origin between 1m and 9m beyond the back of the gallery. A stone wall extends NE-SW across the W arm of the court. A large limestone block on top of a smaller stone lies c. 30m to SW and is known locally as the 'Rocking stone'. An unclassified megalithic tomb (SL035-078----) lies c. 200m to W. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 68-9, no. 110)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a slight E-facing slope. A triangular slightly raised area (max. Wth 8.3m; max. L 11.5m) defined by an earthen bank with a stone at each corner. The S and NW sides are defined by an earthen bank (H 0.3m and 0.4m respectively) while the NE side is defined by a scarp (H 0.35m). The SW and SE corners are marked by limestone glacial erratics (1.2m x 1.9m x 1.65m and 1.75m x 2.2m x 1.2m), that at SW standing on a natural limestone pedestal (H 0.45m). These stones are probably natural depositions. The N corner is marked by a prostrate limestone pillar (L 3.1m; Wth 1.4m; T 0.8m), which may have originally been upright, and which projects into the interior. There is an upright slab (H 1m; 0.8m x 1.6m) at the SW end of the S side. There is a gap (Wth 1m) in the bank at SW. The interior is level and clear of overgrowth and slightly raised to compensate for the hillslope. Noted by Wood-Martin (1883-4, 456) as 'a very peculiar structure'. Though named 'Giant's Grave' on the 1914 OS 6-inch map, this is not a megalithic tomb.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In elevated pasture, on the summit of a ridge with excellent views in all directions. A circular raised area (diam. 7.4m) defined by an earthen bank (int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.5m). Traces of a low external bank (Wth 1.5m; H 0.25m) around the barrow, noted during a previous site inspection in 1993 (SMR (1989) file), are no longer visible.

source_data.original_text:
According to Wood-Martin (1883-4; 1888), this feature was destroyed about the year 1817. The father of his informant had been engaged in its demolition. Wood-Martin (1883-4, 451, no. 8; 1888, 172, no. 8) states: 'It appears to have been oblong in form; it lay right in the centre of the present road, and most of the slabs of which it was composed are now in the fences on either side'. In 1836 it was recorded as 'Gliopach Mór' (OSL, 242). There is a possibility that the feature referred to was a megalithic tomb. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 99, no. 25)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on a roughly oval ,SW-facing terrace on the W slope of a low N-S ridge, in an area of sharply undulating terrain broken by limestone outcropping. At the SW–W edge of the terrace, the slope drops into a relatively narrow, natural NNW-SSE depression, on the opposite side of which ground rises again to another broad ridge.
A previous inspection in 1993 found that the cashel was densely engulfed in overgrowth which impeded examination (Egan et al. 2005, 148, no. 820). Since then, it has been largely cleared of scrub.
It consists of a roughly oval area (27m NW–SE; 19.5m NE–SW), which conforms to the natural shape of the terrace. The perimeter at NE–SE is defined by an inward-facing scarp or slope (H 1.7m; Wth slope c. 4m), roughly defined on its upper edge, which coincides with the level ridge top, by stones, boulders and tree stumps. At SW–W the perimeter is bordered by a fall of ground, and is partly defined by limestone outcropping. Remnants of an original enclosing wall can still be traced at the NNW and SE edges of the terrace: At NNW a short length (L 5m) of wall footings (Wth 1.55m) remains in situ, and on the SE arc a low moss-covered stony rise (Wth c. 1.4m) is evident. 
The interior slopes down from NE to SW, mirroring the natural slope of the terrace, levelling out in the S third of the enclosure. The ground surface is rough and uneven, broken by outcropping and strewn with loose stones, with small clumps of brambles, blackthorn and hawthorn scrub in parts. 

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of revised upload: 10 February 2020

source_data.original_text:
In a small valley, on pasture broken by limestone outcrops. A gallery (L 5.2m; Wth c. 1m) is segmented by jambs into two chambers. The entrance, at the NE, is marked by a pair of jambs but no evidence for a court survives. Single stones form the sides of the chambers and the rear of the gallery. A roofstone, apparently broken, covers part of the inner chamber. A low field bank extends N-S across the front of the gallery. There is a low mound (14m NW-SE; 9m NE-SW) around the sides and back of the gallery. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 77-8, no. 123)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rocky gorse-covered pasture, on level ground at the base of, and built against a 10m high W-facing cliff. The ground slopes down gently to the W. The remains of a rectangular structure (8.55m N-S; 2.4m E-W) with earth and stone walls (int. H 0.6m; ext. H 0.4m) on the S, W and N sides; the E side is formed by the cliff. The internal face of each wall is revetted with limestone slabs. The entrance (Wth 1m) is in the W wall, off-centre to S, revetted on both sides with courses of unmortared rubble limestone. The interior is slightly sunken. Though named 'Giant's Grave' on the 1914 OS 6-inch map, this is not a megalithic tomb but rather, as suggested by Ó Nualláin (1989, 99, no. 28), the foundations of a building. It was noted by Wood-Martin (1883-4, 456).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In rocky pasture, on the summit and towards the N end of a steep-sided ridge. A circular area (diam. 18m) defined by a moss-covered collapsed stone wall (int. H 0.65m; ext. H 0.65m). Remnants of internal and external facing of limestone blocks, laid in rough courses with rubble limestone fill, were noted NW-NE. The interior, which is divided by a N-S drystone wall to W of centre, is undulating and densely covered with overgrowth on the W side of the dividing wall. This cashel is indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map, perhaps mistakenly, as a much larger enclosure (diam. c. 50m).

source_data.original_text:
On a rocky NE-facing slope, in a natural rock outcrop at the base of a near vertical cliff. Two large horizontal slabs of rock, the lower of which projects 0.6m out from under the upper on the NE side. The lower slab is level and has a small roughly D-shaped round-bottomed depression (0.33m by 0.37m; D 0.1m), that appears to be natural, on its upper surface. Water flows from between the two slabs into the depression via a short V-shaped channel (L 0.2m; Wth top 0.03m; D 0.02m) at the SW and exits through a small notch on the NE side. There is no evidence to indicate recent holy use.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In gently undulating pasture, on a level area with a steep natural break of slope to the S. The lintelled entrance (Wth 0.45m; H 0.2m) to the souterrain is located at the base of the S side of a drystone field boundary wall and is largely blocked by earth and stone making access impossible. According to local information, a passage extends N for 12m from the entrance to another access point which is now blocked and evident as a depression (1m x 1m; D 0.3m). Burnt and unburnt animal bones were noted in spoil around the depression during a previous inspection in 1993 (SMR (1989) file). The area between both entrances is disturbed by badger sets. A hut site (SL041-053----) lies c. 65m to NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In a paddock, 50m NW of a derelict farmhouse. Named 'Tobercaleen' on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. An oval depression (2m N-S; 2.6m E-W) defined SE-NE by earth and rock (int. H 1.2m) and NE-SE by a muddy gently sloping ramp to the exterior. The base of the well is of rock and mud and holds 0.4m of water. Water is piped from it to water troughs nearby. According to local information, there are no cures associated with this well and no tradition of 'patterns' or pilgrimages. There is, however, a local tradition that it has moved from upslope to W to its present location. There is another holy well (SL041-046----) c. 200m to NW in Cloystuckera townland. Templecaleen church (SL041-048001-) is c. 90m to S. Another church (SL041-049----) lies 150m to S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In wet pasture, on a slight E-facing slope. Fragmentary remains of a rectangular structure (int. 11.5m E-W; 3.8m N-S) with walls (T 0.8m) of uncoursed mortared sandstone. The external corners have sandstone quoins, the best of which are at the SW corner where the lowest quoin rests on a large boulder (H 0.6m). There is a break in the N wall (L 2.6m) and sections (L c. 2m) of the E and W walls are reduced to 1m in height, possibly indicating the position of window opes. This structure is named 'Templecaleen' on the 1838 OS 6-inch map, but the name is transferred on the 1914 OS 6-inch map to an adjacent church site (SL041-048001-) 50m to the N. There is a holy well (SL041-047----) 150m to the N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

Not  listed in either the SMR (1989) or RMP (1995). In rough pasture, on a steep N-facing slope overlooking a river 30m to N. A roughly circular roofless structure (diam. 1.2m) with a sunken interior (max. D 0.85m) lined with roughly coursed unmortared rubble limestone. The floor is level and strewn with rubble limestone. The entrance (Wth 1m) is on the N side and consists of two parallel earth and stone banks (H 0.4m; L 1m). At external ground level, the rim of the interior is defined by an earth and stone bank (ext. H 0.3m), possibly the remains of a collapsed roof. This is probably post-1700 AD in date.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

source_data.original_text:
In the NE corner of a modern subrectangular pasture field, located at the NW edge of a low flat-topped ridge, in an area of sharply undulating terrain broken by limestone outcropping.
This greatly ruined enclosure, possibly a cashel, is not shown on the 1838 and 1914 OS 6-inch maps. It consists of a subcircular area defined at NW–SSE by levelled remnants of a drystone wall. The original diameter is uncertain, possibly 35m. The surviving arc of enclosing wall is evident as a low, broadly slumped moss-covered stony rise (Wth c. 2m; int. H 0.1-0.2m; ext. H 0.4-0.45m). At NE–ESE the outer edge of the wall is incorporated into a N–S field fence/hedgerow which more or less respects the curve of the enclosure. The enclosing wall cannot be traced with certainty on the W arc; it may coincide with a break of slope, where there is a natural fall of ground. A farm track skirts the base of this slope at S–SW.
A later N–S field wall, now reduced to low, moss-covered wall footings (Wth 0.8-1m; H 0.1-0.2m), cuts through the W sector of the cashel. It appears to intersect with a perpendicular wall, also ruined, which extending to E through the SE quadrant of the cashel. Surface spreads of loose stones to E of the N–S wall appear to result from efforts to levelling it. In the NE quadrant another concentration of stones, c. 5m across, is focused on a slightly sunken feature, obscured by overgrowth. 

Notified to NMS by Brain Doyle. 

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 13 March 2020

source_data.original_text:
In pasture on the outskirts of Geevagh village, located in an area of lowlying, damp rush-grown pasture, overlooked to NE by a high ridge.
This possible enclosure is not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps. It is evident in aerial imagery. 
It is evident at ground level as a slightly raised subcircular flat-topped area or platform (21m E−W; 24m N−S) defined by a slight scarp (H 0.3-0.4m). The scarp has a hint of a raised internal rim at NW and E. There are poorly defined low areas or gaps in the scarp at W E and NE. A slight depression (Wth 1.6m) can be traced outside the scarp on the W arc. The remains are very low profile.
The nature of this possible enclosure is uncertain: According to local information, it was created in the mid 1990’s when earth was spread here to level up a hollow.

Attached image: SL035-124---- viewed from W

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 5 November 2020

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on the top of a narrow NWW−SSE by a high ridge, with steeply sloping sides. There are excellent views: to W over a broad valley of boggy ground; to N−NE over gently undulating hilly terrain.
This structure/possible enclosure is not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps. It is evident as a D-shaped raised area (18m NE-SW; 10-11m NW−SE) defined on the NW curving side by a low stone and earth bank, and bordered on the straight side at SE by a NE−SW field ditch and field fence. The remains appear to represents the NW half of an originally circular enclosure/structure.
The bank (Wth c. 4m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.8m) is best preserved at SW−W, lower and somewhat degraded at N. It retains a low internal lip, and has a broadly slumped slope on its external face. Remnants of drystone facing protrude in parts from the top and external slope. The low inner face of the bank slumps seamlessly into a shallow concave interior. 
The straight side at SE is created by a field ditch (Wth c. 0.8m), which cuts through the enclosure. The field ditch is bordered on its SE side by a field bank (Wth 1-1.2m; H c. 1m), which serves as the townland boundary. The portion of the enclosure which lies to SE of the field bank appears to have been levelled, but it is difficult to be certain that no remains exist here because this area is engulfed in a dense thicket of blackthorn and brambles. 
This appears to have been a relatively small, circular enclosure or structure with a stone-faced perimeter bank and a concave interior, and no evidence of an external fosse. Its exact function/nature is uncertain. It might be some form of barrow, however, the stone facing of the bank is unusual. It must pre-date the construction of the current field bank/townland boundary. It is possible that it is of the early modern era: According to local information, in the past structures/reservoirs were built on these ridge tops to hold water.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 11 November 2020

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on a terrace on a high, limestone ridge, overlooked to the N by a higher ridge. Approximately 20m to N of the enclosure, there is a precipitous drop into a deep, narrow pass which intervenes between the two ridges. Immediately to E of the enclosure the ground rises to a higher terrace; to S and W ground falls away to lower terraces.
Roughly oval area (26m N−S; 22m E−W) enclosed by a low, moss-covered stone bank (Wth 1.6m; H 0.3-0.4m). The stone bank is poorly preserved and gapped on the W arc; the largest breaks are at S (Wth 6m) and N (Wth 4m). On the E arc the perimeter of the enclosure is cut into rising ground to form an inward-facing sod-covered scarp (H 0.7m), which has a low external lip (Wth 0.8m; ext. H 0.2m) at NE. The interior is not raised. It is bisected to E of centre by a field wall/property fence on a NNW-SSE axis. 
There is a rath (SL035-010----) 150m to W.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 11 November 2020

A motte and bailey (SL028-012----) lie c. 250m to W in the adjacent townland of Carrownagilty.

In elevated rocky pasture, on a slight SW-facing slope. An oval slightly raised area (24m N-S; 19m E-W) enclosed by a stone wall (int. H 0.3m; ext. H 1.6m) consisting of limestone rubble and some larger limestone boulders. The interior is rocky and undulating and slopes gently down to SW. There is a souterrain (SL028-021002-) in the SE quadrant. A roughly circular annexe (diam. 24m) (SL028-021003-) is conjoined to the cashel at SW. It is defined by a degraded stone wall (int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.5m) which joins the cashel wall at S and SW. The interior of the annexe is level and strewn with moss-covered rocks.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified as 'Enclosure' and 'Settlement Deserted' respectively. It is in wet elevated pasture, on a slight NE-facing slope with a sharp natural break of slope immediately to the N. A deserted settlement of six rectangular stone structures, all aligned NE-SW, is delimited to the W and N by a NE-SW earth and stone bank (H 1.1m) and on E side by a drain (D 0.4m). The smallest structure measures 3.2m x 3.8m while the largest measures 15.9m x 2.8m, the latter being divided into three rooms by crosswalls. Two of the structures have no obvious entrances, and two additional structures are c. 60m SW of the main complex. These structures are all shown on the 1st edition OS 6-inch map (1837) and are probably of 18th or 19th century date. This structure (ext. dims 10/6m NE-SW; 5.1m NW-SE; int. dims 8.5m NE-SW; 3.5m NW-SE) has block limestone walls (T 1.05m; max. H 1.2m) with entrances on the on the NW (Wth 0.95m) and SE (Wth 0.6m) long walls and it may have a separate room (int. dims 3.2m x 2.2m) at the SW end.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on top of a rise with commanding views of the surrounding countryside and within an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL035-052004-). The roofless ruin of a rectangular church (ext. 17.5m E-W; 7.6m N-S) built of uncoursed limestone rubble bonded in a lime mortar. The walls have a slight batter and rest on a foundation plinth. No gables are evident and both end-walls stand to the same height as the side-walls. The interior is divided into two compartments by a cross-wall. At the E end (int. 10.95m E-W; 5.5m N-S) is the church, while at the W end is a smaller vaulted room (int. 5.5m N-S; 3.65m E-W). The entrance doorway is in the N wall, at the NW corner of the church; its surround has a cusped pointed arch with a chamfer, but its jambs are missing. The church is lit by three single-light windows, one each in the N, E and S walls. The light of the E window has an ogee-arch whilst the S window has a rounded arch. The lintelled doorway into the vaulted room is near the S end of its E wall. The room is covered by a rounded wicker-centred vault, and lit by a single-light window in its N and S walls. On the exterior of the S wall and just E of the window lighting the room, is a feature consisting of two close-set corbels arranged in the manner of a 'box machicolation' but which could be the base of a latrine chute (M. A. Timoney 2002b, 57). Lying on the ground outside the SW corner of the building is a collection of loose stones including one of the jambstones from the entrance doorway. The ruin is that of the late medieval parish church of Shancough. The church lies off-centre to the NW within a rectangular enclosure (65m NW-SE; 40m NE-SW) (SL035-052003-). This enclosure is defined by an earth and stone bank (int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.85m) on the NW and SE sides and part of the NE side; elsewhere the remains of the bank are topped by a drystone wall. The NW, NE and SE sides are straight but the SW side kinks inwards at the W corner. There are numerous small breaks (Wth 0.8m to 1.1m) in the bank. Traces of internal and external revetment of limestone slabs are evident, especially on the NW and NE sides. The undulating interior is divided roughly in half by a NNE-SSW drystone wall incorporating the E gable of the church. A 'furnace bottom' was noted in this wall during a previous site inspection in 1993 (SMR (1989) file). This area may have functioned as a graveyard though no graveyard is named on the OS 6-inch maps and there is no evidence of burials. A souterrain (SL035-052002-) is located 31.5m to NNE of the church and another (SL035-052005-) is 50m to WNW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Straddling the broad summit of a high rise. A roughly rectangular area (115m NW-SE; 71m NE-SW) defined by an earth and stone scarp (H 1.7m) on the SE and SW sides and by the remains of a bank topped by a drystone wall on the NW side. The NE side is defined by a steep natural slope. Traces of an external stone revetment are evident in places along the scarp on the SW side where three to four courses of limestone rubble-walling are evident. On the NW side three limestone slabs (H c. 1m; Wth c. 1.2m; T c. 0.03m) also indicate the remains of the revetment. The interior is undulating. The late medieval parish church of Shancough (SL035-052001-) lies roughly within the centre of the interior and is surrounded by a rectangular enclosure (SL035-052003-) which occupies most of the S half of the enclosure. There are two souterrains, one (SL035-052005-) in the NW quadrant and the other (SL035-052002-) in the NE quadrant. According to Gwynn and Hadcock (1970, 404), 'St. Patrick ordained Ailbe an archpresbyter in Senchua'.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on a gentle N-facing slope; in Foyoges graveyard (SL035-067002-). An E-W line of loose stones in the W half of this small graveyard is the only evident trace of the church indicated as a rectangular structure (c. 25m NW-SE; c. 7.5m NE-SW) on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. Described in an inquisition of James I, dated 1619-20, as 'a ruinous cell or chapel called Templenefahoge' (Clyne 2010, 72), the church was referred to in 1836 as 'an old church (ruins) and burial for children and strangers called Killamy' (OSL, 237). There are no visible remains of the 'Bishop's Grave' (SL035-067004-) indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map c. 30m to the NE of the church though there are praying stones (SL035-067005-) at this location. There is a souterrain (SL035-067003-) c. 20m to NW .

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

M. Clyne, The rental of Holy Trinty abbey, Lough Cé. In T. Finan (ed.), 'Medieval Lough Cé. History, Archaeology and Landscape'. (Dublin, 2010), 67-96.

Revised by: Paul Walsh

Date of revision: 9 September 2010

source_data.original_text:
A rectangular area (20m NW-SE; 14m SW-NE) enclosed by a stone wall (H 1m) with a rectangular projection to the NW. Traces of a church (SL035-067001-) are evident in the W half. There is a piered entrance gate in the centre of the NE wall. The interior slopes gently down from the NE. There are a number of low uninscribed grave-markers as well as five 20th-century headstones. Two well-shaped grave-markers (H c. 0.32m; Wth 0.3m) occur in the W half, both roughly inscribed with plain crosses (H 0.32m). The graveyard is still in use. There is a souterrain (SL035-067003-) c. 20m to NW. The graveyard was referred to in 1836 as a 'burial for children and strangers called Killamy' (OSL, 237). There are no visible remains of the 'Bishop's Grave' (SL035-06704-) indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map c. 30m NE of the graveyard though there are praying stones (SL035-067005-) at this location.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In mountain bog, on a SW-facing slope and 8m SW of a 'St Elba's Grave' (SL035-073002-). A U-shaped well (max. L 1.7m NE-SW; max. Wth 0.5m NW-SE; max. H 1.3m from the base to the roof) with walls of roughly coursed limestone rubble (T 0.4m) roofed with limestone flags. The roof slopes gently down from the front to the rear. The opening into the well (Wth 0.7m; H 0.8m) faces SW. The base of the well is stone-lined and holds water. It was recorded in 1836 that the well was named after Saint Eilibh, a sister saint of Lasair (OSL, 239). In 1942-4 it was recorded as being named after Saint Ailbe and that it was visited by persons suffering from any diseases (but particularly mental diseases) from 15th August to 8th September though it was then only infrequently visited (ITA). There is a penitential station (SL035-073003-) c. 10m to E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In mountain bog, on a SW-facing slope and 8m NE of 'Toberelba', a holy well (SL035-073001-). 'St Elba's Grave' consists of three elements: a flat slab, an upright slab and a modern cross. The flat uninscribed rectangular limestone slab (L 3m; Wth 1m; T 0.3m; long axis NE-SW) is obscured along its edges by peat and moss. At the NE end of this slab is an upright rectangular limestone slab (Wth 0.46m; H 0.85m; T 0.15m) cemented to the SW side of the plinth on which the modern cross stands. The slab has been shaped, but not dressed, to give angular corners and is inscribed 'I H S' (the 'S' being reversed). Cemented to the top of this slab, on the same alignment, is a roughly square limestone flag (Wth 0.5m; H 0.4m; T 0.08m). To the NE of the flat slab is a modern granite cross (inscribed 'A M D C' across the arms facing SW) on a plinth of three tiers (base 2.05m square; H 2.9m). On the lowest tier (H 1.1m) are tokens, including some euro coins in a tin, indicating recent pilgrim visits. According to tradition, the large flat stone is the grave of Saint Aillbe and people suffering from illness who sleep soundly overnight on the stone are cured of their ailments (ITA). There is a penitential station (SL035-073003-) 1.6m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In mountain bog, on a SW-facing slope and 1.6m to SE of 'St Elba's Grave' (SL035-073002-). The 'station' house is a partially collapsed roofless roughly rectangular structure (int. dims. 2.9m NE-SW; 2m NW-SE) with walls of roughly coursed drystone rubble limestone (T 0.5m; max. H 2m). The entrance (Wth 1m) is at the NW end of the NE wall with a limestone slab (Wth 1.15m; H 0.9m; T 0.15m) that was used to block it still leaning against the NW side. The SW wall (T 1.3m) is thicker than the other walls and extends beyond the NW and SE corners of the structure by 0.4-0.65m. It also bulges halfway along its length suggesting a previous collapse and repair. 'Toberelba' holy well (SL035-073001-) is c. 10m to W.

source_data.original_text:
On sloping ground in thin-soiled pasture with an outlook to the S. The tomb stands in a subrectangular mound (19.5m N-S; 12.5m E-W) (SL035-097002-). Two possible kerbstones are exposed inside the edge of the mound at the SE and another at the NW. The tomb, which faces N, consists of the scant remains of a court represented by an entrance jamb to the E and alongside it a courtstone leading to a gallery (L 9m; Wth 2m) divided into a very short antechamber and three main chambers. A transeptal chamber opens off each side of the first main chamber and just over 2m beyond the gallery a subsidiary chamber opens to the E. A jamb just 0.4m behind the eastern entrance jamb separates the antechamber from the first main chamber. Two stones form each side of this chamber and gaps between them allow entry to the transeptal chambers, the western formed by two stones on each side and a backstone and the eastern represented by opposed stones at its inner end and a backstone. Two jambs, the eastern possibly partly displaced, separate the first main chamber from the second each side of which is formed by two stones. A long sill, flanked at either side by jambs, separates the last from the rear chamber. The W side of this chamber is formed by two stones, only the innermost orthostat survives on the E side, and it is closed by a backstone. The subsidiary chamber is represented by a backstone and two adjoining sidestones. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 69-70, no. 111)
Two previously recorded orthostats were noted in 2020: one at the N end of the W wall of the middle chamber of the gallery; the other at the W end of the N wall of the E transeptal chamber (pers. comm.  Sam Moore).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

See linked document with details from Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume V. County Sligo. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1989)
