source_data.original_text:
In rocky elevated pasture, on a slight NE-facing slope, overlooked by higher ground on the W side. A roughly circular area (58m N-S; 53m E-W) defined by a partially collapsed stone wall (int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.6m; Wth top 1.05m; Wth base 1.15m) NNW-NW and by a drystone field boundary elsewhere. The roughly coursed limestone wall is well preserved SE-SW with vertical sides and a flat top. Large rectangular slabs (c. L 1.5m; Wth 1.15m; T 0.3m) are visible towards the base of the wall in places along this section. Remains of a facing of stone slabs (max. Wth 1.8m; max. H 1.05m) is evident along the external base of the wall SW-NW. The entrance (Wth 2.1m) is at WSW and is defined on either side by a large boulder (Wth 1m; H 0.6m). The interior is undulating with some small limestone outcrops, slopes slightly down to NE and is dry and clear of overgrowth. In the S half of the interior is a slightly raised trapezoidal area (24.4m NW-SE; 24m NE-SW) (SL041-020002-) defined by a limestone rubble wall (int. H 0.55m; ext. H 0.85m) on the W, N and E sides and by the cashel wall on the S side. There are no visible remains of the 'furnace bottom' in the centre of the N wall of the trapezoidal area which was recorded during a previous site inspection in 1993 (SMR (1989) file). A D-shaped annexe (dims. 14m NE-SW) (SL041-020004-), with a straight SW side (L 11m), defined by a sod-covered stone wall (int. H 0.4; ext. H 0.45), is attached to the external side of the cashel wall at NE. It has a possible entrance at W at is junction with the cashel wall. A relict field boundary wall abuts the external face of the cashel wall at SSW. There is a souterrain (SL041-020003-) 30m to N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

On a gentle S-facing slope, c. 100m N of Lough Skean. There are no visible remains of this hut site. It was described during a previous site inspection in 1993 (SMR (1989) file) as an oval structure (5.3m N-S) with sod-covered limestone slab walls (T 1.1m; int. H 1.25m; ext. H 1.3m). The walls were lower on the W side forming an entrance (Wth 0.4m). The interior was scooped out and the E side was covered with overgrowth. A quarry lies immediately to S. Though named 'Giant's Grave' on the 1914 OS 6-inch map, the remains were not those of a megalithic tomb.

source_data.original_text:
In gently sloping rocky pasture. A ruined gallery (L 4.5m; Wth 2.2m) is aligned NE-SW. A prostrate stone at the NE end is a fallen backstone (Wood-Martin 1883-4, 448-9, no. 2; 1888, 169, no. 2). Three orthostats are in place at the more northerly side. Two are alongside to the W and are separated by a gap 1.3m wide from the third which adjoins the prostrate backstone. One orthostat is in place at the NE end of the other side of the gallery. Alongside to the W there is another orthostat that has fallen outwards and is now almost prostrate. The outer end of the last supports a stone, possibly a displaced orthostat (ibid.). A natural oval hillock (SL041-034002-) at the edge of the field c. 100m to SE is possibly what Wood-Martin (1883-4, 449) referred to as a 'sepulchral mound on the summit of a slight rise almost obliterated by tillage'. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 78, no. 124)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

On a SE-facing slope; in a graveyard , just N of an early 19th-century C of I church, in the graveyard (SL041-038002-). Depicted on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as a ruined rectangular structure (c. 14m NW-SE; 8m NE-SW) but only the E corner is shown on the 1914 OS 6-inch map. The elongated nettle-covered mound just S of the centre of the graveyard is the McConmee burial vault. This was probably originally built within the church ruin (O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 246) but there is no evident trace of the church. According to tradition, this was the 'ruins of an old church called Teampull Chill 'ac a Treanuigh, supposed to have been built by St. Macatrany' (OSL, 237), but it is as likely to have been the medieval parish church of Kilmactrany.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In a field to the N of Kilmactranny graveyard (SL041-038002-). Set into the top of a large conglomerate erratic (H 1.3m) is a plain Latin cross with a moulded base (H 1.25m; T c. 0.15m). The N face of the cross is carved with an inscription in false relief, now very weathered and, in parts, almost illegible. The monogram IHS is carved on the head and the remnants of a cross rising from the cross-bar of the H can be traced. The inscription runs across the full length of the arms (3 lines) with the remainder on the shaft: PRAY FOR THE SO/VLE OF [E?]DMOND/ET OWENE MDE[R?]/MOE/[R?][O?][E?]/WHO/EREC/TED/THIS/MONV/MENT/168[6?]. The last digit of the date is unclear though it might possibly be a '0' as noted by J. C. MacDonagh (d. 1960) who gives the following: 'Pray for the soul of Edmond et Owen Mc Dermot Roe … this stone … 1680' (n.d. vol. 18, 19). There is a break in the cross which has been repaired by two iron bands and MacDonagh (ibid.) records the story that it had been accidentally broken by a local landowner who, on the death of his cattle, had a blacksmith repair it. A second 17th-century cross (SL041-038007-) was noted in the adjoining graveyard (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney) but it cannot now be seen. (Crawford 1907, 215; King 1985, 31).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In level pasture. The church, which is indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map as a rectangular structure (c. 10m E-W; c. 5m N-S), is reduced to a scatter of rubble covered by dense scrub overgrowth. According to local information, it was '20ft [6m] long and 14ft [4.2m] wide with a bit of a gable'. A displaced stone (L 1m; 0.2m x 0.2m), to the S of the church, is said to have been an altar stone. There is also a local tradition of an associated graveyard (SL041-048004-) but no visible remains of this are apparent. There is a holy well (SL041-047----) 90m to the N. The church is named 'Templecaleen', on the 1914 OS 6-inch map, but on the 1838 OS 6-inch map this name is given to a nearby site (SL041-049----), 50m to the S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, on the summit of a small drumlin on a slight E-facing slope. The W and S sides of the drumlin are covered with mature deciduous trees. An oval area (25m N-S; 29m E-W) defined by a low scarp (ext. H 0.4m) E-NNE. The scarp is topped by earth and stone field boundaries SSE-S and NNW-N. The steep natural slope of the drumlin breaks immediately outside the scarp S-NW. The interior slopes down to E and is under patchy grass. An internal division, described in the S half of the rath during a previous site inspection in 1993 (SMR (1989) file), has been levelled and only traces of it are now visible as a bank of stony soil (Wth 1.8m) enclosing an area c. 12m E-W and c. 8m N-S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified as 'Enclosure' and 'Settlement Deserted' respectively. It is in wet elevated pasture, on a slight NE-facing slope with a sharp natural break of slope immediately to the N. A deserted settlement of six rectangular stone structures, all aligned NE-SW, is delimited to the W and N by a NE-SW earth and stone bank (H 1.1m) and on E side by a drain (D 0.4m). The smallest structure measures 3.2m x 3.8m while the largest measures 15.9m x 2.8m, the latter being divided into three rooms by crosswalls. Two of the structures have no obvious entrances, and two additional structures are c. 60m SW of the main complex. These structures are all shown on the 1st edition OS 6-inch map (1837) and are probably of 18th or 19th century date. This structure (ext. dims c. 8m NW-SE; c. 5m NW-SE) defined by a grass-covered stone spread (max. H 0.4m) is c. 60m SW of the main complex.

Compiled by: Michael Moore

Date of upload: 31 January, 2017

source_data.original_text:
On the E shore of Lough Arrow, at the mouth of Loughbrick Bay. Inspection was difficult due to dense overgrowth. An oval area (c. 25m NE-SW; c. 30m NW-SE) defined S-NE by a stony bank, NE-E by a low stony rise (Wth 1.1m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.4m); elsewhere the enclosing element is obscured by overgrowth. The bank is most substantial (Wth 3.5m; int. H 0.55m; ext. H 1.1m) at S and WNW-NNE. From SW-W, adjacent to the lake, the bank is reduced to a low stony scarp (H 0.6m) topped by a slight internal stony rim. A broad fosse-like depression (Wth 8m; D 0.9m) outside the bank N-E, continuing E-ESE as an inward-facing scarp (H c. 0.9m), appears to be the result of relatively recent quarrying into the gently rising ground immediately to E and SE. A shallow depression (Wth c. 2m) is visible outside the bank at S. The level interior is bisected by a NE-SW field boundary wall NW of centre. The NW quadrant is firm and dry underfoot but much of the rest of the interior, especially the NE quadrant, is very damp and marked by a dense growth of irises and reeds.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In undulating pasture, on a slight NE-facing slope and c. 40m SW of the Feorish River. A raised circular area (20m N-S; 21m E-W) defined by two banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank (int. H 0.6m; ext. H 1.1m) of earth and stone is evident all round and is faced internally and externally in many places either with single upright limestone slabs (up to 1.2m square) or un-mortared limestone blocks in two to three courses. The inner bank is broken at SSE (Wth 0.9m), S (Wth 1m), WNW (Wth 0.8m) and NNW (Wth. 0.9m). The intervening fosse (Wth 4m at base) is evident NW-N and E-SE. The outer bank (int. H 0.65m; ext. H 0.45m) is earthen and evident only E-SE, at WNW and NNW-N. The interior is raised to compensate for the hillslope and is level dry and clear of overgrowth. There is a field clearance cairn (diam. 2m; H 0.3m) to E of the centre.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified as 'Sweathouse' and 'Sweathouse Site' respectively. In poorly drained pasture, on the E-facing slope of a low rise between two farmhouses. source_data.original_text:
In Lough Bo, c. 60m from the stony E shore. A roughly circular low-cairn crannog (20.75m N-S; 22.4m E-W; H 1.2m above the muddy lake-bed) consisting of a partially submerged plateau of small shattered stones (diam. c. 0.05m) with patches of sand in between them and a mix of dark brown mud and sand. The plateau has an even surface and slopes gradually down towards the edges where shattered stones are mixed with muddy marl. In the centre of the plateau, and rising above the water level, is a small oval loosely packed collection of stones, mainly sandstone. Some of the stones are flagstones but there are also subangular and rounded stones (dims. c. 0.45m x 0.4m). On the edge of the plateau at S is a U-shaped indentation in which is exposed an irregular double row of wooden posts leading out into the water. Horizontal timbers can also be seen under the stony surface material of the crannog. There is also a stony ridge (L 14m) leading from the centre of the oval stony area out into the water in a SE direction, possibly the remains of a jetty. The edges of the crannog slope gently under the water towards the W and open water, while there is a more abrupt edge at the E towards the shore.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classsified 'Sweathouse'. In a coniferous forest on the S side of a narrow valley at a meander of a stream. The remains of the sweathouse comprise a roughly circular domed structure (diam. top 2m; diam base 6m; H 2m) with a rectangular opening (Wth 0.45m; H 0.6m; D 0.4m) on the N side facing the stream. It is constructed of rubble limestone in rough courses, bonded with lime mortar. The splayed lintelled opening, which is flush with the external wall face, has jambs of roughly shaped limestone blocks. Internally there is a single rectangular cell (1.8m N-S; 1.7m E-W; H 1.6tm) with a corbelled roof and a level floor of packed earth. The internal surface of the wall, which is unrendered, is faced with shaped limestone rubble bonded with lime mortar. The sweathouse is overgrown with briars. It is marked on the 1914 edition of the OS 6-inch map but not on the 1838 edition, an indicator that it is probably 19th century in date.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Date of upload: 04 January 2012

source_data.original_text:
In pasture at the head of a narrow valley opening to the NW. This well-preserved tomb, known as 'The Labby', faces uphill to the SE. It consists of a chamber (L 2.1m; Wth 0.9m at the front, 1.5m at the rear) with sides and back of single stones. The front of the chamber is formed by two portal-stones (H 1.4m) and a doorstone 0.3m lower than them. The structure is covered by a large rectangular roofstone (L 4.8m; Wth 3.4m; T 1.6m) resting on all the orthostats save the more southerly sidestone. There is peat-growth on top of the roofstone. Two raths (SL034-153----; SL034-154----) lie c. 80m to SE. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 63, no. 102)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
At the northern end of a plateau in pasture. This is a circular cairn (diam. 25m; H c. 3m) now substantially grass-grown. There is an OS trigonometrical station on top of the cairn and a massive erratic has been incorporated in its northern end. The top of the cairn has been disturbed and there is a hole on the western side. A trench (L c. 10m; Wth c. 2m; D c. 1m) extends from the cairn edge at the SE towards the centre. There is a possibility that this could indicate the position of a collapsed or largely demolished passage and chamber. Wood-Martin (1883-4, 462) has recorded that the site was known as 'Seelewey'. He also recorded a claim that many years ago a Lady L. Tennison and others had cut a trench into the cairn discovering only some bones. Abuts circular enclosure (SL034-156----) to S. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 93)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In open water in Ballindoon bay, c. 100m from the N shore of Lough Arrow with a clear view of Carrowkeel and Kesh Corann to SW. The whole crannog is submerged, but the surface can be seen clearly under the water. An oval high-cairn crannog (19.1m N-S; 17.9m E-W; H 2.05m above the sand and gravel lake-bed) consisting of a firm surface of rounded to subangular stones (diam. 0.2-0.3m). Some larger stones (diam. c. 0.5m) at the SSE edge may be structural. There is a central oval cairn (4.1m N-S; 3m E-W) of stones (max. diam. 0.6m). The cairn is surrounded by a plateau consisting of small stones forming an even surface at a depth of 0.85m below the water. The plateau slopes gradually down to E, S and W while the drop to the N is more abrupt. The submerged edges appear to be distinct in material. Another crannog (SL034-239----) is situated to the NW. This crannog was mentioned as a 'shoal' NW of another crannog (possibly SL034-219001-) by Wood-Martin (1886, 246).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On upland pasture and commanding a view westwards across Lough Arrow to the Bricklieve Mountains. A gallery (L 6m; Wth 1.9m at the front) is represented by three sidestones at its front or WSW end, one on the N side and two on the S side, and by its backstone. Just 0.7m E of the two stones at the S side there is a set stone at right angles to the line of the gallery side which may have functioned as a buttress-stone though it is unusually large for that purpose. About 1m outside the northern sidestone there is an outer-wall stone and 1.3m to the E of it another. Between these and the line of the gallery side there are two more set stones. These seem to represent an intermediate line of walling between the gallery side and the outer-wall. There are a number of prostrate stones at the site. One of these adjoins the N end of the backstone and may be a fallen sidestone. Another at the NW corner of the structure might be a fallen facade-stone. A poorly preserved low mound at the site scarcely extends beyond the confines of the structure. Some uncertainty has been expressed about the classification of this tomb (Ó Nualláin 1989, 64-5, no. 104) but the available indications are that it is a wedge-tomb.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In Ballindoon Bay, in Lough Arrow and between two other crannogs (SL034-215----; SL034-219001-). Wood-Martin (1886, 246-56), refers to a crannog 'close to the shore of Ballindoon demesne' comprising of 'a large pile of stones, evidently deposited by human agency'. A large reed stand (c. 60m N-S; 20m E-W) growing on a stony shoal in the lake-bed is located at a depth of between 0.9-1.1m below the water. The shoal, which has no distinct edges, consists of small stones with some larger boulders (diam. 1-2m) which occur naturally in many places in Lough Arrow. It is not clear whether this is a natural or man-made feature. A possible jetty or causeway leads out from the N end of an adjacent crannog (SL034-219001-) towards this possible crannog.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

Not included in the SMR (1989) but listed in the RMP (1995) and classified 'Kiln'. In elevated undulating pasture, built into a drystone wall (long axis NE-SW) which encloses the base of the cairn of a wedge tomb (SL034-208001-) immediately to NW. A D-shaped kiln (1.35m SW-NE; 1.2m SE-NW; H 1.3m) of rubble limestone. The bowl of the kiln (diam. top 1.75m; wall T 0.6m; H top to base 0.6m) has vertical sides and is slightly in-turned at the top where there is a course of level rubble stone. The mouth of the kiln, which is rectangular in shape (Wth 0.7m; H 0.5m; D to rear wall 0.6m), faces SE away from the cairn of the wedge tomb. It has a lintelled top and sides of rough limestone rubble. The rear wall of the fire pit is vertical and the raking hole is now obscured by earth and rubble. This is probably post-1700 AD in date.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, occupying a shelf on the SW-facing slope of a high ridge. There are good views to W and SW over lowland pasture bordering Lough Arrow. A circular area (c. 24m NW-SE; c. 23m NE-SW) defined N-SSE by a stone bank and S-NNW by a curving scarp (H 1.5m) coinciding with the break of slope at the terrace edge. The perimeter is densely ringed with hazel, ash, hawthorn and brambles, impeding inspection, and clumps of brambles obscure much of the level interior. Where the bank can be seen at ENE and SE it appears as a concentration of stones (Wth 4.5m; int. H 0.55m; ext. H 0.7m) incorporating large slabs and boulders with much stone tumble obscuring the internal and external faces. At S the bank appears to be more compact (Wth 2m). There is a possible entrance (Wth 2.5m) at SE, partially blocked with stones. The natural slope below the cashel has been quarried away to a high vertical face. A rath (SL040-051----) lies c. 100m upslope to NE.

source_data.original_text:
In Lough Arrow, c. 200m E of the Annaghloy peninsula, unusually located almost in open water. Indicated as a small oval islet on the 1914 OS 6-inch map. A roughly oval high-cairn crannog (15.8m N-S; 28.9m E-W; H 2m above the firm sandy lake-bed) with a mid-cairn of loosely packed angular and subangular stones (4.6m N-S; 4.9m E-W) off-centre to W. The edge of the mid-cairn drops distinctly down 0.6m to NW to the surrounding berm. To the E and S, the mid-cairn drops down gradually to a surrounding plateau. In the centre of the mid-cairn is a post to warn boat-users of its presence. It is surrounded on the E and S sides by a plateau of loosely packed stones, the surface of which is uneven and unstable. Animal bones were found among these stones during the site inspection. The berm is quite large and surrounds the whole site. It lies at an average depth of 0.4-0.5m and is narrower to the N (Wth 5m) and S (Wth 1.9m) than to the E (Wth 10.5m) and W (Wth 7.2m) and consists of loosely packed angular stones (diam. 0.3-0.4m). However, there are a number of larger flagstones on the S side of the site. The edges, which consist of stones, were investigated by probing from the surface and they seem to drop down quite dramatically from a depth of 0.5m to 1.4m. As this site has both an unusual location and shape it is classified as a possible crannog. It is mentioned by Wood-Martin (1886, 246) as being man-made.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on level ground with rising ground to S and SW and overlooking Lough Arrow to N. A circular earthen platform (30m ESE-WNW; 28m NNW-SSE) defined SSW-NNE by a stony scarp (H 0.7-0.9m) and elsewhere by a stone wall (Wth 3m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.7m), incorporating some field clearance material. The perimeter is ringed with hawthorn and blackthorn bushes. The interior slopes down gently from the centre to N. An oval cairn (3.5m N-S; 5.5m E-W; H 0.5m), roughly in the centre, is partially obscured by overgrowth. Adjoining the W edge of the cashel is a subrectangular area (27.4m E-W; 28m N-S) defined on the N and S sides by sod-covered stone walls (Wth 2.5m), on the W side by a field boundary and on the E side by the cashel wall. The N wall (H 0.5m) is straight while the S wall (int. H 0.8m; ext. H 0.3m) is gently curved and scarped into rising ground. The interior is level. Another cashel (SL040-182---) lies c. 100m to SSW.

In rough, rush-grown pasture, located on top of a ridge named Mullaghahanny on the 1914 OS 6-inch map, close to the SE shoulder of the ridge where ground falls steeply into a small valley. Good views over the slopes of adjacent ridges to S, SW, and NW, with Lough Arrow visible in the middle distance to SW. Broadly oval area (29m N–S; 26m E–W) defined by a levelled bank with a largely infilled external fosse. The flat, featureless interior appears very slightly raised above surrounding field level. The enclosing bank (Wth 3.5-4m; 2m on top; int. H 0.1-0.2m; ext. H 0.5m) is evident as a broad low rise marked by a growth of greener grass. The fosse is visible as a shallow, damp depression (Wth c. 3m; base c. 2m), distinguished by denser rush growth. At SE–WSW the fosse is incorporated into the line of a later field ditch (Wth 1.6m), with external field bank, which respects the curve of the enclosure.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located the level top of a high ridge, close to the break of slope at NE where ground falls in a long, steep NE-facing slope into a small stream valley. There are excellent views N−SE bounded by a distant high ridge. 
This possible enclosure is not indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map, but is shown on the 25-inch plan and 1914 OS 6-inch map as an arc of hachuring which curves W−NE (cord L c. 25m). A low scarp can be traced W−NE in a broad arc (cord L 29-30m NE−SW). The scarp appears to have been partly levelled in the past; it is very slight at W−NW (H 0.3m; Wth slope 2-3m), but is better preserved at N−NNE (H 0.9m; Wth slope c. 6m) where it coincides with and is enhanced by the natural break of slope of the ridge. A slight surface undulation on a N-S axis, possibly the remains of a field boundary, cuts across the NE terminal of the arc. 
The significance of this curving scarp is uncertain; it may be the surviving NW arc of an originally circular enclosure. There is a rath (MA034-069001-) 275m to W.

In pasture in limestone terrain, on a terrace on a high ridge overlooking the E shore of Lough Arrow. To NE ground shelves up gradually; to SW it falls steeply for c. 400m in a series of rocky terraces, eventually levelling out at the lake shore.
This enclosure is not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps. It is visible in aerial imagery (Digital globe, Google Earth).
Circular area (diam. 21m N−S; 21 E−W) defined by a low remnants of a bank (Wth 1.4m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.3m at E). The enclosure backs onto a slight rise at W bordered by a N−S seam of limestone bedrock. This gives the interior a gentle dip or slightly concave profile. The enclosing bank is evident at NNW−SE as a low grass-covered rise, best preserved at E−SE; it is barely discernible on the W half where it converges with rising ground. The interior mirrors the natural slope, with a gentle fall from the perimeter at W toward the centre where it levels out but is only marginally higher than exterior ground level.  

Notified to NMS by Andrew Goodison.

In undulating rough pasture, near the top of the N-facing slope of a ridge. A raised circular area (diam. c. 20m) enclosed by a substantial earthen bank (Wth 5m; int. H 1.3m; ext. H 1.8m) with remains of a stone kerb visible at intervals around the base of the internal face of the bank. The boggy external fosse (Wth 3m; D 0.9m) is filled with rushes. A possible entrance (Wth 1m) is at N. The possible remains of an outer bank (Wth 1.8m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.6m) curve around the fosse N-NE. The interior slopes down from S to N and there is a possible souterrain (SL034-069002-) in the W half, adjacent to the bank.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In rough pasture, on the N-facing slope of a low rise. A mature sycamore tree grows on the S edge of a penitential cairn (SL034-070002-). Wood-Martin (1892, 372) referred to the many legends and traditions attached to this tree 'some of which are yet current'. In 1836 it was noted that Catholics are said to have performed stations here (OSNB vol. 1, 468). It is known locally as a site of stations or 'pattern'.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, on the N-facing slope of a low rise. A circular cairn (6m N-S; 5m E-W; H 0.9m) of small stones. A cross-inscribed stone (SL034-070004-) is at the edge of the cairn. Nine rounded stones (SL034-07003-) similar to 'cursing stones' and a cross-inscribed slab (SL034-070004-) were noted here in 2003 (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney). There is a holy tree (SL034-070001-) at the S edge of the cairn. The cairn is known locally as a site of stations or 'pattern'. Wood-Martin (1892, 372) referred to stones which are 'so disposed as to simulate the form of a rude altar'. Two quarry holes lie immediately to N of the cairn.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In undulating elevated pasture, on a slight NNW-facing slope. There are excellent views N-SE though views are moderate to poor in other directions. A slightly raised circular area (diam. 22m) defined by a fosse (Wth 2m; D 0.3m) and an external bank (Wth 2m; int. H 1m; ext. H 0.8m). The bank has internal and external stone revetments. In the centre of the interior is a slightly raised circular platform (diam. 6m; H 0.4m) defined by a low bank or sod-covered stone foundations (Wth 0.4m). Extending from it to the inner edge of the fosse at W and N are two linear earthen banks (Wth 1m; H 0.4m; L c. 9m), that to N marked by a boulder at its S terminus. At NNW is a small earthen mound (4m E-W; H 1m), partially incorporated into the enclosing bank but projecting 1.5m from its external face. A N-S field boundary lies immediately to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On gently rolling upland pasture about 2km to the E of the NE corner of Lough Arrow. The remains of a WSW-facing gallery (L at least 3.5m) divided by a septal-stone into a portico (L 1.5m; Wth 1.9m at the front, 1.6m at the septal-stone) and wedge-shaped main chamber, stands at the centre of a substantial circular cairn (20m N-S; 17m E-W; H 1m). Three orthostats, two together about 1.5m W of the front of the gallery and another almost 2m SE of these protrude from the cairn and seem to represent a buried kerb or outer-wall. A single stone forms each side of the portico. The septal-stone reaches to the level of the chamber sides each of which is now represented by two orthostats. Outside the junction of the two stones at each side there is a small stone apparently intended to strengthen the wall and there is another outside the end of the eastern of the two orthostats at the N side. A single roofstone resting on the septal-stone and the gallery sides covers the remains of the main chamber. A fence follows the cairn perimeter at the W and S and there is the remains of a small limekiln (SL034-208003-) at its eastern edge. The central part of the cairn, i.e. that part of it adjoining the structure rises about 1m above the rest of the cairn and includes spoil from the gallery area. This site was dug into at least twice in the 19th century and human remains, a piece of bronze and pottery sherds, among which were the remains of at least three Beakers, are among the recorded finds (Wood-Martin 1883-4, 461-2; 1888, 182-5; Madden 1969, 157-9). (Ó Nualláin 1989, 63-4, no. 103)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a S-facing slope overlooking Lough Arrow and forming the SW corner of Ballindoon graveyard (SL034-211002-), which lies within an early ecclesiastical enclosure (SL034-21104-). The priory is on a ledge from which the ground drops abruptly to Lough Arrow c. 6m below. The remains of the priory (Pl. 52) comprise of the ruin of the church consisting of a nave (int. 13.5m E-W; 6.9m N-S) and chancel (int. 8.2m E-W; 6.9m N-S) divided by a tower with a short transept (int. 4.1m N-S; 4m E-W) at the E end of the N wall of the nave. The church is built of uncoursed limestone in a lime mortar. The interior contains many burial memorials ranging in date from the 17th to the 19th centuries. It is entered through a doorway midway along the N wall of the nave; the chamfered door surround has a pointed arch and a decorated stop-chamfer and a hood-moulding; the doorway is covered by a segmental wicker-centred vault. Inside on its E side, is a stoup with an octagonal basin. The nave is lit by two windows: one in the centre of the W gable and the other near the E end of the S wall. The light of the W window has two mullions rising to three round sub-arches with switchline tracery above. The embrasure is deeply splayed with a rear pointed arch. The window in the S wall has a lintelled embrasure and a double round-headed light which is missing its mullion. The transept is an insertion, entered from the nave through a wide semicircular archway; it is lit by a single window high up on its W gable. The springing stone of the E side, cut from the same stone as the springer for the arch of the tower compartment, is from an earlier arch than that which now gives access to the transept.
The chancel is lit by two windows in the N wall and a central window in the E gable. The E window is similar to the W window in the nave, but is wider with three mullions rising to four sub-arches. The windows in the N wall have lintelled embrasures and single (to E) and double (to W) round-arched lights. Near the E end of the S wall is a doorway facing into the chancel; the embrasure is lintelled and the door surround has a pointed arch. This doorway gives access to the church from the base of a stairs cantilevered from the external face of the S wall of the chancel. This rises to give access to the first floor of the tower at the SE corner. 
The central tower has a unique form which Leask (1960, vol. 3, 54-5) described as 'a magnified screen, rising through and above the roof of the church...the whole conception of this design is most original'. At ground-floor level are three barrel-vaulted compartments, the central one an open passage between the nave and chancel. There are two bell-rope holes in the vault over the passage, and two corresponding holes in the vault overhead. The side compartments are closed at their E end but open to the W (the opening on the S side is blocked by a supporting rubble wall). The central passage is linked to these side compartments by opposite doorways, and each side compartment has an inserted doorway and window in its outside wall. The graveslab (SL034-211007-) of David Duignan, the 17th-century scribe, and his wife, is in the N compartment (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney). At first-floor level the central area contains a similar vaulted passage to that below but with taller arched openings, each with a cut-stone rib on its soffit. However, the sides of the vaulted area are also open with tall arched openings similar to those at either end. These also have soffit ribs, the terminal of the one at the SE corner is decorated with an octagonal rosette below a slight roll. There is a tall narrow window in both the N and S walls at first-floor level; these have double round-headed lights. The stone flashing course for the roof over the nave and chancel survives on either face of the tower and just below each apex is a small rectangular opening. At this level both ends of the tower are gabled but the central part is brought a storey higher and then also gabled (see Leask 1960, vol. 1, fig. 20). 
These are the remains of a Dominican foundation, known as St Mary's Priory, which was 'begun in 1507 by Thomas O'Farrell' (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 222; Conlan 2002, 225; Ó Muraíle 2002, 241, n. 38). The surviving structure, apart from the transept which is an insertion, is consistent with an early 16th-century date of construction. A font (SL034-211003-), which is named 'St Dominick's stone' on the 1914 OS 6-inch map, lies c. 70m to the N (Wood-Martin 1882, 228). There is a holy well (SL034-211006-) on level ground to the SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

Within an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL034-211004-). The rectangular graveyard (c. 60m NW-SE; c. 30m NE-SW) is enclosed by a stone wall and has an entrance on the NE side. The ruin of Ballindoon Abbey (SL034-211001-), a Dominican foundation, occupies the SW corner. The graveyard, which is still in use, is grass-covered and full of 19th- and 20th-century headstones. There is a plain 19th-century barrel-vaulted mausoleum, belonging to the Gethin family, to the NW of the priory. According to local information, burials were uncovered during surface quarrying in the vicinity of the graveyard.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on top of a small pile of stones c. 70m N of Ballindoon Dominican priory (SL034-211001-). It is named 'St Dominick's Stone' on the 1914 OS 6-inch map and known locally by this name. It comprises a roughly beehive-shaped limestone block (L 0.4m; Wth 0.34m; H 0.22m) with a circular round-bottomed depression (diam. 0.13m; D 0.06m) in its upper surface. The block has two vertical sides and one bowed (the N side). The bowed side has four distinct ribs (Wth 0.01m) dividing it into five sub-triangular faces. Two corners are chamfered with slightly bulbous projections at the base of the chamfers. The S vertical face between these corners has a slightly sunken panel (0.24m x 0.14m) with an IHS carved in relief; there is a cross on the bar of the 'H'. This is a late 18th/early 19th-century addition (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney). According to Wood-Martin (1882, 227-8), the water which collects in the stone 'is supposed by the country-people to be a certain cure for warts'.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Surrounding Ballindoon Dominican priory (SL034-211001-) and graveyard (SL034-21102-). Described by Wood-Martin (1882, 227-8) as a 'formidable intrenchment' which surrounded the priory and graveyard on the NE side, stopping at the steep-sided lakeshore. It is indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map as a curved hachured scarp N-E and as a hachured bank E-SSE with a short extension to the E. None of these features are evident in a field of reclaimed grassland which surrounds the graveyard. However, a denuded linear earthen bank (L 32m; H 1.35m) (SL034-211005-) was noted parallel to, and c. 32m from, the NW wall of the graveyard. The area between this bank and the graveyard is gently undulating and slopes gradually down to the W. In a wooded area c. 80m SE of the priory is a holy well (SL034-211006-).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In a wooded area, on level ground to c. 80m SE of Ballindoon Dominican priory (SL034-211001-) and on the S side of a 6m high cliff. The well is now covered by a pump-house (2.7m x 2.7m). A small muddy stream flows SW from the pump-house toward Lough Arrow. No pilgrimage tokens or other signs of recent use are evident. According to Wood-Martin (1882, 228), the well gushed forth from the base of the cliff and stations were held there on St Dominick's Day, the 4th of August.

source_data.original_text:
In the N side of Lough Arrow, c. 150m from the E shore and c. 250m SE of another crannog (SL034-215----), with a clear view of Carrowkeel to SW, Kesh Corann to W and Ballindoon Castle (SL034-220001-) to ESE. An oval high-cairn crannog (37.4m N-S; 21m E-W; H 2.3m above the lake-bed). It has a mid-cairn (8.4m N-S; 7.5m E-W) in the S half consisting of small stones (sandstone and limestone) set in dark crumbly soil. There is a square stone-lined depression (1.4m x 1.4m) in the SW quadrant of the mid-cairn. The mid-cairn is surrounded by a stony plateau, stretching out 6m to N, 3.5m to E, 4m to S and 3m to W. The E and W edges are distinct with a sharp drop to the lake-bed, the S edge slopes more gradually while that to N is less well defined. There is a circular depression (diam. 2m) in the plateau, immediately NE of the mid-cairn. A possible jetty or causeway leads out to the N towards a possible crannog (SL034-239----). Mentioned by Wood-Martin (1886, 245) as the largest crannog of a group, not far from Ballindoon Abbey (SL034-211001-); he also noted that soil had been brought to it in recent times.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Close to the E shore of Lough Arrow, on a steep W-facing slope. The site occupies the W edge of a terrace overlooking the shoreline. The remains consist of an earthen platform (c. 25m N-S; c. 15m E-W) (SL034-220002-) from which the ground falls steeply down, over 8m, to the lake shoreline. At the S end of this platform are the sod-covered remains of a stone-built structure (int. dims. 11m x 7.5m) which was probably rectangular in plan but the remains are very fragmentary. The interior area is strewn with loose rubble. An earth and stone bank (Wth 0.7m; H 2.5m) extends downhill from the N end of the platform towards the lakeshore. At the foot of this are the remains of a rectangular structure (int. dims. 2m x 4m) with a small secluded boat dock on its W side. A tumbled field boundary wall links the S end of the platform with the shoreline. Most of these remains are covered by trees with an undergrowth of briars and bushes. 
On the shoreline, immediately N of the end of the field boundary wall, is the 'Armourer's Well'; Wood-Martin (1882, 227) suggested that water from the well was used to temper weapons of war. The well consists of a roughly circular depression (1.4m N-S; 1.5m E-W; max. D 1.4m), lined on the N side with rocks, with an irregular outflow gully (L 1.5m) on the NW side. The base of the well is muddy with some rocks protruding through it and the gully is roughly lined with small rocks. The well was filled with lake water when inspected but according to local information, it also holds water during the summer months when the lake level is lower.
The castle of Baile-an-Duin was captured and dismantled by Hugh O'Conor in 1352 (ibid.). It was later a possession of the MacDonaghs (O'Dowd 1991, 72). According to local tradition, Ballindoon House (SL034-213----), c. 0.9km to the NW, was built using material from the castle (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on a flat-topped ridge on the E shore of Lough Arrow. The remains of Ballindoon Castle (SL034-220001-) are at the SE corner. A subcircular area (int. dims. 36m x 39m) enclosed by an earth and stone bank (Wth 0.7m; H 2.5m) on the E side which continues down the ridge on the W side to the lakeshore. The remains of a rectangular structure (int. dims. 2m x 4m) are built against the internal wall. There are the remains of a small secluded boat dock on the W side. There is an Armourer's well (SL034-220003-) within the perimeter to S.

The well consists of a roughly circular depression (1.4m N-S; 1.5m E-W; max. D 1.4m), lined on the N side with rocks, with an irregular outflow gully (L 1.5m) on the NW side. The base of the well is muddy with some rocks protruding through it and the gully is roughly lined with small rocks. The well was filled with lake water when inspected but according to local information, it also holds water during the summer months when the lake level is lower. Wood-Martin (1882, 227) suggests the well was used to temper weapons of war. No trace of any tokens to indicate holy use and no local information that there were any cures associated with it.

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, overlooking a stream and steep-sided valley to N. Incorporating a low flat-topped natural hillock and truncated at W by a drystone field boundary. A roughly semicircular area (28m N-S; 21.5m E-W) defined by a moss-covered stone wall (int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.9m) N-S. The wall consists of rubble limestone with occasional larger blocks and the only evidence for an external facing is a single upright limestone slab (H 1.25m; Wth 1m; T 0.4m) at E. There are no visible remains of this wall S-N. A fosse (D 0.8m) is evident N-NE. Due to the natural hillock the interior is raised above the level of the enclosing wall. The hillock is roughly circular and flat-topped (7m N-S; 6m E-W; H 0.75m) with gently sloping sides. There is a souterrain (SL035-015002-) in the interior.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the S shore of Inishmore Island in Lough Arrow, within a possible graveyard (SL040-050002-). The ruins of a rectangular structure (int. 8.5m NW-SE; 5m SW-NE) are situated in an area covered by scrub overgrowth. Only fragments of wall-facing survive (uncoursed limestone; T 0.6m) and most of the walling is of loose drystone construction. No feature of this is consistent with that of a church though it appears to be the structure named 'Monastery (in Ruins)' on the 1914 OS 6-inch map. There is no known record of a monastic foundation here (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 365).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In a thicket of hazel and hawthorn scrub, utilising a level terrace on a S-facing slope. An oval area (30.6m NW-SE; 23m NE-SW) enclosed by a collapsed, moss-covered wall of limestone rubble (Wth 3m). In parts at E and SE large slabs and blocks are visible protruding from the rubble, remnants of the basal course of an internal and external stone facing indicating that the wall was originally c. 2m in width. From SE-SW, where the wall coincides with the break of slope at the edge of the terrace, it is reduced to a thin scattering of stone topping a scarp (H 1m) covered with stone tumble. The scarp drops to a level terrace (Wth 3m) from which the ridge slopes down steeply. The interior is level and broken by rock outcrops in places. A N-S field boundary wall (Wth 0.6m) clips the perimeter W-NW. There is a gap (Wth c. 1.5m) at NW, now partially blocked by a field boundary wall. There is a possible hut site (SL040-055002-) in the NW quadrant, flanking the entrance.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on an E-facing slope adjacent to the W shore of Lough Arrow. Listed in the RMP (1995) as 'Brick kiln(s), possible'. The remains consist of a sub-circular or squarish area (5.5m N-S x 5m E-W) bounded by a sod-covered stone bank-like feature. It has a low internal rim and is built up slightly on the SE to compensate for the slope. The exact nature of this feature is unclear and that it might represent the remains of a kiln cannot be ruled out. There is no evidence to suggest that these are the remains of a brick kiln and there is no local information of such. Immediately SE is a raised rectangular platform (SL040-168004-), to the SE a possible structure (SL040-0168002-) and to the NE the remains of a house (SL040-168003-). Although the date of these features cannot be determined with any degree of accuracy it is likely that they date to the post-AD 1700 period.

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 17 January 2012

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on an E-facing slope adjacent to the W shore of Lough Arrow. Listed in the RMP (1995) as 'Building'. The remains consist of a substantial rectangular building (ext. 14m NNW-SSE x 8m ENE-WSW) defined by a low ruined wall which survives as a sod-covered bank (Wth 1.5m; H 0.6 at SW and 0.2m at NE). There is a pronounced external dip at the E and SE where the structure has been built up to compensate for the slope and create a level interior. A possible entrance is visible as a break at the N end of the W wall. To the SW are the remains of a possible kiln (SL040-0168001-) and another structure (SL040-168002-) and further to the WSW is a raised rectangular platform (SL040-168004-). Although the date of these features cannot be determined with any degree of accuracy it is likely that they date to the post-AD 1700 period.

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 17 January 2012

This rath is possibly one of the two forts, named 'Mullaghmore Fort' and 'Lisnaspeenoge Fort' respectively, which were recorded in 1836 in the S side of Ballysumaghan townland (OSNB vol. 1, 157).

source_data.original_text:
On the SE side of a broad shallow NE-SW valley of boggy ground, overlooked SE-SW by hilly terrain broken by rock outcrops. A stream, which marks the county boundary between Sligo and Leitrim, skirts the monument E-SE. 
This is a National Monument in state ownership (no. 277). A conical oval mound (c. 42m NW-SE; c. 35-40m NE-SW; H 5m) with a flat top (15.5m NW-SE; 10m NE-SW) and steeply sloping sides. Occasional large stones protrude randomly around the top edge of the mound, possibly remnants of an enclosing wall. The mound appears to be a modified natural ridge and this fact has cast some doubt on its status as a motte (Glasscock 1975, 109; Graham 1988, 121).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating rocky pasture, on the summit of a small hillock with a stream at its base on the W side.
This cashel is a national monument in State care (no. 277). An oval area (21m E-W; 16m N-S) enclosed by a substantial drystone wall (Wth 3m; int. H 1m; ext. H 2.4m). In parts, a low foundation plinth of prostrate slabs protrudes slightly at the base of the external face. This was necessary in order to stabilise the wall, which is built almost at the break of slope at the top of the hillock. The entrance (Wth c. 1.2m) is at ENE and is now partially blocked by large stones displaced from the collapsed S jamb. From the entrance the gentle ramp-like slope of the hillock drops to a spine of elevated ground forming a natural routeway to E. Immediately outside the entrance, slightly to N of the N jamb, there are two large contiguous upright slabs set perpendicular to the cashel wall. Another large upright slab is located c. 5m down slope to ENE, adjacent to a concentration of stones. In the centre of the level grassy interior two large prostrate slabs (max. dim. 1.2-1.7m) are embedded in the ground. A dilapidated field wall (Wth c. 1m; H 0.5m), largely obscured by overgrowth and superseded by a post and wire fence, encloses the base of the hillock NW-SW, continuing to W beyond the cashel. No evidence of a chamber noted by Milligan (1890-91, 577) in the thickness of the wall, which was entered by a small square-headed door (H 2 ft 6 ins [0.76m]; Wth 2 ft [0.6m]) to which access was not gained as it was filled with rubbish and rubble. According to local tradition, the chamber gave access to a secret passage, which led to the bottom of the hill (ibid.). Skeletons were frequently found in the ground outside the cashel (Milligan 1890-1, 577). Recorded in 1836 as 'Badhbun Buidhe' (OSL, 254) and in 1894 as 'The Bauven Crin' (the fortress of Belonna) (Kerr Kirker 1894, 278). Recorded as 'Caisleán Oir or Caisleán Uabhair (castle of pride)' (Faughnan 1943). A possible souterrain (SL021-028001-) is associated with this cashel. Another cashel (SL021-027----) is located c. 120m to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In hilly terrain overshadowed to N by Killery Mountain, commanding excellent views along a valley to SW. A subrectangular area (35m N-S; 39m E-W), utilising the natural defences of a high steep-sided rocky spur on its S, W and N sides; the gradually sloping E side allows access to the top of the spur. The E side is defined by a scarp (H 1.4m) that drops down to a broad terrace. The remains of a stone wall are evident in parts, most clearly S-SSW as an arc of moss-covered horizontally laid slabs at the cliff-edge, in one instance surviving to two courses. Along the W and NW arcs, single stones which occur at intervals and are set back 0.5-1m from the edge of the spur may also be part of the enclosing wall. The base of the spur E-S is faced with drystone walling of relatively recent date.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a low ridge. The inner end of a court at the E opens into the remains of a gallery (L 4.4m; Wth c. 1.7m). Three courtstones flank the S side of the gallery entrance and one the N side. Wood-Martin (1887-8, 295-6; 1888, 203-4) noted four extra stones at the N which would suggest that there may have been a full court here. Two stones remain of the N side of the gallery and three of the S side. The inner ends of both sides are missing but the backstone survives. There is no indication of segmentation in the gallery. Beyond the backstone and more or less in line with the N side of the gallery there is a thin, low stone on edge. Its function is unclear. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 51-2, no. 80).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In rough, rushy pasture, on the top of a high ridge at a break of slope on the E side with extensive views N-S. An oval platform (c. 30m N-S; c. 20m E-W) defined by an earthen bank (Wth c. 5m; int. H c. 0.5m; ext. H 1.75m) SW-N and by a scarp (H c. 2m) elsewhere. An external fosse (Wth 5m) evident SSW-NNW is broad, deep and flat-bottomed. It is bordered on its outer edge by a substantial townland and field boundary (Wth 3m; int. H 1.7m; ext. H 1m) that continues beyond the enclosure to NW and SE but may preserve the line of an outer bank. Elsewhere the fosse is a slight depression (Wth 4-5m) of soft, wet ground. From NE-SE the ridge slope falls away abruptly from its outer edge. The entrance (Wth 0.7m) is at ENE, partially faced with large stones. Stones are also visible protruding from the external face of the bank in this area. The rath is ringed with hazel and the interior, which appears to slope down gently to E, is engulfed in a thicket of impenetrable blackthorn bushes. The townland boundary between Mullaghfin and Toberanania skirts the rath S-NNW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On a rocky rise, in rush-grown pasture. This unclassified megalithic tomb is a National Monument in State ownership (no. 277). An orthostat (L 1.3m; T 0.3m; H 1.3m if upright) aligned SW-NE and leaning to the S is the only set stone here. In addition four large slabs lie at the site. One (max. dim. 2.7m) adjoins the NE end of the orthostat and beyond this is another slab of similar size. Immediately S of the orthostat there is a large slab (max. dim. 2m) and alongside this to the SW there is another. There are also seven smaller prostrate stones at the site. The stones seem to represent the remains of a megalithic tomb or perhaps an abandoned attempt to build one (Ó Nualláin 1989, 53, no. 83). The presence of two large slabs one resting above the other some 15m to the S is cited as support for the view that construction of the monument may not have been completed. A court tomb (SL021-104----) lies c. 50m to ENE.

source_data.original_text:
On top of a roughly circular knoll, surrounded by a flat expanse of bog but connected by a low spine of elevated ground to a high ridge at SSW. The circular flat top (16m N-S; 17m E-W) of the knoll is enclosed by scant remains of a stone wall. The wall survives as a jumble of moss-covered stones, occasionally protruding from which are individual stones that appear to be in situ facing stones of the foundation course. The inner face of the wall coincided with the break of slope at the top of the knoll with the outer wall face constructed slightly downslope. It appears to have been 2.5m in width. The interior is strewn with stone and there is considerable stone tumble on the steep sides of the knoll. From an entrance (Wth 0.8m) in the wall at ENE a line of contiguous stones, perpendicular to the wall, extends downslope for c. 5m. There is also a break (W 1.6m) in the wall at SE. A stand of hazel, holly and hawthorn covers the knoll, with a dense thicket of blackthorn extending to the N. At the base of the knoll on the E side a low natural terrace (c. 20m N-S; 20m E-W) of dry ground extends into the surrounding marshy ground. A cashel (SL021-073----) lies c. 400m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In sharply undulating grassland of knolls and low ridges, broken by rock outcrops. An oval area (14m N-S; 18m E-W), encompassing the top of a low knoll, enclosed by a ruined stone wall. The knoll has a steep slope to N and S but a more gradual incline to E and W. The enclosing wall appears to have faced a low scarp (H 0.6-0.7m) encircling the top of the knoll and is topped with a slight moss-covered stony internal rim (Wth c. 0.6m). A single hawthorn tree grows on the wall at N. The interior has a level but uneven surface. A line of moss-covered stones crosses the interior on a N-S axis, 2.7m from the wall at W. There is a possible entrance at E where there is a break (Wth c. 3m) in the wall and the interior ground level grades gently to the exterior. The scant remains of a wall are visible on the steep N slope of the knoll, 1.5m above the base. It follows the E-W contour of the knoll and is probably associated with two small rectangular fields to E of the knoll. Ruined moss-covered walls (Wth 0.5-1m; H 0.3m) enclose the fields. The smaller field (17.7m N-S; 7.7m E-W) is located at the base of the E slope of the knoll. Its SE corner is linked by a short E-W stretch of wall to the NW corner of a somewhat larger field that extends across the intervening space between this cashel and another (SL021-071----) c. 60m to SSE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On top of a small knoll in sharply undulating pasture, broken by rock outcrops. The flat circular top (16m N-S; 19m E-W) of the knoll is enclosed by a ruined stone wall. The wall survives as a sod-covered stone bank without clearly defined edges. There is a considerable over-spill of stone on the knoll slope giving a width in parts of 3.5m. The interior, which is strewn with moss-covered stone, slopes down gently to E and SE. The entrance (Wth 2.5m) is at ESE. A linear depression (Wth 2.6m) cuts through the wall at SE and extends for 7m to NE into the interior, expanding at the NE end to a deep pit (Wth 3.5m; D 0.8m), partially infilled with stone. It appears to be the result of relatively recent disturbance. A ruined field wall skirts the base of the knoll intersecting at W and S with remnants of a rectilinear grid of fields (SL021-113----). A cairn (SL021-114----) lies c. 18m to SE, a cashel (SL021-069----) c. 400m to NW and rath (SL021-079----) c. 400m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified as 'Enclosure' and 'Enclosure Site' respectively. It is indicated on the 1913 edition of the OS 6-inch map as a triangular area defined on the N and E sides by linear field boundaries and on the SW by a hachured line. The word 'fort' is marked in pencil on the NMI copy of the 1838 edition of the OS 6-inch map. In poorly drained pasture, at the base of a N-facing slope. Upon inspection in 2002 a flat D-shaped terrace (c. 14m E-W; 13.5m N-S) created by quarrying into the base of the slope was identified. The curving side E-W is defined by a N-facing scarp (H 2.8m at S) cut into the natural slope. The scarp diminishes in height at E and W. The straight N side of the terrace is bordered by a low N-facing scarp (H 0.7m) dropping to an E-W field drain. This is not an archaeological monument.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

On a low spine of elevated dry ground extending from the W end of a high E-W ridge through poorly drained rushy pasture. A circular platform (27.5m N-S; 27m E-W) defined by an earthen bank, an intervening fosse and an outer bank, with an external fosse evident SW-NW. The banks appear as low grass-covered rises protruding from a sea of rushes engulfing the interior of the rath and the fosse. The inner bank (Wth 4m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 1.65m) has a low flattened internal lip but a pronounced external scarp. The intervening fosse (Wth 3m) is visible as a slight depression of soft wet ground. The outer bank (Wth 4.5m; int. 0.3m; ext. H 0.35m) survives SW-SE as a broad flattened grass-covered rise. The entrance (Wth 1.8m) is at ENE with a corresponding low area in the outer bank but no obvious causeway over the fosse. Stones protrude randomly from the terminal of the inner bank on the S side of the entrance. A remnant of a N-S field boundary crosses the outer bank at E. The interior is mostly level but with a slight slope down to ESE in the E half towards the entrance.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On a poorly drained low-lying patch of ground about 50m ENE of an unclassified megalithic tomb (SL021-062----). 
This court tomb is a National Monument in State ownership (no. 277). The inner end of a SSE-facing gallery (L 4m; max. Wth 2.6m) is divided by segmenting jambs inset in the gallery walls into a well-preserved rear chamber (L c. 2m) and an outer chamber now represented by two opposed sidestones. The status of an upright stone between these two sidestones and crossing the gallery is unclear. Some 2m to the W of the gallery there is a lone kerbstone and 2-3m E of the gallery there are three others. The alignment of these kerbstones suggest that the structure stood in a cairn of trapezoidal plan. There is some cairn fill in the gallery and between it and the kerbstones. There are a number of displaced stones at the site including a group of four large examples just S of the surviving gallery structure. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 53-4, no. 84)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Not included in the SMR (1989) but listed in the RMP (1995) and classified 'Field System'. Not marked on any edition of the OS 6-inch map.  In undulating average pasture, broken by rock outcropping. A cashel (SL021-073----) is located within the limits of the field system. The system consists of a rectilinear grid of ruined field walls, surviving as low sod-covered stone banks (Wth 0.5-0.8m; H 0.3m). They appear to be associated with a ruined farmstead (shown on the 1913 edition of the OS 6-inch map), probably 18th/19th century in date, located c. 50m to SW of the cashel. The stone foundations of a cluster of small rectangular buildings can be made out beneath heaps of field clearance rubble. The grid of fields extends to E of the farmstead and are laid out axially along the natural contours in a series of roughly E-W lines (varying in width from 20-50m) with transverse sub-divisions. A connecting wall encloses the base of the knoll on top of which cashel (SL021-073----) is sited.This system dates to the post-1700 AD period.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Date of upload: 11 January 2012

source_data.original_text:
In a wet meadow, 120m N of the drained Tunnagh Lough and below the earlier shoreline. The lake is surrounded by drumlins which restrict views in all directions. A roughly circular platform-mound crannog (8.5m N-S; 7.5m E-W; H 0.5m). The surface is even and the site is quite distinct topographically but not in material. While there is not much surface material to confirm this as a crannog, a drain cut 4m S of it exposed a number of rounded stones and a brushwood and timber floor. Indicated as an oval islet at the NE end of the lake on the 1838 OS 6-inch map.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a break in slope in undulating terrain. Indicated as a rectangular structure on the 1838 OS 6-inch map but only the E wall (int. L 13.4m; T 1.2m), with returns of the S (int. L 6.15m) and N (int. L 0.7m) walls, now stand. The wall is of uncoursed limestone and stands to a uniform height (H c. 4m) over most of its length but much of the inner facing stones are missing. At ground-floor level, the wall is pierced by eight irregularly spaced gun loops: five in the E wall and three in the S wall. These have a plain rectangular front opening (H 0.25m; Wth 0.1m) behind which the embrasure is splayed (Wth on inside face c. 0.5m) and covered by stepped lintels. The absence of door and window opes suggests this may be the remains of a small bawn; Moygara Castle (SL044-052001-) has a much larger bawn that is pierced by gun loops in a similar fashion. According to local tradition, this is the remains of a castle built by the MacDonaghs (ITA).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

Some rushes grow in the interior. In 1836 it was recorded as 'Tunnagh Fort' (OSNB vol. 1, 128).

source_data.original_text:
Incorporated in the upper courses of the external face of the W wall of a ruined stone building which forms part of a cattle pen, is a triangular sandstone slab (Wth at base 0.54m; T 0.15m; H 0.3m) with a carving of a human head in raised relief on one side. The head (Wth 0.16m; H 0.16m) has a flat top, broad angular cheeks and a flattened chin. The oval heavy-browed eyes are the most prominent facial features flanking a clearly defined almost triangular nose. The mouth is a barely discernible short horizontal groove. The provenance and date of this carving are unknown.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on the gentle S-facing slope of an E-W ridge, bordering the N side of a small, shallow valley. Two raths are located immediately upslope, crowning the top of the ridge, one (MA021-074----) 25m to N, and the other (SL021-075----) 40m to NNE. A third rath (SL021-076----) is located 90m to SSE on top of the low ridge which defines the S side of the valley. An E−W drain cuts through the wet, rushy ground in the base of the valley.
This enclosure is not indicated on the 1836 and 1913 OS 6-inch maps. It is visible on current aerial mapping. It consists of a circular area (30m E−W; 28m N−S) defined by a levelled bank. At ground level the bank can be traced as a barely discernible, broad low undulation (Wth 3.4-4m). It is almost entirely obliterated at E. Outside the bank on the W−N there is a hint of a depression/cropmark (Wth c. 3m), marked by soft, poached ground and a growth of yellower grass; this may indicate an enclosing fosse. The interior is not raised relative to exterior ground level; it mirrors the natural contours of the ridge slope, exhibiting a gentle slope down from N to centre, where it levels out.
Although located in close proximity to three raths, this enclosure differs from them in its siting and morphology: it is located on the slope rather than on top of the ridge, and its interior is not raised relative to exterior ground level. It may be a rath or it may be an enclosure dating to an earlier period.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on the narrow, level top of a steep-sided E−W ridge, in an area of hilly, undulating terrain interspersed with damp valleys. It is sited at the highest point of the ridge, and there are extensive views in all directions, with many natural landmarks clearly visible on the horizon: Carrowkeel and Kesh Corran Mountains to S, Knocknashee to SW, the Ox Mountains to W, Ben Bulbin and the Dartry Mountains at N−NE. 
This enclosure is not indicated on the 1836 and 1913 OS 6-inch maps. It is visible as an arc of bank on current aerial mapping.
An arc (C. 24.5m NE−SW) of upstanding bank (Wth 5-6m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.75m) curves SW−N, and appears to represent the W half of a circular enclosure (diam. 25-30m). There is, however, no trace at ground level or in aerial views of the E half of the enclosure. The bank has broadly slumped sides: the external slope is quite pronounced, especially at SW; the internal slope is low and merges seamlessly with surrounding ground. A section (L 4-5m) of the bank at NW is lower than the rest. The SW terminal of the bank coincides with the break of slope of the ridge top, where ground falls away very steeply. Outside the bank there is a slight depression (Wth 2-2.5m) marked by soft, rush-grown ground; this may indicate the presence of a fosse. 
Remnants of cultivation ridges traverse the ridge top on a roughly N−S axis, including the area that would have encompassed the enclosure interior.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 16 November 2018

In pasture, located on top of a low, narrow E-W ridge. There are good views over the surrounding landscape of small knolls and low, undulating ridges, broken by limestone outcropping.
Raised circular area or low platform (17m N−S; 16.5m E−W) defined by a slight scarp (H 0.4-0.5m). The enclosure spans almost the full width of the narrow N−S ridge top, and the scarp at N and S is partly enhanced by the natural fall of round. The scarp is barely discernible on the E arc, and the W edge of the enclosure is overlain by later drystone field wall, on a NNW−SSE axis, which is engulfed in brambles and hawthorn. A few stones protrude slightly from the scarp, with one stone rising more prominently from the SW edge of the circuit.

In pasture, located on a hill, just below the crest of the hill on its S side. Immediately to N, E and S of the enclosure, the slopes of the hill fall steeply into damp-based valleys; the level top of the ridge extends to W.
Not indicated on any edition of the OS 6-inch mapping. The outline of a possible enclosure is visible in aerial imagery as a subcircular area (diam. 30-35m) defined on its perimeter at SW−N by a curving cropmark. It is bordered at E by a straight NW−SE field boundary/hedgerow and at S by a straight NE−SW feature/possibly a field drain. There is almost no visible trace at ground level. A slight curving scarp may correspond to the S arc of the possible enclosure; it is clipped at SE by a linear NE−SW field drain, now infilled and indicated by a dark line of dense rushes. Another area of slightly denser vegetation at W may indicate the SW−W arc of the possible enclosure. The N arc cannot be traced, and a NW−SE field fence, engulfed in a blackthorn and hawthorn, cuts across the E edge.

source_data.original_text:
In rough damp pasture, occupying a low rise surrounded on all sides by high ground, mostly rounded hillocks/drumlins and low ridges. There is a stream 100m to W. Views are of the rising slopes of the surrounding hillocks, with a somewhat more open aspect to W along a small valley. A N−S field boundary lies 10m to E of the enclosure, and to E of that there is a farm shed and bay for storing silage bales.
This enclosure was partly levelled at an unknown date in the past. It is not indicated on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps; it is visible in aerial imagery.
It is evident at ground level as a slightly raised circular area (26m N−S; 27m E−W) defined by a low, but clearly visible scarp (ext. H 0.3-0.4m), best defined at SE, SW and NW. The scarp is barely discernible at E (Wth 3m) and a portion has been levelled at SE−S (Wth 4m). A low undulation is visible c. 2m outside the enclosing scarp on the N side; this may be an outer bank, however, it is not fully concentric with the enclosure and cannot be traced around the full circuit; it may be the remnant of a later field division which skirted the enclosure. 
The interior has a very slightly domed profile, more pronounced on the N−S axis.

Notified to NMS by Jean-Charles Caillère.

source_data.original_text:
In rolling drumlin pasture, in the S half of Killerry graveyard (SL021-011002-). The ruin of this rectangular church (ext. c. 19m E-W; 7.35m N-S) is of at least two phases: the N and E walls (Wth c. 0.9m) are considerably thicker than the S wall (Wth 0.55m) and a cross-wall (Wth 0.6m). Also the N wall is constructed of uncoursed cyclopean masonry; probably matching this are massive quoins at the NE corner and the lower courses of the E wall. The church appears to have been subsequently rebuilt, possibly in the 18th century, when the E wall was built up to a gable. This gable had a central window ope which held a wooden-framed light. Also at this time the church may have been reduced in size by the insertion of the cross-wall, 10.75m from the E gable. The upper part of the S wall and most of the return of the W wall have fallen. A slight sod-covered rise, c. 3.4m to the W from the present end of the N wall, probably marks the original line of the W wall, which may have incorporated a room at the rear of the church (M. A. Timoney 2002b, 57). The interior is under grass; against the N wall is a flat graveslab dated 1830, and there are two headstones of more recent date. The ruin is that of the parish church of Killerry.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On the W side of a road. A rectangular graveyard (60m E-W; 55m N-S) enclosed by a low stone wall. The ruin of the parish church of Killerry (SL021-011001-) forms part of the S boundary wall. The graveyard is under grass and contains many 19th- and 20th-century headstones and some low uninscribed grave-markers as well as several chest-tombs and several recumbent graveslabs. It is still in occasional use. In the NE quadrant are several curing stones and a straining stone (SL021-011003-). According to Wood-Martin (1892, 364), this graveyard was 'cleared and levelled' in the 19th century.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).
