source_data.original_text:
In the NE quadrant of a graveyard (SL021-011002-). Set into the upper surface of a thin stone slab (D c. 0.05m; 0.75m x 0.8m), now broken and sod-covered, are two round (diam. c. 0.25m) and five oval (c. 0.15m x c. 03m) stones known as the 'Curing Stones' (Walsh 1999-2000, 8). Amongst these is a smaller angular stone. Adjacent to this arrangement is a rectangular stone (L c. 0.3m) to which is tied a piece of string, known as the 'straining thread'. The string or thread is reputed to cure strains, pains, and aches. These are part of a curative ritual (see O'Rorke [1889], 319-20; Wood-Martin 1892, 364-5; Crawford 1913a, 267-8). The tradition is associated with St Patrick and according to the caretaker in 1913, there was 'a spring of good water under the slab' (Crawford 1913a, 267). Another 'straining stone' (SL021-025004-) is located 3.5km to NE. (Weir 1980, 209-10)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
At the W end of a spine of elevated ground broken by rock outcrops and engulfed in a dense thicket of hazel and blackthorn, rising from an expanse of flat poorly drained pasture. A roughly circular area (c. 23m NE-SW; c. 20m NW-SE) defined by a scarp (H 2m) topped by a low moss-covered rubble bank (Wth c. 1m; int. H 0.3m) with rough external facing (H 0.6m) of large upright slabs and boulders. Skirting the base of slope N-SE is a scarp cut into the natural slope with an intervening gap or terrace (Wth c. 2m). It is truncated at SE by a later field fence on a NE-SW axis. The scarp is faced with large roughly coursed blocks of stone and is topped by a low bank of rubble (Wth 1.5m). At SE it incorporates massive boulders. Extending from it to E is a S-facing scarp (H 1m) of similar construction which follows the natural contour of the elevated ground. A possible souterrain (SL021-022002-) and hut site (SL021-022003-) lie at the centre of the overgrown interior. A possible cashel (SL021-023----) is located on elevated ground c. 80m to SSE and there is a burnt spread (SL021-116----) immediately to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
A D-shaped area (dims. 52m N-S) enclosed W-E by a dilapidated sod-covered stone bank, with the straight side (L c. 58m E-W) to the S bordered by a field boundary wall topped with a post and wire fence. The sod-covered stone bank has traces of an internal and external facing of large stones, best seen N-NE. It is engulfed by blackthorn bushes NE-E. The wall is poorly preserved (Wth 1.8m; H 0.35m) W-NW where it kinks to incorporate a natural undulation but is more substantial (Wth 3m; int. H 0.65m; ext. H 0.65m) NW-E where it curves to form a regular arc. The wall (Wth 0.6m; H 0.6m) defining the S side surmounts a low N-facing rocky scarp (H c. 0.6m). The interior is predominantly level but to the N of the centre a N-facing slope crosses the width of the graveyard and marks a drop (H c. 1.5m) in ground level to a flat wet area. According to local information, this area was used as a burial ground and is locally called 'the roilig' (Faughnan 1943). No graves or grave-markers are visible anywhere within the interior. A 'straining stone' (SL021-025004-) is located to the NE of the centre. A possible church (SL021-025001-) lies immediately outside the graveyard to the SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on a hillock overlooking a small stream. A long earthen mound (c. 56m E-W; 10m N-S; H c. 1.4m) incorporating part of a natural rise. The W end of the mound slopes down to W, is wedge-shaped (18m E-W; 8m N-S at E end; 7m N-S at W end) and revetted with large boulders. A large limestone slab (L 2.6m; Wth 1.8m; T 0.4m) (SL021-026001-) resting on three smaller boulders (dims. of one: 1.1m x 0.85m; H 0.26m) forms the E side where a straight line of boulders joins these stones to the S side of mound. The eastern portion of the mound (L 40m; Wth 10m), E of the boulders and slab, is convex in profile. The mound is ill-defined at the E end with a scarp revetted by smaller stones continuing on the N side for a further 20m. A narrow rectangular field is indicated here on the 1838 OS 6-inch map.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

On the top of a high ridge, close to a break of slope on the N side. A slightly raised circular area (c. 26m E-W; c. 27m N-S) enclosed by an earthen bank (Wth 2m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 1m) with an external fosse. The fosse is evident NE-SE as a shallow flat-bottomed, waterlogged depression (Wth 2.5m) and is recut (Wth 1.7m; D 0.5m) at W to serve as a field drain. The fosse becomes a flat terrace (Wth 2m) of damp ground NNW-NE, its outer edge coinciding with the top of the steep ridge slope. A N-S field drain (Wth 1m; D 0.4m) cuts across the W edge of the rath, more or less on the inner face of the bank. The external face of the bank at S is incorporated into an E-W field boundary. There is a possible entrance (Wth 1.6m) at E with the remains of stone facing. The entrance is partially obstructed on the inner edge by two large stones. There is a hint of a causeway across the fosse. The rath is engulfed in a thicket of hazel, blackthorn and brambles. The interior is level. There is a souterrain (SL021-031002-) in the NW quadrant.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On a spine of elevated rocky ground, at the E end of a low narrow ridge. An oval platform (16m N-S; 19m E-W) defined on top by scant remains of a moss-covered stone wall, and enclosed by an outer wall NE-W with an intervening gap (Wth 3m). The oval platform is in effect a modified natural rise, defined NW-NE by a steep drop (H 3m) and elsewhere by a more gentle fall of ground (max. H 1m). The interior is level but with an uneven surface broken by a scattering of stone. The W third is covered by low scrubby blackthorn bushes. A shallow depression (Wth 2m; D 0.4m) extends from the S edge of the oval platform into the interior to N for 6.5m, probably the result of quarrying. The entrance was most likely at E where the interior is lowest relative to external ground level and where a slightly raised stony causeway-like feature (Wth 1.3m) bridges the gap between the enclosing walls. There is a possible souterrain (SL021-032002-) in the interior, adjacent to the entrance at E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

The interior is uneven with numerous stones protruding from the sod; the shallow depression of a possible souterrain (SL021-064002-) is evident at S. There is a terrace (c. 25m E-W; c. 12m N-S) immediately down slope to E, defined by a curved scarp (H 1.4m) along the N arc (which is revetted with a single large slab at the E end), and by a linear NE-SW field boundary to SE. There is a rectangular arrangement of upright and prostrate stone slabs (c. 8m E-W; 3m N-S) at the N end of the terrace. An enclosure (SL021-065----) lies c. 50m to SW.

In pasture, on a gentle NW-facing slope. A circular area (40m NW-SE; 41m NE-SW) enclosed by an earthen bank (Wth 1.5m; int. H 0.75m, ext. H 0.9m) NNE-SE and by a scarp (H 1.55m) elsewhere. The bank is relatively narrow and insubstantial and resembles a field boundary. The scarp has a slight internal lip and is topped NW-N by a concentration of stones (Wth 1.4m). The interior is split-level with the change in level marked by a low NW-facing scarp (max. H 0.6m) bisecting the interior slightly NW of the centre. The scarp retains dilapidated stone facing in parts. To SE of the scarp the interior is level, grassy and clear of overgrowth. The area to NW of the dividing scarp slopes down to NW and is strewn with moss-covered stone and dotted with clumps of bushes and brambles. There is a possible souterrain (SL021-099003-) in the N half of the interior and a holy well (SL021-099002-) in the NW quadrant.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a drumlin; in Kiltycloghan graveyard (SL027-011002-), just N of the centre. Only the W wall stands (L c. 9.6m; H c. 2m; Wth 0.8m) of the church indicated as a rectangular structure (c. 15m E-W; c. 10m N-S) on the 1914 OS 6-inch map. A survey of the graveyard in 1942 (SMR (1989) file) recorded two stones which were part of ogee-headed window lights; one of these is now in the NMI. Both arches are cusped and have recessed spandrels. Also recorded was part of a door jamb and a moulded arch-stone. These stones (SL027-011005-; SL027-011007-) are all 15th/16th-century in date and came from the church. This was the parish church of Ballysumaghan which was noted in an inquisition of 1584 (O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 248-9).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

This was recorded as 'Ardleebeg Fort' in 1836 (OSNB vol. 1, 156).

A trapezoidal graveyard (c. 60m NW-SE; c. 40m NE-SW at NW end; c. 50m NE-SW at SE end) enclosed by a stone wall. It was extended c. 25m to the NW prior to 1894 and quernstones found here are in the NMI (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney). A small walled-off area against the W wall is the burial place of the Cogan family. The fragmentary remains of the medieval parish church of Ballynakill (SL027-094001-) are in the centre of the interior. It has been noted that the memorials are arranged in an arc in the SE quadrant, perhaps indicating the former existence of a curved enclosing element around the graveyard (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, on a rocky bluff, c. 40m NW of the Douglas River. A raised circular area (21.5m N-S; 21.6m E-W) defined S-NE by a stony bank (Wth 3m; int. H 0.25m; ext. H 1.5m) with a pronounced external face and a low internal lip and elsewhere by the steep fall of ground (H 4m) which drops to a narrow terrace from which there is a further fall to the base of the bluff. Many rough angular stone protrudes from the sides and top of the bank. The stony top of the bank at W appears more regular and may represent wall footings (Wth c. 1m). The interior is generally level but with an uneven surface. A low N-facing scarp (H 0.5m) marks a drop in the ground level in the N half (3m SSW of the bank). Traces of a similar scarp on a NNE-SSW axis are evident in the E third of the interior. At NE an irregular depression (c. 5m NW-SE) is quarried into the scarp and extends c. 5m to SW into the interior. A small portion (c. 3m NE-SW; 2m NW-SE) of the scarp at SW is also dug away.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In boggy ground, at the W end of a former lake named 'Castle Lough' on the 1838 OS 6-inch map and below the former shoreline. Views are restricted due to the surrounding drumlins. A roughly circular low-mound crannog (17m N-S; 18.5m E-W; H 1.1m), indicated by a broken circle on the 1910-11 OS 6-inch map. The surface in the centre is fairly even with only a few stones exposed and it slopes gently down towards the edges. Two depressions were noted, the larger (7m N-S; 8m E-W; D 0.2m) at the SW edge, the smaller (1.5m N-S) at the SE edge. Just inside the E edge are two piles of stones, 1.5m apart (N pile: 1.65m N-S; 1.3m E-W: S pile: 2.45m N-S; 1.2m E-W). The piles, which face the lake, may represent an entrance. The edge of the crannog drops c. 0.45m sharply in all directions and is skirted by a 4m long chain of subangular stones (diam. 0.4m) along the NE arc. The crannog is generally overgrown with grass and surrounded by a band (Wth 7m) of high rushes that may indicate its full extent. A lacustrine enclosure (SL027-163003-) is c. 100m to NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

On the top of a gravel knoll (c. 80m E-W; c. 60m N-S) surrounded by bog and reclaimed grassland. The knoll is approached via a causeway (L c. 30m; Wth c. 4m; H c. 0.8m) from the SE. On top of the knoll is a rectangular bawn (20m N-S; 26m E-W) with fragmentary remains of a tower (SL021-068----) at its SW corner and a gateway near the S end of its E wall. The bawn gateway is situated near the S end of the E side, overlooking the causeway. Only the S side of the gateway opening survives; there is no indication of a structure inside but the ground level dips steeply down towards the opening. Flanking the gateway is a single gun loop on either side. There are no other apparent features on the bawn wall though stretches of it have been repaired and rebuilt in the recent past.

Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC with revisions by Patrick F. O'Donovan and Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 20 June 2011

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, within the demesne of Markree Castle (SL026-038----). An oval steep-sided conical earthen mound (H 5.5m), with an oval summit (30.5m N-S; 21.5m E-W) which slopes down gently from the rim towards the centre. Attached to the N side of the mound, but separated from it by a fosse (Wth 3m; D 0.5m), is a rectangular area (50m E-W; 15m N-S), possibly a bailey (SL026-031001-) which is raised c. 2.5m above the external ground level. This area is covered by dense scrub overgrowth, but the mound is under grass. The castle was probably built to command a ford, in the vicinity of Ballygrania Bridge c. 400m to the W, across the Arrow or Unshin River.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, straddling a low ridge with a steep W-facing slope at the base of which is an expanse of flat damp pasture. A substantially raised circular platform (28.6m N-S; 26m E-W) defined by a scarp (H 2.45m at E, 3.55m at W), topped by a low slumped stony bank (Wth 2-3m; int. H 0.5m) NW-W. The base of the platform is surrounded by a fosse (Wth 6m) NNW-SSW outside of which is a berm (Wth 10-11m). The berm continues around the base of the platform SSW-NNW, where the fosse is absent. A low bank (Wth 1.5m; H 0.2m) tops the inner edge of the berm while a similar bank (Wth 1.5m; H 0.4m) is evident SE-S on its outer edge. At its outer edge the berm has a pronounced scarp (H 1.7m at E; 3.5m at W) that drops to an external fosse (Wth 3.5m) NNW-SSW. On the W half of the rath the enclosing elements are built up or adapted to compensate for the steep natural slope. Both fosses are clearly defined NW-SSW where they cut through elevated ground but peter out elsewhere. The interior has an even surface with much stone protruding randomly from the sod. The W and SW portions of the interior are raised to compensate for the natural hillslope. The entrance is at E where there is a broad poorly defined gap (Wth 6m) in the bank and a ramped slope to corresponding causeways (Wth 3m) across the fosses.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In flat marshy pasture, bordered to E by a low ridge. A high oval mound (c. 50m NE-SW; c. 35m NW-SE; H 4m) with broad steeply sloping sides and a flat top (36.5m NE-SW; 20m NW-SE), possibly a modified natural feature. The base of the mound is defined by a fosse (Wth 3m), visible as a slight depression S-NE but more clearly defined NW-NE; elsewhere the fosse appears to be masked by an expanse of marshy ground. Outside the fosse at SW is a low stony rise (Wth 3m; H 0.3m) that may be the only remnant of an outer bank. Occupying most of the top the mound is an oval flat-topped platform (21m NE-SW; 12m NW-SE) defined by a scarp (H 0.6m). A gap (Wth 1m) separates the platform from remnants of a bank (Wth c. 2m; ext. H 1m) along the edge of the mound S-NE. Where there is no bank the gap that separates the platform from the edge of the mound is wider (Wth 1-2m). Immediately outside the bank SSE-SW, a gently sloping terrace (Wth 2.5-3m) breaks the steep slope of the mound. A shallow linear depression (6-7m N-S; 2m E-W) at the N end of the platform appears to be the result of quarrying. A semicircular quarry pit (4-5m N-S; 3m E-W) dug into the N slope of the mound has partially destroyed a possible causewayed entrance ramp. Another enclosure (SL026-035----) lies c. 50m to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

Crowning the N end of an elongated oval hillock bordered to S and W by a flat expanse of boggy ground. A roughly oval level area (14m E-W; c. 19m N-S) defined SW-E by a low scarp (H 0.5m), cut into the natural break of slope, and elsewhere by a slight stony rise. Outside the N half of the enclosure, the hillslope is steep (H 4-5m at W and E, c. 3m at N) but at S is more gradual. The N slope of the hill appears gently terraced and the base of the slope NW-N is scarped (H 1m). A low bank (Wth 2m; H 0.5m), 2.6m to N of the scarp, curves NNW-N around the base of the hill and is possibly the remains of an outer enclosing element. There are field boundaries immediately to N, E and S. Another enclosure (SL026-034----) lies c. 50m to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In a coniferous forest, on flat ground. A row of three stones, two of which are upright, aligned NNE-SSW. The NNE stone (c. 0.75m x 0.6m) is prostrate but when upright would have been at least 1.6m high. The centre stone is the tallest (H 1.7m; 0.8m x 0.55m) and its long axis is transverse to the alignment of the row. The SSW stone (H 0.6m; 0.6m x 0.6m) is also upright. The stones are known locally as 'Clogh a gadaide or the Thief's stone' (O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 239). (Kilgannon 1926, 241-2)

source_data.original_text:
On the NE end of a low steep-sided ridge with excellent view in all directions. A circular area (int. diam. c. 36m N-S; c. 38m E-W) defined NNW-ESE by a round-topped earthen bank (Wth 1.7m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 1.8m) and WSW-WNW by a low scarp (H 0.6m). No visible remains of the enclosing element elsewhere. The steep natural slope of the ridge marks the limit of the rath. The bank is skirted externally by a broad level platform (Wth 5.2m) from which the ground slopes down naturally. The rath is named 'Lisboy Fort' on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. There is a possible souterrain (SL020-221001-) in NE quadrant. The bank and platform are engulfed in overgrowth and a coppiced hazel wood occupies a large part of the interior. There is a lane immediately to NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Not included in the SMR (1989) but listed in the RMP (1995) and classified 'Bridge'. This is an overgrown humpbacked road bridge (Wth 6m; long axis NW-SE) over an unnamed stream. The roadway is no longer in public use and is now used as farm track. The bridge comprises a single segmental arch (span c. 4.5m) with rough voussoirs which are in poor repair. A low parapet wall is evident in the undergrowth. The bridge is 18th/19th century in appearance. This bridge probably dates to the post-1700 AD period.

source_data.original_text:
On a knoll in good pasture c. 150m E of Lough Dargan and c. 500m WSW of a court tomb (SL021-020----) at Carrownagh. The tomb stands in a low, oval mound (28m E-W; 12.5m N-S; max. H 1.5m). A largely destroyed full court (L 7.5m) at the E leads to a gallery (L 6m; max. Wth 2.7m). Two jambs define the entrance to the gallery and two more divide it into two chambers. The court is represented by five stones, one flanking each entrance jamb and three at its outer end. A gap between two of three outer stones may form the entrance to the court. A large stone standing on edge at the inner end of the court may have rested on the entrance jambs as a lintel. The gallery sides are intact save for a gap at the inner half of the N side of the front chamber. There are two displaced stones in this chamber. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 50-51, no. 78)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On a knoll in good pasture c. 500m ENE of the court tomb (SL021-019----) at Arnasbrack. The tomb consists of an E-facing gallery (L 5.7m; Wth 1.7-2.4m). Two courtstones flank the N side of the gallery entrance which is formed by two jambs. Another pair of jambs divide the gallery into two chambers. Two orthostats form the S side of each chamber and the N side of each is now represented by a single sidestone. There are two prostrate slabs in the court area, the larger possibly a displaced roofstone. There is no trace of mound around the structure but the gallery contains a considerable amount of fill. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 51, no. 79)

In flat wet rough grazing. Indicated as an embanked circular area (diam. c. 40m) on the 1838 OS 6-inch map and as a roughly circular raised area on the 1913 OS 6-inch map. A large steep-sided subcircular mound or natural knoll (c. 50m NW-SE; c. 45-50m; H 4-5m) with a flat oval top (c. 20m NW-SE; c. 10m NE-SW) is now evident. However, extensive quarrying of the NW-SE slopes of the knoll has obliterated its original form. On the W side the knoll has a terraced profile. From the level top there is a gentle slope (H 1.3m) that levels out to a terrace (Wth 3.7m) defined at outer edge by a scarp (H 1m). Stones protrude from the scarp in parts. The scarp drops to another gently sloping terrace (Wth 3.4m) from which there is a fall of 1.75m to the base of the knoll. The base of the knoll is scarped to a vertical face (H 0.9m) but this appears to be a relatively recent feature. To S there is a shallow depression (Wth 2.7m) at the base of the knoll, defined on its outer edge by a slight rise in ground level. It may represent a fosse or a drain but cannot be traced elsewhere. A hut site (SL021-117----) is located on a low elevation c. 30m to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In undulating grassland, prominently sited at the top of a steep SSE-facing slope. A conical earthen mound (H c. 3m) with a flat oval summit (27m E-W; 22.5m N-S) is enclosed along its rim by a moss-covered stony bank (Wth 2m; int. H 0.55m). Externally the stony bank merges with the steep sloping side of the mound. The base of the mound is enclosed by a shallow and indistinct fosse (Wth c. 3-4m) except WSW-W where it is steep-sided (D 0.7m; Wth 4.3m). Ash trees, hawthorn, blackthorn and brambles grow around the perimeter of the mound and blackthorn bushes and clumps of brambles dot the summit. At ENE is a gentle ramp-like slope on the mound's side, corresponding with a gap in the bank (Wth 2.3m) at the summit. According to Milligan (1890-91, 577), this may be one of the castles captured by O'Donnell in 1516 during one of his raids. Killross parish church (SL021-056001-) lies 700m to the ENE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, located in the level base of a broad natural depression ringed by rising ground. The Ballygawley Mountains form a dramatic backdrop on the horizon at N-NE. A circular area (45m E-W) enclosed by a broad earth and stone bank (Wth 5.5m; int. H 0.7m; ext. H 0.7m) with the remains of stone kerbing along the internal bank face along the E arc. The entrance (Wth 9m) is at E. A field boundary curves around the bank along the NE arc.
There is a mound barrow (SL021-102---) 300m to NE and a portal tomb (SL021-058----) 380m to NNE.

Straddling the NE-facing slope of a low rise, bordering flat marshy ground to NNW and undulating rising ground E-SW. H 0.3m) is evident NE-W. The entrance is at NE, where the scarp is very low and there is hint of a causeway across the fosse. The interior has an uneven undulating surface. In the SE quadrant there is a very slightly raised U-shaped area (c. 8m E-W; c. 6m N-S) defined N-SE by a slight stony scarp (H 0.3m). An earthwork (SL021-119----) lies c. 50m to WNW.

source_data.original_text:
On rolling pasture with a view northwards to Slieve Daeane and north-westwards to Knocknarea. The structure is aligned W-E and stands in a mound of irregular plan (L 16.7m; max. Wth 8.8m; H 1.5m at W falling to 0.2m at E). Three collapsed stones at the W may represent a facade. To the E of these there is a gallery (L at least 7m; max. Wth 1.8m) represented by five orthostats to the N and six to the S. About 1.5m beyond the E end of the S side of the gallery there is another stone which could be an outer-wall stone or buttress. A line of outer-walling represented by three orthostats and two fallen examples lies to the N of the gallery. At the E end of this line there are three small displaced stones and another just south of them. A further example rests on the E end of the mound. There are three displaced stones in the gallery the largest of which stands on end. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 52, no. 81)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on the NW-facing slope of a ridge. The remains of a sunken flat-bottomed linear road (L 81.6m NW-SE; Wth 6.5m; D c. 0.8m) are visible in the SW corner of a field. An aerial photograph (IASAP, 3043088-9) shows faint traces of the road continuing into the field to NW. This is possibly the remains of a mass-path which is known to have existed in this area (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). The remains of the late medieval Kilross church and graveyard (SL021-056001-; SL021-056002-) are c. 100m to the N.

raw_items.raw_text: investigated in the 1920s by Henry Morris

source_data.original_text:
In undulating grassland, located on top of a low ridge, close to the break of slope on the N side, where ground falls away steeply. The elevated position provides extensive views. The Ballygawley Mountains loom on the near horizon at NW−NE, with gaps in their range allowing views of Knocknarae at NW and the Dartrys to N. There are distant views of Kesh Corann at S, Knocknashee at SSW and the Ox Mountains at SW.
Compact circular mound (7m N−S; 6m 6−W; H 1.15m at N, 0.7m at S) with a domed profile, slightly flattened on top. The N slope is higher, and somewhat more broadly slumped, enhanced by the natural fall of ground. The mound appears to be largely earthen, but medium to large-sized stones protrude in parts. It is grass-covered and a single sycamore tree grows on top. According to local information, this mound was investigated in the 1920s by Henry Morris (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney), but the results of this investigation were never published.
There is a portal tomb (SL021-058----) 135m to N, and an embanked enclosure (SL021-051----) 325m to WSW.

raw_items.raw_text: built by Cornet Cooper in the middle of the 17th century
Markree Castle was rebuilt in the 18th century
in 1802 it was enlarged and castellated
in 1866 it was further enlarged and remodelled
ornate gothic gateways built in the 1830s

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, in a mature demesne landscape. The remains of a 17th-century house survive where they were incorporated into the SW end of the present 18th/19th-century Markree Castle. The 17th-century remains consist of three walls (T 1.35m), three storeys high, built of random rubble limestone with roughly dressed quoins. The SW wall (L 19.1m) retains its full length, the NW wall (L 20.9m) is incomplete, whilst there is only a short return (L 5.85m) of the SE wall. Numerous window and door opes have been inserted into the walls. The NW wall has a slight external base-batter. A very slight ledge, on the exterior wall-face, marks the division between the basement and ground floor. According to O'Rorke ([1889], vol. 2, 349) the earlier house was built by Cornet Cooper in the middle of the 17th century. Markree Castle was rebuilt in the 18th century as a three-storey structure and in 1802 it was enlarged and castellated; in 1866 it was further enlarged and remodelled (Bence-Jones 1988, 201-2). The demesne retains many estate features including ornate gothic gateways built in the 1830s (Howley 1993, 98 and fig. 162) and a large icehouse. Two raths (SL026-039----; SL026-075----), a circular enclosure (SL026-072----) and a possible earthwork (SL026-166----) are within the demesne.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on top of a rise; the ground slopes down to E and S of the rath. A circular platform (diam. at top 29m; diam. at base c. 55m; H c. 5m) with sloping sides, enclosed on top by an earthen bank (Wth 4m; int. H 0.6m) topped by one course (Wth 1m) of loose stones. The base of the platform is defined on the upslope by a fosse (Wth 5m; D 0.6m) NW-NE and by a terrace (Wth 2.5m; H 1.1m) elsewhere. The fosse and terrace are in turn enclosed by another terrace, widest along the N arc of the rath (Wth 19.5m; H 3m) but still substantial along the S arc (Wth c. 10m; H 2m). The entrance (Wth 2m) at NNE, with remains of stone lining, has been widened to c. 5m and is approached from the exterior by a gently sloping ramp and a causeway across the fosse. The interior slopes distinctly down to E. Recorded in 1836 as the 'Big Fort' (OSNB vol. 1, 159).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In poorly drained undulating pasture, at the E end of a ridge. A raised circular area (int. diam. 26m) enclosed by two earthen banks with an intervening fosse. The inner bank is highest along the E arc (Wth 4m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 1.1m) with only a slight internal lip along the W arc. The outer bank (Wth 2.6m; ext. On a low rise, in low-lying poorly drained rough grazing. A raised circular area (diam. 21m) enclosed by two earthen banks with an intervening fosse (Wth 3m) and traces of a possible third bank. The inner bank (Wth 3m; max. int. H 0.8m; ext. H 1.6m) is generally low internally (H 0.4m) with traces of internal and external stone kerbing. Gaps (Wth 1m) occur in the inner bank at N and NE. The middle bank is substantial (Wth 4.5m; int. H 1.1m; ext. H 1.2m) SW-N, truncated by a drain and field boundary at N and elsewhere evident as a low grass-covered rise (Wth 3m). Traces of a possible outer bank (Wth 3m; int. H 0.6m; ext. H 0.2m) were noted 3m outside the middle bank in places S-NNW. The interior is grass-covered and the perimeter is overgrown with trees. Another rath (SL027-062----) lies c. 60m to NE. According to local information, the name 'Bullaunoge' indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map c. 30m to E, applied to a spring well now disused and choked with overgrowth.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Located in a pasture field, on the E-facing slope of a small hillock, 100m W of Kilross church (SL021-056001-) and graveyard (SL021-056002-). There is a stream 30m to E. 
This medieval cross, of unusual and striking design, lay on its side partly buried in the ground, its sculpted features concealed, until it was uncovered and set upright in August 2018.
It consists of a massive rectangular sandstone block (total H c. 1.4m; Wth 0.65m; T 0.49m), sculpted with short protruding arms to create the effect of a cross. The stubby arms (projecting Wth 0.16m; H 0.17m; L 0.34m) are rectangular in shape, and disproportionally small relative to the bulk of the stone. They protrude 0.16m from the narrow sides of the stone, 0.24m below the top. They are flush with the NE face of the stone, separated only by a slight dressed indentation. They do not, however, extend across the full thickness of the stone, ending 0.15-0.16m short of the SW face. The arm on the SE side is somewhat rougher in form, possibly at least partly as a result of weathering.
On the broad NE face of the stone, there is an incised outline of a double-line Greek cross (H c. 53m; Wth 0.52m) with a square centre and expanded rectangular terminals; the design is now partly eroded. The incised cross fills most of the space on the top half of this side, with its horizontal arms, which span almost the full width of the stone, in line with the protruding stone arms.
High on the opposite (SW) side, an oval sculpted protrusion (H 0.21; Wth 0.19m) stands 0.08-0.1m proud of the stone surface. This represents a human head, but its surface is now rough and abraded, with no clearly defined facial features evident. The two corners at the top of the stone, on either side of the head, have each been cut back to a broad sloping angle, which serves to accentuate the 3-dimensional form of the head. The position of the head, relative to the stone arms of the cross, appears to reference the crucified Christ. Lower on the same side, 0.95m below the top, a horizontal moulded band (H 0.1m) extends across the width of the stone; it is evident as a shallow, double shelf, protruding c. 0.05m from the stone surface. This provides a decorative base to the cross, below which it is likely to have been embedded in the ground or set in some supportive structure.
A rectangular, vertical-sided, flat-based slot or socket (L 0.3m; Wth 0.11m; D 0.13m) is cut into the flat top of the block. The upper edge of each long side is slightly splayed. This socket is likely to have held another element of the cross, now lost: possibly a sculpted stone cap or another smaller cross of stone or even wood.
A number of very small hemispherical pits or hollows (max. diam. 0.02-0.03m; D 0.015-0.02m) can be seen on the NE side of the stone, above and to the side of the incised cross. Some are surrounded by a slight discoloration oF the stone surface. The nature of these holes is as yet uncertain.
Shallow, narrow fissures or indentations, part of the natural fabric of the stone, are evident on all sides. Two pronounced fissures/cracks on the NE side extend from close to the base of the stone obliquely across the surface, and intrude on the lower part of the incised cross.

The history of the cross -where it stood originally and how long it was buried at its current location- is uncertain. In the mid-1800’s the OS name books recorded ‘two stones, holy water pots (fonts), one is built in the road’ (SL021-055001-; SL021-055002-) (OSNB no. 2, 246); they were indicated on the 1837 OS 6-inch map as ‘Fonts’, located in the field boundary on the S side of this field, a few meters from the current position of the cross. Later in the 19th century, Wood-Martin (1882, 352), recorded the following local tradition: ‘The church and burial-ground at Kilross were reputed to have been formerly situated on the opposite side of the rivulet which flows near them. One night, in council assembled, the occupants of the graveyard came to the conclusion that they were too tightly packed, and next morning the church and church-yard were found transported to their present position. The two wells, however, which were in the old burying-ground remained in their original position, and two large rocks, one of them sculptured, and called the "holy-water stone" mark the site of these “fonts”.’ 
Wood-martin’s large ‘sculptured’ rock may have been a bullaun stone, but it may well have been this cross: the socket on the upper surface naturally fills with water, and could have been interpreted locally as a 'holy water stone'. 
In light of the discovery of the cross, the legend of the changed location of the church and graveyard is interesting, and may reflect a folk memory of an ecclesiastical site which was older and more extensive than the current church remains suggest.
In the 1980’s two 'pillar stones' (SL021-105001-; SL021-105002-) were noted lying on, or embedded in, the ground in this general area; one of these may have been the buried cross.

source_data.original_text:
Located on terrace on an E-facing terrace on a ridge in sharply undulating terrain. Ground rises to W, restricting views, and falls away to E to flat, damp ground. 
This enclosure is not indicated on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps; it is visible in aerial imagery. 
It was levelled at an unknown date in the past, but the ephemeral outline of a roughly circular area (diam. c. 28m) can still be traced at ground level, crossed roughly centrally by a N−S field fence/property boundary. 
To W of the field fence, a slight curving scarp (Wth slope 3.5-3.8m; ext. H 0.6m) can be traced on the SW arc, petering out at NW to an area of irregular N-sloping ground. To E of the fence, the NE arc can be traced as a levelled scarp (Wth slope c. 4m; ext. H 0.5m) following a natural contour, which becomes increasingly indistinct on the SE arc. There is a rath (SL027-003----) 180m to ESE and a wedge tomb (SL021-054----) 260m to NNW.

Notified to NMS by Jean-Charles Caillère.

In 1836 'two holy water pots (fonts)' (see SL021-055002-), one of which was built into the road, were recorded in Kilross townland (OSNB no. 2, 246). These were indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map and named 'Fonts', c. 80m W of Kilross Church (SL021-056001-). The area is covered with overgrowth and they were not located. Wood-Martin (1882 vol. 3, 352) mentioned that two wells in this area were marked by 'two large rocks, one of them sculptured, and called the "holy-water stone"...' The precise nature of these 'holy water pots' is uncertain, and the possibility that these were bullaun stones cannot be excluded.

The precise nature of these 'holy water pots' is uncertain, and the possibility that these were bullaun stones cannot be excluded.

In the SE quadrant of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL020-171003-). An arc of a stone wall (C c. 16m; Wth 2.3m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 1.3m), which is over 1m thicker than any adjacent walls, defines the graveyard WSW-NW. The wall comprises a basal course of large stones topped with smaller stones. Burials are located in a roughly oval area (c. 11m E-W; c. 8m N-S) defined by a collapsed stone wall at N and S, by a low scarp (H 0.6m) along E arc, while at the W arc it is open onto the graveyard wall. Burials marked by uninscribed stones are randomly scattered in the E half of the oval area while in the W half they occur in three parallel rows (on a NNE-SSW axis) roughly 0.9m apart. There is a standing stone (SL020-171004-), known as 'Cloghanaspig' [Cloch an Easpaig-the Bishop's stone], at SW. The graveyard is indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as a small rectangular enclosure (c. 12m N-S; c. 10m E-W) and named 'Killeran Grave Yard'. It is known locally as a 'children's burial ground' (SL020-171010-). There is a tradition of a possible church (SL020-171001-) within the interior. There is a holy well (SL020-171005-) c. 80m to the S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

H 1.6m) to SSE (T 1.4m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 1.9m). In general, the base of this wall, which is composed of large stones at S and NW, retains the external face of a natural scarp. A cashel (SL020-171006-) abuts the edge of the enclosure at NE. A graveyard and a possible church site (SL020-171002-; SL020-171001-) and a standing stone (SL020-171004-) are in the SE quadrant. A holy well (SL020-171005-) lies c. 50m to the S.

Inside the SW edge of a graveyard (SL020-171002-). An upright rectangular limestone pillar (H 0.9m; Wth 0.5m; T 0.26m; long axis NNW-SSE). Small moss-covered stones are piled around its base. O'Rorke ([1889], vol. 2, 247) recorded that the stone, popularly known as 'Clogh an Easpuig' [the Bishop's stone], marks the resting place of a bishop and, according to local tradition, the part of it which is sunken in the ground is ogham-inscribed. A small roughly oval stone (L 0.3m; Wth 0.25m; T 0.7m) lies at the base of the E face of the pillar. It has a flat base and a slightly rounded upper surface which contains five shallow circular holes with rounded bottoms (diam. 0.02m; D 0.03-0.05m) which, according to local tradition, were used to hold candles.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In low-lying wet ground interspersed with rock outcrops, at the southern foot of a low ridge. A damp grass-covered area (diam. c. 3.5m) is defined on its W side by a 4m long arc of mostly contiguous stones; a single stone (0.65m x 0.9m x 0.5m) lies 1m E of the N end of the arc and another (0.8m x 0.5m x 0.35m) 3.8m E of the S end. According to local information, the well was formerly completely enclosed by a stone wall but this was partially demolished when an adjacent ash tree fell during a hurricane c. 1958. O'Rorke ([1889], vol. 2, 247) mentioned that the well was '…till recently…frequented by crowds from all quarters including the town of Sligo'. In 1942-4 it was recorded as 'Tober Domhnaigh' and also that it had become known as 'Tobervanny' and was no longer visited (ITA). There is an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL020-171003-) c. 50m to N and a graveyard (SL020-171002-) c. 80m to N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, midway on a gentle E-facing slope and abutting the NE edge of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL020-171003-). A D-shaped area (dims. 21m NE-SW) with a straight SW side (L 26m) defined NW-SE by the remains of a substantial stone wall, covered with overgrowth; the straight side is shared with the adjoining ecclesiastical enclosure (SL020-171003-). Inner and outer stone facing is evident at E giving a total wall width of 3.75m; some outer stone facing is also evident at W and N. Field clearance stones have been piled against the outer face of the enclosing wall NW-ENE as have a couple of large boulders (L 3m; H 2m) at SE. The entrance (Wth 0.8m) is at S where the cashel wall meets that of the adjoining enclosure. Immediately E of the entrance is a short stretch of collapsed wall (L 2.5m). The interior is level and under pasture; the E half is 0.5-2m higher than the surrounding ground while the W half is c. 1m lower than the interior of the adjoining enclosure. Along the W arc the straight cashel wall revets a natural scarp. Along the N and S arcs the cashel wall is topped by a later stone wall.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on top of a sheer cliff, overlooking Lough Dargan immediately to its N. The remains of a castle built in 1422 by Conor Mac Donagh (Timoney and O'Brien 2000) now survives in two sections, 25m apart. Both are built of uncoursed limestone rubble bonded with a lime mortar. The E block consists of a SE corner (8.85m E-W; 3.5m N-S; T 2.1m) now standing to two storeys but originally higher. At ground-floor level, where the wall breaks off, part of a doorway survives. This gives access to mural stairs, lit by a series of slit windows, that rise to the SE corner and then continue through the E wall to first-floor level where a door, now fragmentary, gave access to a first-floor chamber. There is a large ruined window embrasure in the S wall. The ground-floor chamber was covered by a rounded wicker-centred vault but only the springing courses of this now survive, along the S wall. There are four blocks of fallen masonry, parts of a vault, lying on the ground in the vicinity of the E block. 
The W block also stands to two storeys, but was originally higher, and only a N-S length of walling survives (L 5.2m; T 2m). At ground level is an angled passageway, with a lintelled door. At the S end of the passage is the corner of a chamber covered by a rounded wicker-centred vault. At first-floor level there is a short right-angled return on the W face of the wall. A curved scarp, partially rock outcrop and partially stone facing, arcs between the two blocks on their S side. This is probably the footings of a bawn wall (SL021-045004-); the W block is likely to be a mural tower connected to the bawn wall, whereas the E block is probably the remains of the main tower. Immediately S of the castle are the ruins of a number of 18th/19th-century buildings (SL021-045002-, SL021-045003-) and a walled garden(s), that were still in use in the 1830s (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). The site continued to be part of the estate of the nearby mid-18th-century Castledargan House.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On the top of an E-W ridge at the edge of a N-facing limestone bluff overlooking Lough Dargan. A slightly raised roughly D-shaped area (dims. c. 30m ENE-WSW) with a straight N side (L 30m). The interior is defined on the straight side by the bluff and elsewhere by a ruined stone wall. The wall survives as a sod-covered stone bank (Wth c. 1.7m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.65m) but stones protruding in parts indicate that it is composed of a rubble core with internal and external stone facing. It is best-preserved NE-S but is very degraded and broken by numerous gaps SW-NW. The interior is level but uneven, broken by E-W bands of limestone pavement. A faint linear cropmark crosses the E edge of the interior on a NNW-SSE axis intersecting at the N end with a perpendicular line that can be traced for c. 10m to WSW across the N of the interior. These features may be the remains of later field boundaries. The cashel is located towards the W end of the cliff at a point where a series of broken terraces allow access to the base of the cliff and from there to the lakeshore. A cashel (SL021-046003-) is visible on a lower undulation of the same ridge c. 150m to SW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

On top of an E-W ridge, at the edge of a steep bluff. An oblong area (26m E-W; 16m N-S) defined NNW-NNE by the break of slope at the top of the bluff and elsewhere by a slight moss-covered rise (Wth 1.5m) outside which the ground falls away gently in a natural slope. At the base of the slope, at a distance of 8-10m from the inner wall, is an outer enclosing wall. It is difficult to trace NE-SE and is truncated in parts by small areas of quarrying. It survives S-NW as a sod-covered stony bank (Wth c. 3m) topping a low scarp (H 0.7m). A third wall and outer fosse are visible as cropmarks in an aerial photograph (IASAP, 3043089-90) along the WNW arc outside and separated from the second wall by an intervening fosse. A cliff-edge fort (SL021-046002-) is visible on higher ground c. 150m to NE. The remains of a field system (SL021-046004-) lie in the surrounding field to E, S and W. There is a possible hut site (SL021-046006-) c. 20m to SW.

In pasture, on top of a ridge. A fragmented pattern of field boundaries, covering an area c. 300m x 90m, is visible in an aerial photograph (IASAP, 3043089-90) radiating to E, S and W of a cashel (SL021-046003-). On the ground, the field boundaries are evident as slight stony rises covered with moss. Immediately to W of the cashel, the walls enclose small subrectangular fields of unequal size (e.g. 25m N-S x 12.5m E-W; 16m N-S x 45-50m E-W) laid out axially along a natural E-W elevation. The shape of the fields is largely dictated by natural contours. A possible hut site (SL021-046006-) is located c. 20m SW of the cashel and appears to be associated with this field system.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating marshy terrain, on the N side of a road, in the NW corner of Kilross graveyard (SL021-056002-). Only the SW corner of the church stands (int. 4.95m E-W; 2.8m N-S). This is built of mortared roughly coursed limestone. Along the internal face of the W wall is the springing line of a wicker-centred vault which covered a ground-floor apartment at the W end of the church. A window lighting this area survives in the S wall, and has a splayed and lintelled embrasure and a single flat-headed light. At first-floor level part of W side of another window embrasure survives. This is the remains of the late medieval parish church of Kilross (O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 247; M. A. Timoney 2002b, 57). A road (SL021-057----) lies c. 100m to the S. In 1836 'two holy water pots (fonts)' (SL021-055001-, SL021-055002-) were recorded in this townland (OSNB vol. 2, 246); these were probably the two 'Fonts' indicated and named on the 1838 OS 6-inch map, c. 80m to the W. This area is covered with scrub overgrowth and these features could not be located.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
A rectangular graveyard (c. 50m E-W; c. 30m N-S) enclosed by a low repointed stone wall. It is entered through a gateway, with plain limestone piers and a wrought iron gate, in the S wall. In the NW corner are the fragmentary remains of Kilross parish church (SL021-056001-). Most of the headstones are of 19th- and 20th-century date but the earliest noted was dated 1721. There are also a number of low uninscribed grave-markers, six chest-tombs and a number of recumbent slabs. The most notable plot is a 19th-century walled enclosure, with three memorials to the Ormsbys of Castledargan, which overlies the line of the S wall of the church. There are no visible remains of the foundations of a possible building (noted by M. B. Timoney, pers. comm.) (SL021-056004-) to the ESE of the church. Three quernstones (SL021-056003-) have been found in the graveyard, two of which are in the NMI. A road (SL021-057----) lies c. 100m to the S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

raw_items.raw_text: unpublished archaeological assessment report for Castledargan Golf Course, 2000

source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified 'Castle Possible' and 'Castle Possible Site' respectively. It had originally been classified as a possible castle because, according to Martin Timoney (pers. comm. SMR (1989) file), there was the 'stump of old tower behind house'. This tower was not located according to the SMR (1989) file. According to Timoney (unpublished archaeological assessment report for Castledargan Golf Course, 2000, 12) the above information was given by a local in the mid-1970s and that Martin Timoney had not seen the tower himself. In his report he describes the above as 'an old water pump' with a walled garden curving around it which could have been 'interpreted as being a tower'. In relation to the Country House, O'Brien (2000, 6) states in his report that, there is no documentary evidence relating to a building date. However in the light of a possible mid-1700s date suggested by architect Dr. F. O'Dwyer (Timoney c. 2000, 13), O'Brien (2000, 6) states that because of 'the improving family circumstances … and the presence of more that one household in the 1949 Elphin Census, the building of Castledargan House in the mid-1700s would not be and unreasonable supposition.' Martin Timoney (phonecall July 2003) adds that three large beams of worked oak with mortice holes and dowels were found in the house, reused as lintels. The house is dated to c. 1750 with much rebuilding in the 1850s.


Compiled by Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Date of upload: 11 January 2012

Not included in the SMR (1989). Listed in the RMP (1995) and classified 'Church'. This folly is incorporated into the SSE wall of an enclosed orchard immediately to E of Castledargan House (SL021-109001-). The avenue to the house is located on the SE side of the wall. An intervening border of rhododendron bushes obscures the SE face of the wall. The wall (8.4m NE-SW; H 2.7m) consists of coursed, mortared stone. A round-arched doorway with cut-stone surround is centrally placed in the wall. To E of the door is a round arched window with a cut-stone surround. Both the door and window openings have been carefully blocked up with drystone walling. At the NE end of the wall, two coursed stones protrude from the base of the NW face, possibly a remnant of a return wall to NW. This is not a church or any ancient feature but rather a demesne feature or folly in the walled garden of Castledargan (ibid.). This monument is post-1700 AD in date.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

In pasture, within the demesne of Markree Castle (SL026-038----). The possible motte (SL026-031----) consists of an oval steep-sided conical earthen mound (H 5.5m), with an oval summit (30.5m N-S; 21.5m E-W) which slopes down gently from the rim towards the centre. Attached to the N side of the mound, but separated from it by a fosse (Wth 3m; D 0.5m), is the possible bailey, a rectangular area (50m E-W; 15m N-S) which is raised c. 2.5m above external ground level. This area is covered by dense scrub overgrowth, but the mound is under grass. The castle was probably built to command a ford, in the vicinity of Ballygrania Bridge c. 400m to the W, across the Arrow or Unshin River.

source_data.original_text:
This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn M in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. About 400m S of a passage tomb K (SL040-093----) and a possible passage tomb (SL040-094----) and c. 80m N of another passage tomb (SL040-102----) on the N edge of a small plateau with views limited to local horizons. A small, roofless, NW-facing cruciform passage tomb rises clear of a substantially grass-grown circular cairn (diam. c. 10m; H 1m). A passage (L 1m; Wth 0.7m) is separated by a sill from a central space (L c. 0.8m; Wth c. 0.6m) opening off which are two opposed side-chambers, one to the right (L c. 1m; Wth c. 0.9m), another to the left (L c. 0.8m; Wth 0.4m) and an endchamber (L c. 0.8m; Wth 0.4m). None of the tomb orthostats exceeds 0.8m in height. Some slabs lie prostrate on the mound forward of the passage which according to Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger (1912, 330) was originally 10 feet (c. 3m) long. A small excavation of the cairn (Bergh 1987, 32) led to the recovery of human bone at the edge of the tomb. Radiocarbon dating of a human tooth yielded a date in the interval 2451 to 2039 cal BC and of charcoal a date in the interval 3370 to 3042 cal BC (Bergh 1995, 105). (Ó Nualláin 1989, 83)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn C in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. On the bog-grown northern slopes of the Bricklieve Mountains and 10m N of possible passage tomb (SL040-087----). A circular cairn (diam. 17-19m; H 1.5m) with a slight bulge at the W where there has been some slippage downslope, is crossed by a field boundary wall. Just W of the centre of the mound there is the remains of a passage (L 3m; Wth c. 0.5m) opening to the WNW. A massive lintel covers the inner end of the passage. Beyond this the N or left-hand side and rear of the chamber area is represented by tiered corbelling which extends for a further 3m to the ESE. At about mid-length the line of corbelling bulges to the N indicating the possible presence of a side recess. The corbelling rises above a substantial body of fill that hides the orthostatic structure. Some 1.2m to the S of the line of the passage and more or less opposite the northwards bulge already referred to, a roofed polygonal chamber (max. dims. 1.7m x 1.7m) is accessible from the top of the cairn. The field wall crossing the monument separates this chamber from the rest of the tomb structure and obscures their relationship but it would seem that this is a recess opening off the right-hand side of the chamber area at the end of the passage. Two orthostats form the E and W sides of this chamber and a single example closes the S end. At the northern end there are three stones arranged in the manner of a doorstone between two jambs which support a lintel now partly displaced. The design here supports the likelihood of a connection between this chamber and the structure to the N of the field wall. The roofstone of this chamber is somewhat precariously supported on a single layer of corbels, including the lintel just mentioned. The design of this tomb is uncertain but the indications are that it is cruciform in plan (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 322-3; Ó Nualláin 1989, 82)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

See linked documents with details from Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume V. County Sligo. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1989) together with a plan and sections of the monument (surveyed 1997).

On the bog-grown northern slopes of the Bricklieve Mountains and 10m S of a passage tomb (SL040-086----). The disturbed basal layers of a circular cairn (diam. 17-19m) are partly covered by a layer of peat. Structural remains are scant. Some kerbstones are visible almost 2m inside the present perimeter at the ENE and 1.5m N of these a large slab lies prostrate on the mound. Almost 3m W of the surviving kerbstones there is a set stone (L 0.7m; Wth 0.3m; H 0.75m). Some 3m NW of the last there is a set stone (H 0.85m) now leaning slightly. A large slab, one end partly buried in the cairn, leans against this stone. Some 4m to the S and close to the centre of the cairn there are two set stones at right angles to each other. One is 0.9m long and the other 0.7m and the latter, the taller of the two, is 1m high. (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 323; Ó Nualláin 1989, 82)

source_data.original_text:
This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn G in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. High on the N slope of Barrnabinnia, one of the bog-grown N-S aligned ridges forming the Bricklieve Mountains. A possible passage tomb (SL040-088----) lies c. 40m to NW and a passage tomb (SL040-09001-) c. 50m to S. A circular cairn (diam. 18-20m; H 3m) covers a well-preserved cruciform passage tomb opening to the NW. The tomb (L 5m) consists of a passage (L 2m; Wth c. 1m) leading to a chamber (L 1.7m; Wth 1.9m; H 2.3m) opening off which there are two opposed side-chambers, one to the right or W (L 0.85m; Wth 0.95m; H 1.3m), another to the left or E (L 0.85m; Wth 1.1m; H 1.4m) and an endchamber (L 1m; Wth 1m; H 1.3m). The tomb is constructed of tall, generally pillar-like uprights and these support a series of lintels and oversailing corbels capped by a large flat slab above the main chamber. Sillstones divide the passage into two compartments and are in place at the front of the two side-chambers and endchamber. Investigation of the tomb in 1911 (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 327-8, 334-5) showed that large flat slabs (some of which are still visible) had been laid as floorstones along the passage and in the chambers. The tomb contained a considerable quantity of burnt bone, some pottery fragments, stone pendants, beads and balls. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 83)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

This feature, first shown on the 1914 OS 6-inch map, lies c. 30m SE of a passage tomb (SL040-090001-) in the Carrowkeel passage tomb cemetery. A fragmented block of limestone (c. 1.7m x 1.2m x 0.5m) rests on four low rounded sandstone boulders partly buried in peat. These boulders are substantially obscured by the constituent parts of the limestone block which are tilted downwards and it is unclear if they have been deliberately placed in position or occur naturally. According to Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger (1912, 330-31), there were also three limestone slabs set on edge at the site, 'apparently placed with the intention of forming a cist'. What may be one of these stones can be recognised but its status remains uncertain. It would be necessary to remove the broken limestone block to form a reliable assessment of the nature of this feature. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 99, no. 27)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). A roofless rectangular cist (2m N-S; 1.2m E-W) constructed of four stones. One stone (L 2.15m; T 0.3m; H 0.5m) forms the E side and another (L 1.9m; T 0.4m; H 0.75m) the W side. A stone (L 1.6m; T 0.35m; H 0.55m), set slightly beyond the end of these two sidestones, marks the S end of the cist. The N end is closed by a stone (L 1.05m; T 0.2m; H 0.4m) set between the ends of the sidestones. Five stones, protruding from the ground just beyond the N end of the cist, are of uncertain origin. Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger (1912, 331) reported a local claim that the cist had been roofed but that the covering slab had been broken up by rabbit hunters. There is a passage tomb (SL040-093----) c. 20m to SW.

This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn K in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. About 130m S of and somewhat upslope from the megalithic structure (SL040-091----), 10m E of a possible passage tomb (SL040-094----) and c. 400m N of another passage tomb (SL040-101----). A round cairn (diam. 21.5-23m; H 3.5m) covers a well-preserved cruciform passage tomb opening to the NNW. The tomb (L 7.7m) consists of a passage (L 4.5m; Wth 0.65-1.1m) leading to a chamber (L 1.4m; Wth 1.9m; H 3.4m) opening off which there are two opposed side-chambers, one to the right or W (L 1.35m; Wth 1.4m; H 2.2m), another to the left or E (L 1m; Wth 1.2m; H 2.1m) and an endchamber (L 1m; Wth 1.4m; H 2m). The tomb is constructed of orthostats with dry-wall infill which support a series of lintels, a number now cracked, and oversailing corbels capped by a large flat slab above the main chamber. Sillstones divide the passage into three sections and are in place at the front of the two side-chambers and endchamber. Investigation of the tomb in 1911 (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 329) produced burnt bones, stone pendants, beads and balls, mushroom and poppy-headed antler and bone pins, and a decorated Bronze Age bowl (Ó Riordáin and Waddell 1993, 130). There is a cist (SL040-092----) c. 20m to NE. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 83)

This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn L in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. On a mountain ridge, 10m W of another passage tomb (SL040-093----) and c. 400m N of a third passage tomb (SL040-101----). This is a damaged round cairn (diam. c. 18m; H 1.5m), its perimeter peat-grown. source_data.original_text:
This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn E in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. On the bog-covered cliff-walled northern tip of one of the N-S aligned ridges that form the Bricklieve Mountains. Another passage tomb (SL040-096----) lies 200m to S. A long cairn (L 40m; min. H 2m), its perimeter partly obscured by heather-grown bog, is aligned NNW-SSE. Visible kerbstones indicate a max. width of 11m at the S. Close to the N end of the cairn there is a cruciform passage tomb. This consists of a NNW-facing main chamber (L 4m; min. Wth 0.6m, max. Wth 1.35m) divided by sills into four compartments. Opposed side-chambers, both polygonal in outline, and both c. 1m by 0.7m in dimension, open off the taller main chamber. Four orthostats are in place on each side of the main chamber and a fifth example has collapsed inwards at the inner end of the E side. Six orthostats form the sides and back of the well-preserved eastern side-chamber which is entered from the main chamber over a sillstone. Four orthostats are in place around the sides and back of the western side-chamber. Each side-chamber is roofed by a single large slab supported on corbelling. A slab laid lintel-like on the outer pair of opposed sidestones of the main chamber is a modern feature. Immediately in front of the main chamber there is a tall stone which projects outwards from the line of the E side of the structure. This stone and at least three other large stones which seem to be displaced to a lesser or greater degree suggest there may have been further structure at this end of the tomb. Bone fragments, a minute sherd of pottery, a poppy-headed and a mushroom-headed pin and portion of a boar's tusk were recovered from the tomb in 1911 (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 323-4, 332-3). At the southern end of the cairn there is a setting of stones which has been compared to a court (Ó Nualláin 1989, 75-6, no. 120, 82). If, as appears to be the case, it opened onto the end of the cairn it would have measured 5m N-S and almost the same dimension E-W. A large orthostat (L 3.3m) forms the inner end of this feature, there are two on its more westerly side and one on the opposite side. Some 2.5m NE of the court-like feature there is a small chamber opening onto the E side of the cairn. Two pairs of opposed sidestones are visible at the front of this chamber (min. L 1.5m). A roofstone and three corbels, all now partly displaced apparently due to the investigation of the site in 1911 (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 323-4, 332-3), obscure the rear of the chamber.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

See linked documents with details from Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume V. County Sligo. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1989) together with plans and sections of the monument (surveyed 1997).

Date of upload: 27 May 2013

On a little knoll in rocky pasture at the foot of the E flank of the Bricklieve Mountains. This is a gallery (L 6.3m; Wth 2m at front, 0.8m at rear) entered between two jambs at the NW, the more easterly of which is flanked by a single courtstone. There are three stones on the W side of the gallery and four on the E and it is closed by a backstone the top of which has been broken off and now lies on the ground. The gallery contains grass-grown fill which reaches to the level of the sidestones and this extends beyond the front of the monument for about 1.5m. A slab, apparently a roofstone, rests on this fill at the back of the gallery. A stone fence runs E-W across the middle of the gallery. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 75, no. 119)

This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn O in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. At the northern end of Doonaveeragh, the easternmost of the N-S aligned ridges forming the Bricklieve Mountains. A circular cairn (diam. 18-20m; H 2.5m), its lower levels grass-grown, contains towards its southern end a partly roofed chamber (L 2m; max. Wth 0.8m; H 0.9m). Built of orthostats and dry-wall infill, a narrowing of the chamber indicates a division into a shorter and narrower compartment, now roofless, to the S and a slightly wider and longer northern compartment, roofed by two slabs, one overlying the other. Both ends of the chamber are closed. It was investigated in 1911 (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 330, 336-7) when entry was gained through the roof. A decorated Bronze Age bowl was found within the chamber, resting on a pile of burnt and unburnt bones intermixed with small sandstone slabs (ibid.; Ó Riordáin and Waddell 1993,130). There is a Neolithic settlement (SL040-108----) on the lower ground to N. A cairn (SL040-100----) lies c. 200m to SSE. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 83-4)

This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn N in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. About 80m S of another passage tomb (SL040-101----) on a small plateau with views limited to local horizons. A small, roofless, NW-facing cruciform passage tomb rises clear of a substantially grass-grown circular cairn (diam. c. 7m; H c. 0.3m). A passage (L 0.8m), its right or W side missing, is separated by a sill from a central space opening off which are two opposed side-chambers, one to the right, another to the left, and an endchamber. The chambers are poorly preserved and cannot be precisely measured. The overall length of the chamber area from the inner end of the passage to the rear of the structure is 2m and overall width measured from the back of the right-hand side chamber to the back of the opposite example is 2.4m. It is clear that the right-hand side chamber is larger than that to the left. None of the tomb orthostats exceeds 0.6m in height. (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 330; Ó Nualláin 1989, 83)

source_data.original_text:
In heather-covered rough grazing, in the centre of a circular flat-topped spur of a ridge in the Bricklieve Mountains. The ground drops steeply into an upland valley to N and E and a narrow ravine separates the spur from rising ground to W where a cashel (SL040-154----) is located c. 50m to WSW. Breaks in the surrounding high ridges give views ENE to Lough Arrow, to S and on a distant ridge to N, two of the Carrowkeel passage tombs are visible. A roughly circular cairn of stones (7.5m N-S; 9.6m E-W; H 1.25m) located off-centre to N within a circular enclosure (SL040-105001-). The cairn is largely sod-covered and very dilapidated. It has been partially quarried out at NW and as a result presents an irregular, slumped profile. A ruined field boundary wall (Wth 1.5m; H 0.25m), visible as a linear heather-covered rise, bisects the enclosure on an E-W axis and clips the S edge of the cairn. From the base of the cairn the ground slopes down gently to the edge of the enclosure N-E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rough, heather-covered upland pasture in the Bricklieve Mountains, located in a shallow natural hollow on the E side of a broad plateau on top of a NNE−SSW ridge. The stone stands close to the break of slope on the E side of the ridge where ground falls away steeply into a narrow valley. It is overlooked immediately to S by a higher level of the ridge top. Upright block of limestone (H c. 2m; L 1.73m NE−SW at base; T max. c. 1.05m at base) which narrows from a broad base to a pointed top, giving the stone a pronounced triangular shape. The stone has a rough surface, partly colonised by lichen, moss and grass. There are two passage tombs (SL040-101----; SL040-102----) on a parallel ridge to E; it is possible that these were visible in the past from the stone but they are now low, heather-covered mounds and cannot be seen. Two other passage tombs (SL040-095----; SL040-096----) are located on ridge tops c. 440m to NNW and 340m to NW respectively, but are not visible from the standing stone. 

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Revised upload: 2 September 2016

source_data.original_text:
On top of a plateau of exposed limestone pavement, at the lower N end of Doonaveeragh ridge. Rising abruptly from the S end of the plateau is the upper tier of the dissected ridge on top of which is a possible passage tomb (SL040-099----) and a cairn (SL040-100----). The sides of the ridge are formed of limestone cliffs and steep scree-covered slopes. To W, a gorge separates Doonaveeragh and the higher ridge of Carrowkeel. A dense concentration of roughly circular stone-walled huts (diam. 7-15m) cover the full E-W width of the ridge. Clusters of conjoined huts intermix with huts more loosely linked by short stretches of walling or by intervening walled courtyards. In many cases the enclosing walls (Wth 1.2-1.5m) consist of an inner and outer face of slabs or boulders with a rubble core. In some instances construction appears to involve the quarrying of karst to create the interior while leaving some bedrock in situ to define the perimeter. Internal partitions and entrances flanked by large jamb slabs also occur. Herity (1974, 157-8) suggested that this complex may have been a 'passage grave township' and notes that since many of the huts are covered with blanket bog a date of before 1000BC would be probable for the complex. About 24 huts are indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map while Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger (1912, 331-2) recorded 47. An aerial photograph (CUCAP, AJO 35) taken in 1964 shows c. 80 huts. In the summer of 2003 a survey and trial excavations were carried out by Stefan Bergh, Department of Archaeology, NUI Galway, and some 152 huts were identified; a preliminary examination of the finds, which includes a plano convex flint knife, concave scrapers of chert, chert debris, pottery and bones, has led the excavator to suggest a Neolithic date for the complex (The Sligo Champion, 16-7-2003). A similar complex of huts (SL032-013004-) has been identified on Knocknashee c. 22km to NW (Norman and St Joseph 1969, 24-5).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In rough upland grazing, on a gently sloping terrace at the base of an E-facing slope in the Bricklieve Mountains. The SE side of the terrace is defined by a small rocky ravine linking two upland valleys. An oval area (31.4m N-S; 24m E-W) enclosed by a substantial sod-covered stony bank (Wth 3m; int. H 0.9m; ext. H 0.25m). The interior is grass-covered and slopes gently down to E. Abutting the wall at NW, a level semicircular area (4m NW-SE; 3m NE-SW), open to SW, is defined N-SE by a low stony scarp (H 0.45m). A gapped line of sod-covered stones, probably a ruined wall, extends from the cashel wall at ESE for c. 9.6m to NW towards the centre of the interior. Towards its NW end is a perpendicular wall extending to S. A cairn (SL040-105---) lies c. 50m to ENE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).
