source_data.original_text:
Discovered during the construction of the Curlew bypass and excavated in 1995 (Channing 1998a, 154). Two peat-covered spreads of heat-shattered stones and charcoal were found on the edge of wet ground close to Lough Arrow. The main spread (c. 11.5m x 10m) contained two roughly circular unlined troughs, 1.1m apart, cut into the subsoil. The N trough (1.95m E-W; 1.95m N-S; D 0.5m) was roughly circular in plan with straight cut sides. The S trough (1.92m N-S; 1.5m E-W; D 0.25m) was more oval in plan. The second spread (c. 5.5m x c. 2m) of burnt stones and charcoal lay c. 5m to E. The area between the two spreads had been truncated by machinery during the road construction and the excavator implies that both spreads were part of the one monument. (Channing 1995, 1-8)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rough, upland karstic pasture, located on a terrace on the NW edge of a narrow N-S ravine. The ravine forms a passage linking broad boggy valleys to N and S. Immediately to SW of the enclosure, the ground rises abruptly to a rocky plateau on the SE slope of which, c. 160m to S, there is a cashel (SL040-154----). On the ridge top on the opposite side of the ravine there is a cairn (SL040-105----) c. 150m to SSE. A ruined, vernacular stone cottage is located c. 50m to NNW. 
Sub-circular area (diam. c. 22m N-S; 23m E-W) defined by remnants of a sod-covered stone bank/wall which coincides at N-E with the rocky edge of the ravine. The curving arc of the enclosing wall (Wth c. 1.5-2m; H 0.3m) can be easily traced at SE-W where is appears as a low moss-covered rise from which large stones protrude. At SW-W it is built against rising ground and as a consequence has a more pronounced internal slump (H 0.4m). The wall peters out at W-N, and is also difficult to trace at NNE-ESE where it coincides with the break of slope at the edge of the ravine, and is overlain by a later linear field wall. The interior of the enclosure is not noticeably raised, and is marked by a growth of rushes. The surface is occasionally broken by stones. The entrance is not clearly defined but is most likely to be at NW.

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, in the Bricklieve mountains, located at the SE end on top of a limestone ridge. The ridge forms a flat topped, roughly oval island of raised ground (c. 200m NW–SE; c. 90m NE–SW), rising several meters above an undulating valley of rough pasture and bog. The ridge is defined on its perimeter by a vertical escarpment of exposed limestone, which is several meters high and relatively sheer at the E-S and W sides, but in parts at SW and at N-NE forms an easily accessible terraced slope. It is overlooked 50m to N, 100m to E, and 200m to SW by much larger, higher ridges defined by steep, limestone cliffs. There are excellent views in all directions from the enclosure, in particular, to N along a narrow valley which provides a routeway between the ridges, and immediately to SE to a broad gap which provides a natural routeway out of the mountains to lowlying grassland at S.
This consists of an oval area (21m NE–SW; 16m NW–SE) defined by a stone bank/wall. The stone bank is evident evident as a low, moss and sod-covered stony rise (Wth 1.8-2m; H 0.2-0.3m). The interior is flat and not raised above exterior ground level, and the surface is uneven and broken by low moss-covered hummocks of limestone bedrock. The outline of the enclosure is not easily discerned amidst the proliferation of irregular, moss-covered hummocks of limestone bedrock which cover the plateau surface.
Immediately to SW is the barely discernible outline of a possible enclosure (SL040-246001-) defined by a gapped line of moss-covered stones, and distinguished by its relatively stone-free interior. The two enclosures are not conjoined; there is appears to be a slight gap of less than a meter between their respective enclosing walls.

SL040-246----_02.JPG: viewed from N

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

source_data.original_text:
In rough upland pasture, located on a ridge-top terrace or narrow plateau on the E flank of the Bricklieve Mountains. The location gives excellent views over Lough Arrow. On its E side the enclosure utilises a slight natural kink or expansion at the break of slope of the terrace; from here the ground drops c. 2m to a lower terrace, and then drops more steeply in a series of further terraces before levelling out at the shores of Lough Arrow. To W of the enclosure, the plateau drops gently into a shallow valley of rush-grown, boggy ground, beyond which there are views of undulating upland terrain and higher ridges of the Bricklieves.
The enclosure consists of a circular area (diam. 16m E−W; 16m N−S) defined by a low, moss- and heather-covered stone bank (Wth c. 2m; H 0.3-0.4m). The bank is poorly preserved, slumped and gapped. A short stretch at NE, denuded of its thin covering of peaty soil, reveals that it consists of a concentration of small limestone stones. A break (Wth 2m) at SE may be an original entrance. The interior is grassy, flat and featureless, with a single hawthorn tree growing in the NW quadrant. A few hawthorn bushes grow on the stone bank/perimeter at SE−S.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a slight rise on a broad undulating upland terrace. There are excellent views to NE, E and SE over the lowland surrounding Lough Arrow. The ground rises to W and NW in series of terraces to a high ridge. A circular area (21.6m N-S; 21.6m E-W), encompassing a low natural rise, defined by an inner degraded sod-covered stony scarp (H 0.3m) with a slight internal lip (Wth c. 1m), most clearly defined SSE-SSW. An outer degraded stony scarp is evident all round, separated from the inner scarp by a narrow intervening gap (Wth 1.2m), both truncated at W by a fragment of a field boundary wall. The outer scarp is topped NNW-E by a stony bank (Wth 1.8m; H 0.4m) with traces of an inner kerb of large stones. At ENE the stony bank turns outward for c. 4m, possibly indicating the position of the entrance, and corresponding with a particularly degraded section of the inner scarp. There is a possible souterrain (SL040-125002-) in the NW quadrant of the interior and another (SL040-125003-) in the S half.

source_data.original_text:
Carn B in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. At the cliff-walled northern extremity of one of the N-S aligned ridges that form the Bricklieve Mountains. This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). A N-facing undifferentiated passage tomb, exposed in 1911 (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 321-3), stands towards the northern end of a circular cairn (diam. 27m; max. H 5m). Around the southern half of the perimeter and half way down the cairn there are traces of the internal revetment of a drystone wall (ibid.). Surviving kerbstones indicate an original cairn diameter of 23m. The roofed chamber measures 2.85m from a sillstone at the front to the backstone. It widens from 0.6m at the front to 1.25m at the rear and increases in height from some 0.9m to c. 1.5m. Two further sillstones divide it into three compartments, the innermost slightly longer and also wider than the others. The innermost sillstone stands between two jamb-like stones set inside the chamber walls. It would seem that this feature is incorrectly surveyed on the published plan (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, Pl. 17) and interpreted as a cist. Passage tomb art has been discovered on the N jambstone and adjacent orthostat (Hensey and Robin 2012). Three large slabs roof the tomb. The published plan shows a recess to the right of the sillstone at the front of the tomb. It does seem that this is not an original feature but the result of partial collapse. Immediately forward of the front sill there are two opposed slabs, the bases of both exposed, and each apparently deliberately propped against the outer ends of the sides of the tomb. Their status is uncertain. During the 1911 investigation burnt human bone and some pottery fragments were found in the tomb and two short cists (SL040-097002-), apparently secondary, were uncovered on the E side of the cairn of the passage tomb. A cashel (SL040-082001-) and field wall (SL040-082002-) lie c. 80m to W. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 82)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Revised by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 24 September 2012

See linked documents with details from Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume V. County Sligo. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1989) together with plans and sections of the monument (surveyed 1996).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on top of the S side of a narrow ravine, with sheer sides of exposed limestone, in the Bricklieve Mountains. A level D-shaped area (dims. 29m E-W; 24m N-S) defined NE-SW by two stony banks with an intervening fosse and on the straight N side by the edge of a ravine. The inner bank (Wth 7.4m; int. H 1m; ext. H 0.85m) is evident E-SW as a sod-covered stony rise. Elsewhere the interior is defined by a straight scarp of limestone bedrock, probably the result of recent quarrying, that drops 2m down into the fosse. The fosse (Wth 2.4m) is flat-bottomed and relatively shallow E-SW but at W expands to a broad deep depression (Wth 6.8m; ext. D 1.35m) that slopes down toward the cliff-edge at N. The greater width of the fosse in this section may be due to the quarrying away of the inner bank but it also appears to kink outwards slightly to incorporate a natural undulation. Within the fosse on the W side, close to the cliff-edge and slightly recessed into sloping ground, is a ruined limekiln (SL040-080005-). The outer bank (Wth 1.9m; int. H 0.55m; ext. H 0.77m) is compact and relatively narrow. At E it is truncated by a small subrectangular annexe (12.5m E-W; 9.6m N-S at W, 7.6m at E) (SL040-080004-), defined by a low compact stone bank (Wth 2m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.6m), that projects from the E edge of the rath. The level interior of this annexe is slightly raised. Projecting from, but partially incorporated into, the inner face of the stone bank at SSE is a hut site (SL040-080002-). Two parallel E-W banks (Wth 1.9m; H 0.6m), separated by a slightly sunken gap (Wth 1.1m), extend eastwards into the interior from the bank at SW; the S bank is slightly longer (L 8.5m) than the N bank (L 6.85m). The function of these banks is unclear. In the NW quadrant of the interior is a small stony rise (4.8m E-W; 1.5m E-W; H 0.3m) abutted on the N side by another rise (1.4m N-S; 1.5m E-W; H 0.3m).

source_data.original_text:
On an upland ridge in the Bricklieve Mountains. On the rising ground immediately to N of a ravine, on the S edge of which Treanmacmurtagh cliff-edge fort (SL040-080001-) is located, there is a subrectangular walled enclosure (c.150m N-S; 100m E-W; indicated on the 1914 edition of the OS 6-inch map. The wall (H 1.7-2m) resembles an estate wall and is probably 19th-century in date. It is constructed of drystone limestone rubble topped with coping stones. According to local information, the enclosure incorporated a stone house, the S façade (17.3m E-W) of which was incorporated into the S wall of the enclosure. A blocked-up doorway and the stone sills of two windows can still be seen.
The area within the walled enclosure is sub-divided by sod-covered banks of earth and stone (Wth 1.3-2m; H 0.5m) into a series of irregular and subrectangular plots (e.g. 31m N-S; 55m E-W) with ephemeral evidence of ridge and furrow cultivation. A few partial and poorly defined smaller sub-divisions are at S, possibly representing the remains of structures. While use of these field plots must be contemporary with the walled enclosure and the house, the stone banks extend to N beyond the walled enclosure indicating that the patchwork of subrectangular fields pre-dated the construction of the walled enclosure.
To S of the ringfort, the plateau-like top or the ridge presents an open expanse of upland pasture. Traces of ridge and furrow cultivation on an E-W axis are visible. The N half of the ridge top is sub-divided on an E-W axis (i.e. transversely to the line of the ridge) by three widely spaced (30-60m apart), defunct walls, surviving as sod-covered banks of earth and stone (Wth 1.2m; H 0.3-0.4m). Appended to the S side of the middle of the three E-W field walls is a slightly sunken rectangular feature (10.8m E-W; 4.3m E-W; Irish Grid Reference 73285 11477) defined by a sod-covered stony bank (Wth 1.5m; H 0.4m), probably a house site. To W of this slight undulations appear to be the levelled remains of associated rectangular field-plots. At the W end of the southern of the three E-W field divisions, appended to a dog-leg in the wall is a low rectangular platform (8m E-W; 5-6m N-S; H 0.4m; Irish Grid Reference 73243; 11436).
The W-facing slope of the ridge is steep-sided and broken by rock outcrops. At NW the slope drops to a shallow terrace where the partial outline of two rectangular structures, probably house sites, defined by sod-covered walls (Wth 0.7-1m; H 0.3m) are visible. The N structure (c. 9m E-W; 3m N-S; Irish Grid Reference 73173 11508) is located 6m to N of the S structure (c. 7-8m E-W; 3m N-S; Irish Grid Reference 73174 11495). A fragmentary pattern of relict field walls in the vicinity appears to have defined associated subrectangular field-plots.
The surviving field walls in the vicinity of the cliff-edge fort (SL040-080001) appear to post-date the fort. The rectangular structures/house sites resemble house sites and associated field systems (SL040-079----; SL040-063----) found on parallel upland ridges to NW and W, probably dating to the 18/19th centuries.

Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC with revisions by Patrick F. O'Donovan and Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 20 June 2011

In upland pasture, on a broad shelf on a W-facing slope in the Bricklieve Mountains. An irregular area (35.4m N-S; 30m E-W) defined NNE-SSW by an arc of ruinous stone wall (Wth 2.2m; H 0.5m), on the almost straight W side, where there is a steep W-facing slope at the terrace edge, by traces of a stone wall and on the straight N side by a linear field wall (Wth 1.3m) that continues to E beyond the limit of the enclosure. Boulders protrude randomly from the curving wall, which is low and sod-covered. The interior ground level appears slightly higher in the W half than elsewhere. There is a small sod-covered heap of stones (2.6m E-W; 2.3m N-S; H 0.4m) to E of the centre. An E-W field boundary wall crosses the S edge of the interior. There is a gap (Wth 0.3m) at S, flanked by two upright slabs, set 0.3m back from the terminals of the enclosing wall. A larger gap (Wth 2.3m) at SSE is now infilled by the E-W field boundary wall. There is a cashel (SL040-085002-) on a higher terrace on the same slope c. 100m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In upland pasture, on a fairly level terrace at the base of a precipitous W-facing ridge slope in the Bricklieve Mountains. The W edge of the terrace has a naturally raised rocky lip that hides the cashel from view and an undulation in the ridge slope shelters the cashel at SE and S. A broadly oval area (19.6m NW-SE; 16.5m NE-SW) defined by a collapsed stone wall (Wth 1.8m; H 0.6m) of large limestone slabs and boulders, largely sod-covered. The wall is low and dilapidated. At SE where it backs on to rising ground it has a pronounced internal slump but barely rises above the external ground level. The interior is level but a scattering of sod-covered stones produces an uneven surface. There is an entrance feature at NE in the form of a passage (L 2m) flanked by large stones, that narrows from interior (Wth 2.2m) to the exterior (Wth 1m). A possible hut site (SL040-085003-) projects from the external face of the cashel wall at NE. There is a hut site (SL040-085004-) 2m to E; an enclosure (SL040-085005-) abuts the cashel wall at W. Another enclosure (SL040-085001-) is on a lower terrace on the same slope c. 100m to NW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rough grazing, on a low narrow terrace abutting the base of a precipitous NE-facing escarpment in the Bricklieve Mountains. A slightly raised circular area (25m NNW-SSE; 24m ENE-WSW) enclosed by a ruinous sod-covered stone wall (Wth 2m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.6m). At the base of the slope SSW-W the wall is very low externally (H 0.2m) but higher internally (H 1m). External stone-facing is evident, consisting of slabs and boulders bedded on their sides. The entrance (Wth 1.65m) is in the S arc. The interior is clear of overgrowth and mostly flat apart from a small section at W which slopes downwards; a small linear depression (L 1.5m; Wth 2m; D 0.5m), containing a number of stones, is evident at W. A narrow break in the cliff-face, at a point just above the cashel allows access to the plateau-like top of the ridge where there is a hut site (SL040-15904-). One of a line of cashels (SL040-156---, -157---; -161---) spaced at intervals along the long axis of the terrace. Another cashel (SL040-158001-) lies on an elevation c. 150m to NE. An enclosure (SL040-15902-) lies c. 26m to SSE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

Wth 6.3m) (SL040-174002-) lies immediately to NE, attached to the external face of the cashel wall and defined by a stone wall (Wth 1.7m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.36m). The ground drops steeply into an upland valley to N and E and a narrow ravine separates the spur from rising ground to W where a cashel (SL040-154----) is located c. 50m to WSW.

On top of a high limestone escarpment, immediately above a cashel (SL040-15901-) and 20m to NW of a break in the cliff-face which facilitates access from the base of the escarpment. source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, in the Bricklieve mountains, located at the S end of a limestone ridge. The ridge forms a flat topped, roughly oval island of elevated ground (c. 200m NW–SE; c. 90m NE–SW) rising several meters above an undulating valley of rough pasture and bog. The ridge is defined on its perimeter by a vertical escarpment of exposed limestone which is several meters high and relatively sheer at the E-S and W sides of the ridge, but in parts at SW and at N-NE forms an easily accessible terraced slope. The ridge is overlooked at N, E, and SW by much larger, higher ridges defined by steep, limestone cliffs. There are excellent views in all directions from the enclosure, in particular, to N along a narrow valley which provides a routeway to N between the ridges, and immediately to SE over a broad gap which provides a natural routeway out of the mountains to lowlying grassland at S.
Broadly oval area (25m NE–SW; c. 20m NW–SE), which is flat and not raised above surrounding ground level, defined on the perimeter at NW−N and E by a gapped line of moss-covered stones. At SE–W the perimeter coincides with the break of slope at the edge of the plateau: at SE this consists of a low drop to a small terrace, and at SW–W the perimeter coincides with a cliff edge. 
It is uncertain to what extent this is an enclosure; its outline is distinguished mainly as a relatively stone-free space, which contrasts with the proliferation of irregular, moss-covered hummocks of limestone bedrock breaking the surface throughout the rest of the plateau.
It may be associated with the more clearly defined, oval enclosure (SL040-246----) which lies immediately to NE, the interior of which is marked by a similar density of low stony hummocks to the rest of the plateau. It may represent an area cleared for cultivation rather than an enclosure per se, although no cultivation ridges are visible. It could, for instance, be a small field plot associated with two 18th/19th century rectangular houses, which are shown on the 1838 OS 6-inch map at the base of the W side of the ridge.

Attached images:
SL040-246001-_01.JPG: viewed from E, with stone bank of another enclosure (SL040-246----) visible in the foreground.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 28 May 2018

source_data.original_text:
In the SE quadrant of a cashel (SL040-162----), straddling a N−S stony scarp/internal division, which marks a drop in interior ground level in the E half of the cashel.
The visible remains consist of a roofless passage (L c. 7-8m E−W; Wth 0.8m at W end, c. 1.4m at E end; D 0.5m) of drystone construction. The W half of the passage (L 4-4.5m) is evident as a sunken pit faced with drystone walling; the wall face on the N side is relatively intact, but on the S side sections have slumped or collapsed. The extreme W end of the passage is poorly defined, with just a few stones protruding at surface level: it appears to be partly infilled with soil, or perhaps slopes up at this end. The E half of the passage projects to E of the N−S internal division/scarp which extends across the cashel interior. Here, the external face of the walls are built up with a stone bank to compensate for the drop in ground level, so that instead of being sunken, this end of the passage appears raised above interior ground level.
The souterrain is thickly engulfed in overgrowth, and difficult to examine in detail. The original depth of the passage is uncertain as the base is filled with woody debris.

Attached images:
SL040-162001-_01: Souterrain viewed from NW
SL040-162002-_02: Stone facing on N side of roofless passage

In the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. At the northern extremity of a N-S ridge. The cairn, part of the N end of which has slipped over the end of the ridge on which it sits, is of oval plan (18m N-S; 23m E-W; H 2.5m). Some piled stones on the top of the cairn may be a 19th-century OS trigononmetrical station. A small number of kerbstones are intermittently visible around the southern half of the perimeter. A substantially rubble-filled chamber is partly exposed in a hole in the eastern half of the cairn. This consists of two opposed orthostats, 0.7m apart, aligned E-W, which support a roofstone (min. L 2m; Wth 0.8m; T 0.25m). The nature of this chamber is uncertain but it could be the remains of a passage tomb. A short cist (SL040-016002-) was uncovered just inside the W edge of the cairn (Rynne 1969). (Ó Nualláin 1989, 84)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Inside the W edge of the cairn of a possible passage tomb (SL040-016001-). Discovered in 1966 and investigated by E. Rynne (1969, 145-50). Described as an irregular but roughly quadrangular cist (0.8m N-S; 0.5m E-W) with sides composed of single slabs set on edge, apart from SW and SE corners which were closed by two upright stones and by surrounding cairn material respectively. The floor was limestone bedrock. The cist was covered by a single capstone (L 1.15m; Wth 0.52m; T 0.18m) supported on the N and S and possibly the E side by horizontally-laid slabs on top of the sidestones. Small limestone fragments and some unburnt human bones partially filled the cist. The primary burial was found to be the cremated remains of an adult. Two small decorated potsherds were found amongst the cremated bones. In addition, the crouched skeleton of a 10 to 12 year old child with a portion of a small decorated pottery vessel (H 8.8cm; diam. 12.5cm at rim and 4.8cm at base) were found. The investigator suggests that the cist is 'a secondary feature inserted into a pre-existing cairn' (Rynne 1969, 149). A piece of bone from the skeleton has been radiocarbon dated to 3550+-40 BP (GrN-12274) (Ó Ríordáin and Waddell 1993, 37). (Waddell 1990, 133; Ó Ríordáin and Waddell 1993, 131)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On a narrow shelf, on the E-facing slope of a ridge overlooking a narrow upland valley in the Bricklieve Mountains. Remains comprise a cluster of at least six small rectangular houses (SL040-079002-; SL040-079004-; SL040-079005-; SL040-079006-; SL040-218----), a possible structure (SL040-079004-), associated with a lime kiln (SL040-079008-) and a rectilinear pattern of fields in which traces of ridge and furrow cultivation are visible. The houses are visible as low sod-covered wall footings and are almost identical in size (11m x 4.2m) and plan, typically sub-divided into two or more, usually three, rooms. The core of the settlement consists of a row of three houses. The houses are aligned E-W and arranged in a N-S row, dictated by the contours of the terrace. The most northerly of the three is the largest (14.2m E-W; 4.2m N-S) in the settlement and is separated from the middle house by a gap of 10m. A small rectangular enclosure or garden-plot (17m N-S; 14m E-W) (this is indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map) fills most of the intervening space (21m N-S) between the middle house and its neighbour to S. At the NW corner of the rectangular plot is a small sunken subrectangular feature (6m N-S; 2m E-W), possibly the remains of a small shed or lean-to (SL040-079004-). A field-wall extends upslope to W from the NW end of the southern house. Abutting the S side of the wall, 21m W of the house, slightly recessed into the slope, is a ruined limekiln (SL040-079008-). It appears as a small circular area (1.6m N-S; 1.55m E-W) enclosed by a ruined stone wall (Wth 1m; H 0.5m) with an opening (Wth 0.6m) at SE. Another house (SL040-215----) is located 25m to NW of the limekiln, in a natural dip at the top of the ridge. A gap of 9.5m separates the southern house of the cluster of three houses from a rectangular field (27m N-S; 10-2m E-W) subdivided into two roughly equal plots. From here the terrace swings to SW curving around the 'nose' of the ridge. A sub-rectangular depression may indicate the location of  another possible house (SL040-079006-) and beyond this to the SW are the foundations of another house (SL040-79007-) with an associated garden plot (14m NE-SW; 11m NW-SE). Although this is located c. 50m SW of the main cluster (SL040-079002-, Sl0040-079003, SL040-079004-) it is clearly part of the same settlement. To the N of the main cluster of houses, the terrace continues for c. 150m to N ending at a rising slope. It expands in width and has been subdivided into a row of large square fields (c. 30-40m N-S; c. 30-40m E-W) with evidence of cultivation ridges. The settlement is not marked on the 1st ed. OS 6-inch map (surveyed 1837) and appears to have been abandoned by then. While it is impossible to date this settlement a date in the 18th century would not be inconsistent for such remains.

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 17 January 2012

Not included in the SMR (1989) but listed in the RMP (1995) and classified 'Cashel'. Not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch map. In upland pasture, at the W edge of a terrace in the Bricklieve Mountains. A D-shaped area (19m N-S; 15m E-W) defined NNE-S by a ruined sod-covered stone wall (T 2m; H 0.4m) and on the straight W side by a limestone scarp marking a break of slope. The wall continues beyond the D-shaped area down the slope to W. The interior is level and crossed on its W edge by a field boundary wall. It is linked to a rectangular enclosure (SL040-217----) c. 8m to NE by two parallel ruined walls, 1.2m apart. This is probably not a cashel but may be a field, possibly part of a field system associated with an 18th/19th century deserted settlement (SL040-079---) to the NE. Two fields of ridge and furrow cultivation ridges were noted to NW.

A small portion of the enclosure has been destroyed at W due to the construction of a large concrete water tank and a farm building. A break (Wth 1.9m) in the bank at E may mark the original entrance. According to local information, 'passages' which emanated from this enclosure were filled with stones in the 1950s and 1960s.

source_data.original_text:
On a ledge above a scarp, adjacent to the E bank of the Unshin River. There are no visible remains of this short cist; a septic tank is now built on the site. It was discovered in 1970 during construction work (NMI). It consisted of a rectangular cist grave (L 0.71m; min. Wth 0.25m; max. Wth 0.33m; D 0.43m) containing the cremated bones of one human adult and the teeth of a child. Each of the four sides of the cist was formed by a thin limestone slab and the bottom by two large flat stones. The cist was covered by a single capstone and the space between the capstone and the sides was packed with small stones. Small stones also covered the capstone. The cremated remains were heaped in the centre of the floor with a thin spread to all sides. (Raftery 1973, 186; Waddell 1990, 131)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

On the map it is indicated as a feature of oval outline (c. 27m x 15m) with its long axis aligned NE-SW. Wood-Martin (1887-8, 261-2; 1888, 199-200) refers to its destruction but apparently had no information as to its nature. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 97, no. 15)

source_data.original_text:
In the shallow waters of Ballygawley Lough, c. 100m from the SE shoreline. The land surrounding the lake is part of a forest known as Union Wood. A roughly circular high-cairn crannog (27m N-S; 30.3m E-W; H 3m above the sandy muddy lake-bed) on the S half of which is a mid-cairn (6m N-S; 9m E-W). The mid-cairn consists of moderately to well-packed stones with a number of flagstones and rises c. 0.75m above a surrounding plateau. The S edge of the crannog drops distinctly down to the water. A plateau (max. Wth 7m) of loosely packed subangular to rounded stones (diam. 0.2-0.4m), with smaller blackened angular stones in between, surrounds the mid-cairn W-E. The plateau is surrounded by a stone-built berm (Wth 4-8m). At W the plateau is connected to the berm via a stone-built ramp (L 12m N-S; Wth 2.5m). The ramp is mainly stone rubble, but a stone wall is evident along its W edge. The edges of the crannog are stone and are distinct in material and they seem to feather out from the berm. There is an overspill of stones for c. 2m into the water around the perimeter of the crannog. A number of horizontal timbers are visible at NNE and animal bones were also found in the berm in the same area. Wood-Martin (1886, 246-8) mentioned traces of an encircling palisade, mortised beams as well as animal bones here. Apart from the horizontal timbers there are no visible remains of the palisade or mortised beams. This crannog is named 'Sallow Island' on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. A possible crannog (SL020-269----) is c. 60m to S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Not included in the SMR (1989) but listed in the RMP (1995) and classified 'Mill'. On the E bank of the Owenmore river, on the N side of Collooney. Most of the mill complex is demolished though the remains of wheel-pits and arched headraces and tailraces are evident. Some ancillary late 19th-century mill buildings remain, the main blocks are around and attached to a church and graveyard (SL020-203001- and SL020-203002-) on the E side of the cleared yard. The ruins of late 18th-century buildings on the river front and to one side of the lumber yard were noted during a previous inspection in 1992 (SMR (1989) file). A substantial bleach mill complex still stands on the opposite bank of the river (see SL020-272----). According to local information, both mills were owned by the Sims family. Valuation Office Mill Books recorded Alex Sims as the miller of a flour mill in Collooney, powered by a waterwheel (diam. 36ft [10.97m]; breath 8ft [2.43m]), which turned six pairs of stones (Hogg 1998, 108). According to Wood-Martin (1882, 240), Collooney mills 'occupy the site of a much older concern'. This mill is probably post-1700 AD in date.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Date of upload: 12 December 2011

source_data.original_text:
In level pasture, c. 60m SE of the confluence of the Ballysadare and Arrow or Unshin Rivers. The only visible remains are a short length of sod-covered foundation (L c. 4m; Wth c. 1.5m; H c. 0.6m) and two sod-covered mounds of rubble. According to O'Rorke (1878, 52-4), this is the remains of a MacDonagh castle erected in 1408, possibly on the site of a castle erected in 1124 by 'the Connaughtmen' to guard Connacht against attack from Ulster (McGarry 1980, 5). O'Rorke (1878, 52-4) states that much of the castle was 'pulled down and carted away to build Lord Bellamont's mansion in Collooney' (SL020-240----). Sufficient walls, however, remained to be converted into a ball-alley in the 19th century though these were 'thrown down and used as material' for a nearby bridge over the Arrow or Unshin River, a short distance to the N (ibid.).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
A bridge is indicated on the Down Survey (1655-6) barony map on or close to the location of the present bridge over the Owenmore River at the N edge of Collooney. No visible remains of this bridge are now evident. The present road bridge (on a N-S axis; Wth 3.2m) is of eight semicircular arches (span c. 4.4m) with roughly shaped voussoirs. Tall thin piers (Wth c. 1.35m) with tall pointed cutwaters rise to the base of a modern parapet. The core of the bridge is of random rubble limestone. The bridge is extended 3.55m on the downstream (E) side and the extension has similarly shaped stone arches with dressed voussoirs and pointed cutwaters. The arches are heavily underpinned with a thick layer of concrete. The bridge has been extended further in recent times. According to O'Rorke ([1889], vol. 2, 556), Collooney bridge dates to about 1400 but it is not the structure that now exists in this place.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

raw_items.raw_text: finished by one of his sons in 1657
Coote was resident in Collooney Castle in 1659

source_data.original_text:
On the E side of Collooney village, in the NW corner of a walled garden known as 'the castle gardens'. According to local tradition, the S (L 9m; H 3m) and E (L 7.3m; H 3m) walls of a complex containing a garage and outbuildings, are the remains of Richard Coote's house known as Collooney Castle (O'Rorke 1878, 54; M. A. Timoney 1999). The walls are of random-rubble limestone construction, partially covered by a plaster render. The E wall contains one blocked-up rectangular window ope (Wth 1.1m) and the S wall has two similar blocked-up opes. The structure contains no datable architectural features. 
The house was built for Richard Coote by the architect Daniel Thomas and was finished by one of his sons in 1657 (Loeber 1981, 107). Coote was resident in Collooney Castle in 1659 and derived his title Baron Coote of Collooney from the place (ibid.); he was later created Earl of Bellamont. O'Rorke (1878, 52-4) states that much of the castle at Cloonmacduff (SL020-207----) was 'pulled down and carted away to build Lord Bellamont's mansion in Collooney'. It was listed as containing 'ten hearths' in 1662, unusually large for a settler's house (O'Dowd 1991, 141). According to Wood-Martin (1889, 106), 'the fortified house of Lord Bellamount' was located 'close to the new Roman Catholic Church'; it is in fact to the E of the church. Recent archaeological test trenching at the site 'did not reveal any soils, features or finds of archaeological significance' (Conway 2000, 274).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

This tower is probably post-1700 AD in date

source_data.original_text:
Not included in the SMR (1989) but listed in the RMP (1995) and classified 'Building Possible'. In pasture, on a rise on the S bank of the Arrow or Unshin River and on the N side of a disused avenue on the Markree estate. The ruins of a square 2-storey tower (H c. 3.5m; 6.45m N-S; 6.9m E-W) which is built of random rubble limestone bonded with lime mortar. The tower is built on a plinth (projects internally 0.35m) which is in turn built on an earlier plinth (projects externally 0.16m) which is only evident on the E side. There are the remains of window opes on the ground and first floors of the W wall and a door ope in the S wall with a window overhead. A ha-ha curves around the N side. An ornate road bridge is visible to W. The site of a castle (SL020-207-—) lies 220m to W, immediately S of ornate bridge. This tower is probably post-1700 AD in date.

raw_items.raw_text: The nature of the burials and their E-W orientation suggest that the burial ground is Christian in date

source_data.original_text:
Located c. 1.1km NW of Collooney. Human skeletal remains were uncovered by machinery during bridge construction on the Ballysadare-Collooney by-pass road in 1995. Only a small area (14m x 14m) remained undisturbed and was subsequently excavated (Opie 1996, 77). A total of 37 extended inhumations were uncovered during the excavation. The burials were all in a supine position and aligned roughly E-W with the head to the W, except for one individual, possibly a priest, whose head was to the E. Grave-cuts and divides were noted in some burials and one skeleton had an arrangement of three stones under its skull. A bronze ring (int. diam. 12.5mm), which may have been part of a belt, was found on the left radius/ulna of one burial and an iron ribbon torque was found around the neck of another. Skeletal analysis of four of the burials revealed that there were three middle-aged females and one adult male. The nature of the burials and their E-W orientation suggest that the burial ground is Christian in date (Opie 1995). A second burial ground (SL020-266001-) lies c. 15m to W. (Opie 1995; 1996, 77)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In the shallow waters of Ballygawley Lough, c. 70m from the shore and at the edge of the reeds c. 60m S of another crannog (SL020-169----). The lake is at the foot of Slieve Dargan and the surrounding land is forested and views are limited. A circular possible low-cairn crannog (14m N-S; 13m E-W; H 0.58m above the lake-bed of organic mud) consisting of loosely packed subangular stones and probably incorporating a natural rise in the lake-bed. A grass-covered circular area (6m N-S; 6m E-W) in the centre has a row of stones (7m E-W) on its N edge. The edge of the site consists of loosely packed stones and it slopes gently down towards the water; a lot of stone has spilled over the edges. Outside the NW edge are a number of boulders (dims. 1.7m x 1m; 2.2m x 1.4m).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Sited alongside a trackway in extensive woodland in a gap in the Ox Mountains 0.7km NW of Ballygawley Lough. There are a number of mature deciduous trees on the site and the stumps of others. To N and W the ground drops quite sharply to a stream that flows NW-SE. Trees inhibit the outlook from the site but Maeve's cairn on Knocknarea is visible to the NNW. A ring of boulders (19.5m N-S, 17.5m E-W) encompasses a slight platform. There are a number of gaps in the ring of boulders but the indications are that they were contiguously placed. Among the numerous gaps are two that may be original features, one at the SE (Wth 1.3m) and another at the NW (Wth 1.1m). A number of prostrate boulders outside the perimeter may be displaced. Some of the boulders encircling the platform are quite sizeable (the largest is 0.95m x 0.85m x 1.15m high) but others are noticeably smaller. The tops of at least three stones are visible about 3m inside the perimeter at the W. The status of these is quite unclear but their presence suggests that there may have been an inner ring of stones. Somewhat to the W of the centre of the enclosed area four stones lie prostrate. The larger two are about 1.6m and 1.4m in maximum dimensions. These may represent some form of internal feature. The nature of the site is somewhat uncertain but it may be a Carrowmore-type passage tomb. It is indicated as a small oval field on the 1913 OS 6-inch map. Some 100m to the W there is another possible passage tomb (SL020-275----).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Within a possible ecclesiastical enclosure (SL020-21002-). O'Rorke (1878, 98) states that the interior of the enclosure was used as a burial ground up to the end of the 18th century and that 'a row of brick coffins or sarcophagi, of uniform size, such as are often found in the cemeteries of the larger monasteries, was discovered some years since by labourers who were making drains in the place'. No visible traces of the graveyard, or the possible church (SL020-210001-) associated with it, are evident.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Following a storm in January 2015, a large beech tree fell at the location marked on the 1913 OS 6-inch map as 'Kilederdaowen', believed to be the site of a graveyard (SL020-210003-) and a possible ecclesiastical enclosure (SL020-210002-). Part of a human skeleton was brought up encased in the soil adhering to the mass of roots. A rescue excavation (Licence no. 15E0242) was carried out on 14th-16th May 2015 by Dr. Marion Dowd (IT Sligo) on behalf of the National Monuments Service. Bones were retrieved from the exposed root system and from the base of the hole created by the felled tree. The bones derived from one adult individual, a male aged between 17-20 years. The body was in an extended supine position, orientated east-west, with legs to the east and head to the west. Hand bones were recovered in the pelvic region indicating that the hands were originally either by the side or were crossed on the pelvis. Cut marks on the hand bones and ribs revealed that prior to his death the young man suffered violent injuries inflicted by a sharp bladed implement, possibly a knife or sword. Radiocarbon analysis of a bone sample indicates that he died sometime between the early 11th and early 13th century (calibrated 1028-1206 AD - 2 sigma). No trace of a grave cut was apparent and no artefacts were recovered. There were no indications of other burials. (Unpublished final excavation report submitted to NMS by Dr. Marion Dowd, October 2015; Dowd and Lynch 2016).

Date of revised upload: 3 February 2016

source_data.original_text:
In the centre of a former lumber yard surrounded by recent walls and structures; at the W end of a small graveyard, between two 19th-century warehouses. A ruined rectangular structure (16m E-W; 6m N-S) built of uncoursed limestone blocks. The N and S walls are very poorly preserved and the SW corner is missing. A window embrasure, in the centre of the E wall, survives as a rough opening (Wth c. 1.5m); a drawing by Wakeman (O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 344) shows it with a double-ogee light missing its mullion. This window indicates a 15th/16th-century date for the church, which was, according to tradition, built by the O'Haras (O'Rorke 1878, 102-4). It was converted to Protestant use 'soon after the Reformation' but finally abandoned early in the 18th century (ibid.). There are a number of 18th- and 19th-century grave-memorials in the interior, some of which are listed by O'Rorke (1878, 102-4). There is no known historical record of a monastic foundation here (see Gwynn and Hadcock 1970).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
A rectangular graveyard (23m E-W; 12m N-S), no longer used and much covered by overgrowth. The ruin of a late medieval church (SL020-203001-), situated at its W end, takes up most of the space between two warehouses. The interior of the church and graveyard have thirteen memorials 'for some of the leading families of Tirerrill' (O'Rorke 1878, 103). The tomb dated 1707, which O'Rorke (ibid.) noted as the oldest, is no longer evident (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney). An archaeological assessment, carried out in the early 1990s, revealed 'a massive degree of ground disturbance' in the area, but three skeletons and a possible fosse were discovered in small trenches to the SE and NE of the graveyard respectively (Simpson 1994). These suggest a possible early medieval date for the site though there is no documentary evidence for such a foundation (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970). Archaeological monitoring of the site in 2000, prior to development, confirmed that human remains were buried outside the graveyard wall to the E (Halpin 2001, 300-301). According to local information, other human remains were uncovered during the course of the site's development (ibid.). The undisturbed ground (dims. 8m x 5m) to the E did not reveal any further human remains while further E the ground was disturbed and it appears likely that the construction of the basement of Abbey House may account for the ditch or boundary uncovered in the 1994 assessment (ibid., 301).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In low-lying pasture, at the W foot of a low steep-sided ridge. According to O'Rorke (1878, 97), 'the great solitary stone near the northern end of the avenue, through Cloonmucduff, marks the spot near which it [the church] stood'. The stone mentioned by O'Rorke is named 'Cromlech' on the 1913 OS 6-inch map and consists of a boulder resting on two smaller stones; it is a natural feature according to Ó Nualláin (1989, 97, no. 17). No feature consistent with a church is evident in the vicinity of the stone. A possible ecclesiastical enclosure (SL020-210002-) and graveyard (SL020-21003-) are associated with this site.

source_data.original_text:
In a shallow valley with a small stream near the E end of Ballysadare Bay.
There are no visible remains of a 17th-century bridge referred to on a stone (SL014-284009-) with a Latin inscription (now in Sligo County Museum) attributing the building of the bridge to Maria, wife of the soldier Roger Jones in the year 1628 (Sligo Field Club files).
The 17th-century bridge may have replaced an earlier bridge. The placename Belladrihid (Béal an Droichid, ‘approach of (to) the bridge’) is recorded in the Annals of Loch Cé under the year 1495: LC1495.2 ‘Mac Donnchadha of Tir-Oilella, i.e. Tadhg, the son of Brian, son of Conchobhar, was killed by O'Domhnaill, i.e. Aedh Ruadh, son of Niall Garbh, at Bel-an-droichit.’ (pers. comm. Dr Conchubhar Ó Crualaoich, An Brainse Logainmneacha /The Placenames Branch, 2021).
The present bridge is a disused causeway bridge of 19th-century appearance between a railway line and the modern N4 road. It has two semicircular arches, roughly 12m apart, one partially replaced with concrete and the other blocked up leaving only a small lintelled channel.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Revised upload: 21 September 2021

source_data.original_text:
Prominently sited on top of a hill in undulating pasture with excellent views in all directions. A substantially raised circular area (31.2m N-S; 33.5m E-W) defined by two earthen banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank (Wth 5-6m; int. 0.6m; ext. H 2m), evident E-N, is high externally with a slight internal lip. The interior is defined by a scarp elsewhere. The shallow intervening fosse (Wth 3m) is evident all round, marked by long grass. The outer bank can only be traced as a slight rise SW-NW. A gently ramped causeway (Wth 4.5m) across the fosse at ENE, corresponding with a slumped section of the bank, is the most likely the location of the entrance. The interior is slightly higher at the centre with a slight slope down to NE and E. Within it are three depressions or pits (SL026-027002-; SL026-027003-; SL026-027004-), all obscured by long grass, probably the three 'caves' recorded by O'Rorke ([1889], vol. 2, 458) in 'Rathrippon, near Collooney'.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On top of a gravel ridge, c. 1.1km NW of Collooney. A roughly oval burial mound was uncovered by machinery prior to the development of the Ballysadare-Collooney by-pass road. Half of the mound was excavated in 1996 (Opie 1997, 96-7) while the remainder is undisturbed. The remains of at least 83 burials and 28 bone scatters were uncovered during the excavation. The burials were all inhumations in a supine position, aligned roughly E-W with the head to the W, except for one individual, possibly a priest, whose head was to the E. Most of the graves were shallow and cut into the gravel; two were stone-lined and lintelled. Some burials were also found to the S of the mound. A bullaun stone (SL020-26602-) was found in the field in which the unexcavated half of the burial ground is located. The nature of the burials and their E-W orientation suggest that the burial ground is Christian in date (ibid.). A second burial ground (SL020-266----) lies c. 15m to E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008
